observations.text: In 2Thess.2.13 'we ought always to give thanks to God for you' diverges from the meal-blessing sense dominant in the Gospels/Acts/1Cor occurrences of this cluster -- here thanksgiving is a sustained, obligatory disposition ('ought always') directed at other believers' salvation-status (election, sanctification, belief) rather than a single ritual act over food. The impact is to broaden eucharisteo from a punctual liturgical gesture to an ongoing pastoral duty of gratitude for others' spiritual condition.

In 2Thess.2.13, thanksgiving (G2168) co-occurs with M14 (brothers), M51 (beloved), M64 (chose), M16 (firstfruits), M79 (saved), M61 (sanctification), M13 (belief/truth, twice). Thanksgiving is the responsive frame surrounding this entire chain: it is offered specifically because of God's prior acts of choosing, sanctifying, and saving -- thanksgiving here functions as the grateful acknowledgment of the whole soteriological sequence rather than being caused by any single other M-code term alone.

In 2Thess.2.13, arche appears in the specialized sense 'firstfruits' rather than its more common gloss 'beginning/rule/authority' -- a divergence that carries covenantal-agricultural nuance (a consecrated, representative first portion) distinct from the term's dominant temporal or governmental senses elsewhere in the NT.
In 2Thess.2.13 'brothers' sits within the base NT sense of fellow believers; no notable divergence.
In 2Thess.2.13 'beloved by the Lord' sits within the base NT sense of God's settled love for believers; no notable divergence.
In 2Thess.2.13 'chose' sits within the base sense of God's electing choice; no notable divergence.
In 2Thess.2.13 'saved' sits within the base theological sense of eschatological salvation; no notable divergence.

In 2Thess.2.13 the sense shifts from a single concrete act (over food) to an ongoing obligation ('ought always to give thanks'), infinitive form, directed not at provision of a meal but at God's whole saving work (chosen, sanctified, saved) -- the nuance here is thanksgiving as continuous doxological duty rather than a discrete ritual moment, contrasting with the meal-occurrences.

Adding to the prior finding for 2Thess.2.13: from thanksgiving's own vantage, it functions specifically as an obligatory (opheilomen, 'we ought') response, distinguishing it from the other M-codes present (chosen M64, sanctification M61, belief/truth M13) which describe what God has done TO the believers, while thanksgiving alone names the believers' required responsive posture toward that whole complex.
In 2Thess.2.13 Paul and companions ('we', party) initiate the thanksgiving operation, directed toward God (party), on behalf of the Thessalonian brothers (party) for God's saving work toward them.

The large majority of G2168's occurrences (Rom.1.8; 1Cor.1.4; Eph.5.20; Col.1.3; 1Thess.5.18; Rev.11.17; 2Thess.2.13; Rom.16.4; 1Thess.2.13; 2Thess.1.3; 1Cor.1.14; 1Cor.14.18; Phil.1.3; 1Thess.1.2; Phlm.1.4; 1Cor.10.30; Col.1.12; 2Cor.1.11; Eph.1.16) share one core sense across the strong's own full occurrence list: an epistolary/liturgical, habitual first- or plural-person verb of thanking God, usually 'always'/'constantly' and grounded in some grace, faith, or benefit already received in the addressees or the speaker. This is the dominant register of the strong internally and forms the baseline against which the meal-blessing and single exceptional uses (below) stand out.

Thanksgiving is produced by prior reception of grace (M50, 1Cor.1.4), by observing another's faith or love (M13/M51, Rom.1.8, 2Thess.1.3), and by God's qualifying/electing/saving action (M64/M61/M79, Col.1.12, 2Thess.2.13) -- it is consistently downstream of these other characteristics/divine acts.

Deut.12.5 'seek the place' draws on the 'resort to, frequent' sense (1a1) combined with devotional pursuit of the divinely chosen worship-site; a standard extension within the base gloss, no notable divergence.

In Deut.12.5, M15 (choose, of God choosing the place) is present but functions as God's own prior action, not something darash (Israel's seeking) directly modifies; the two characteristics operate on different agents (God chooses; the people seek) within the same verse without direct interaction.

In 1 Sam 24.2 and 26.2, 'seek' carries a hostile-pursuit nuance (seeking to kill/capture David) rather than the neutral/benign 'seek to find' sense; this militarised sense diverges from the more affectionate or petitionary uses elsewhere (e.g. Song 3.1, Exod 10.11), showing the verb's flexibility to carry either amicable or adversarial intent depending on context.
In Isa 40.20 'seeks out' functions within the base gloss of seeking-to-secure (a craftsman), a straightforward practical-search sense with no notable added nuance.
Saul (party) initiates the seek-operation, directed toward David and his men (party), moving into the wilderness terrain to locate them -- a hostile pursuit operation.

M64 (chosen, of the men) is present but concerns selection/election rather than seeking; seeking here targets a person (David) not a quality, so no direct conceptual overlap with the co-present M-code.
Saul (party) initiates the seek-operation, directed toward David (party), in the wilderness of Ziph -- again a hostile-pursuit direction of the operation.
M64 (chosen) is present but pertains to the selection of Saul's soldiers, not conceptually tied to the seeking-of-David action itself.
The impoverished man (implied party, 'he') initiates the seeking-operation, directed toward a skillful craftsman (party) to make an idol -- seeking here serves an idolatrous construction project.

M64 (chooses, wood-selection), M16 (skillful), M23/M55 (setting up an idol) are present but describe separate stages of idol-making; seeking here specifically targets the craftsman, distinct from those other characteristics' own referents.
Terror instead of peace, and fears brought upon.

observations.text: "For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain … I am hard pressed between the two. My desire is to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better. But to remain in the flesh is more necessary on your account."
observations.meaning: Meaning: Paul names death as departing to be with Christ, "far better". He holds it against staying, which is better for others. Implies: the weighing is itself an inner act ("hard pressed", "my desire"). Death is weighed as gain because of who it leads to.

observations.text: A person chooses a thing or place for oneself by sight or use: "the sons of God saw that the daughters of man were attractive. And they took as their wives any they chose" (Gen 6:2); "Lot chose for himself all the Jordan Valley" (Gen 13:11), and they separated; David chose five smooth stones (1Sa 17:40); the bulls of the contest on Carmel are chosen (1Ki 18:23, 25).
observations.meaning: Choosing can follow what the eye finds attractive or useful, and the choice can separate.

observations.text: People select men for battle, leadership or a task, and the word marks fitness: "Moses chose able men out of all Israel and made them heads over the people" (Exo 18:25); "700 chosen men who were left-handed; every one could sling a stone at a hair and not miss" (Judg 20:16); "300,000 choice men, fit for war, able to handle spear and shield" (2Ch 25:5). The same word names the men "chosen from the assembly, well-known men" who rose up against Moses (Num 16:2).
observations.meaning: Here choosing is a judgement of ability: a leader weighs others and takes the fit for a task; being chosen does not secure faithfulness.

observations.text: God chooses a person for a task or office: priests and Levites, the king, David, Solomon, the servant, witnesses. Choosing goes with bringing near: "The one whom he chooses he will bring near to him" (Num 16:5); "Blessed is the one you choose and bring near" (Psa 65:4). The choice is shown, not argued: "the staff of the man whom I choose shall sprout" (Num 17:5). It is followed by a charge: "the Lord has chosen you to build a house for the sanctuary; be strong and do it" (1Ch 28:10). In the servant it is joined to God's soul and Spirit: "my chosen, in whom my soul delights; I have put my Spirit upon him" (Isa 42:1; Mat 12:18).
observations.meaning: God's choosing of a person brings that person near and lays a task on them; the chosen still has to act.

observations.text: God chooses a people, and the verses give love as the ground and deny number: "It was not because you were more in number than any other people that the Lord set his love on you and chose you" (Deu 7:7); "the Lord set his heart in love on your fathers and chose their offspring" (Deu 10:15). The choosing makes them "a people for his treasured possession" (Deu 7:6) and "his chosen ones" (Psa 105:6). It is joined to not casting off, "I have chosen you and not cast you off" (Isa 41:9), and to a purpose: "that you may know and believe me" (Isa 43:10).
observations.meaning: In God the choosing follows the heart set in love, not a quality found in the chosen; it names the chosen, keeps them, and aims at their knowing him.

observations.text: God chooses a place "to make his name dwell there" (Deu 12:11), and the choosing carries his own presence: "My eyes and my heart will be there for all time" (2Ch 7:16). The people's offerings, eating, rejoicing, judgement, reading of the law and prayer are all directed to the place he chooses. The choice can be cast off, "I will cast off this city that I have chosen" (2Ki 23:27), and made again: "the Lord will again comfort Zion and again choose Jerusalem" (Zec 1:17).
observations.meaning: God's choosing fixes where he sets his name and his heart; the people's acts, and their repentance with all their heart and soul (1Ki 8:48; 2Ch 6:38), turn toward what he has chosen.

observations.text: A person chooses the Lord, his ways and the good: "choose this day whom you will serve" (Jos 24:15), and the choice is witnessed: "You are witnesses against yourselves that you have chosen the Lord" (Jos 24:22); "I have chosen the way of faithfulness; I set your rules before me" (Psa 119:30); "who choose the things that please me and hold fast my covenant" (Isa 56:4). Choosing needs knowing and instruction: "when he knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good" (Isa 7:15); "Him will he instruct in the way that he should choose" (Psa 25:12). It can be done together: "Let us choose what is right; let us know among ourselves what is good" (Job 34:4). Preference is stated: "I would rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God" (Psa 84:10); "choosing rather to be mistreated with the people of God than to enjoy the fleeting pleasures of sin" (Heb 11:25).
observations.meaning: The person's choosing of the good rests on knowing and is taught; it binds the chooser as a witness and is kept by holding fast.

observations.text: People choose a king or a side: "your king, whom you have chosen for yourselves, but the Lord will not answer you in that day" (1Sa 8:18); "behold the king whom you have chosen, for whom you have asked; behold, the Lord has set a king over you" (1Sa 12:13). Loyalty follows the choice: "his I will be, and with him I will remain" (2Sa 16:18).
observations.meaning: The people's choosing and the Lord's setting are stated together; a choice made binds loyalty, and a choice made for oneself can meet no answer from the Lord.

observations.text: God sets a choice before a person: "Three things I offer you. Choose one of them, that I may do it to you" (2Sa 24:12; 1Ch 21:10).
observations.meaning: God puts the choosing into the person's hands, and acts on what they choose.

observations.text: Inner-being words stand beside choosing: God's heart in what he chooses, "My eyes and my heart will be there for all time" (2Ch 7:16); his soul in his chosen servant, "my chosen, in whom my soul delights" (Isa 42:1; Mat 12:18); the people's heart and soul turned toward the chosen city in repentance (1Ki 8:48; 2Ch 6:38); the soul's delight in chosen ways (Isa 66:3); the soul choosing death (Job 7:15); the heart given a worth (Pro 10:20); the soul's appetite, "whenever you desire" (Deu 12:21; Deu 18:6); the self humbled in a fast God does not choose (Isa 58:5); "one deeply despised" whom the Lord has chosen (Isa 49:7).
observations.meaning: Choosing is not apart from the inner being: in God it is joined to his heart and soul, in people to the heart, the soul's delight and its appetite.

observations.text: In his suffering Job would choose death over life: "I would choose strangling and death rather than my bones" (Job 7:15).
observations.meaning: Under suffering the soul can prefer death; the choosing follows the weight of what is borne.

observations.text: The word stands for a person's own decision, desire or accord: "whatever my lord the king decides" (2Sa 15:15); "all that you desire of me I will do for you" (2Sa 19:38); "For you must choose, and not I" (Job 34:33); "choosing my words with him" (Job 9:14); "I chose their way and sat as chief" (Job 29:25). The escaped slave dwells "in the place that he shall choose within one of your towns, wherever it suits him" (Deu 23:16). With G0830 the Macedonians gave "beyond their means, of their own accord" (2Cor 8:3), and Titus went "of his own accord" (2Cor 8:17).
observations.meaning: Choosing is the person's own, placed on them and not on another; it can be given freely, beyond means, from one's own earnestness.

observations.text: "Choice" as worth preferred over another: "To get understanding is to be chosen rather than silver" (Pro 16:16); "A good name is to be chosen rather than great riches" (Pro 22:1); "The tongue of the righteous is choice silver; the heart of the wicked is of little worth" (Pro 10:20); also Pro 8:10, 8:19 and Song 5:15.
observations.meaning: Choosing weighs worth: wisdom, understanding and a good name are set above wealth, and the heart is given a worth.

observations.text: "Behold, I have refined you, but not as silver; I have tried you in the furnace of affliction" (Isa 48:10): the ESV renders the word here as testing, the only such verse in the files' pull.
observations.meaning: God's choosing can come through affliction that refines.

observations.text: God chooses what he wants: "Is not this the fast that I choose: to loose the bonds of wickedness" (Isa 58:6), set against a fast of bowing the head (Isa 58:5); "To do righteousness and justice is more acceptable to the Lord than sacrifice" (Pro 21:3); "I will appoint over her whomever I choose. For who is like me?" (Jer 49:19; Jer 50:44).
observations.meaning: God's choosing states what pleases him: justice and freeing the oppressed over outward humbling; his choice is sovereign.

observations.text: A person chooses against God: other gods, "the gods whom you have chosen; let them save you" (Judg 10:14); their own ways, "These have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations" (Isa 66:3); what God does not delight in (Isa 65:12). The verses name what drives or follows such choosing: "your iniquity teaches your mouth, and you choose the tongue of the crafty" (Job 15:5); "Do not envy a man of violence and do not choose any of his ways" (Pro 3:31); "this you have chosen rather than affliction" (Job 36:21). Shame follows: "you shall blush for the gardens that you have chosen" (Isa 1:29); "an abomination is he who chooses you" (Isa 41:24).
observations.meaning: Wrong choosing is taught by iniquity, drawn by envy, joined to the soul's delight and made to escape affliction; it ends in shame and makes the chooser like what is chosen.

claims.text: "God is spirit" (Joh 4:24) stands. But Scripture speaks freely of God's soul ("my soul shall not abhor you", Lev 26:11; "my soul hates", Isa 1:14; "my soul delights", Isa 42:1; he swears by his soul, Amo 6:8) and God's heart (Gen 6:6; Hos 11:8). No ranking of the words follows (dep §3.10)

## Life set before a person

Life is set before the inner being as something to choose. "I have set before you life and death, blessing and curse. Therefore choose life, that you and your offspring may live" (Deuteronomy 30:19). The same chapter also speaks of God's own work on the heart: "And the Lord your God will circumcise your heart and the heart of your offspring, so that you will love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul, that you may live" (30:6). The choice is made by doing, seeking and holding on:
- "if a person does them, he shall live by them: I am the Lord" (Leviticus 18:5)
- "Justice, and only justice, you shall follow, that you may live" (Deuteronomy 16:20)
- "Let your heart hold fast my words; keep my commandments, and live" (Proverbs 4:4)
- "Leave your simple ways, and live, and walk in the way of insight" (Proverbs 9:6)
- "Seek me and live" (Amos 5:4); "Seek good, and not evil, that you may live" (5:14)
- "his soul is puffed up; it is not upright within him, but the righteous shall live by his faith" (Habakkuk 2:4)

Long days are promised with some of the commands. "Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land" (Exodus 20:12). Moses gives the law "that you may fear the Lord your God … all the days of your life, and that your days may be long" (Deuteronomy 6:2). Peter takes up a psalm: "Whoever desires to love life and see good days, let him keep his tongue from evil" (1 Peter 3:10).

The Preacher sets another sight beside this. "There is a righteous man who perishes in his righteousness, and there is a wicked man who prolongs his life in his evildoing" (Ecclesiastes 7:15). And he adds: "Though a sinner does evil a hundred times and prolongs his life, yet I know that it will be well with those who fear God" (8:12). Scripture states both. I leave them side by side.

Death is set before a person just as plainly. "See, I have set before you today life and good, death and evil" (Deuteronomy 30:15). "Behold, I set before you the way of life and the way of death" (Jeremiah 21:8). Proverbs marks where the other way ends:
- "There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way to death" (Proverbs 14:12)
- "In the path of righteousness is life, and in its pathway there is no death" (Proverbs 12:28)
- Wisdom: "For whoever finds me finds life and obtains favor from the Lord, but he who fails to find me injures himself; all who hate me love death" (Proverbs 8:35–36). To hate wisdom is to love death.
- "Death and life are in the power of the tongue, and those who love it will eat its fruits" (Proverbs 18:21). James calls the tongue "a restless evil, full of deadly poison" (James 3:8).

The same word can be death to one and life to another. Paul says of the message he carries: "to one a fragrance from death to death, to the other a fragrance from life to life. Who is sufficient for these things?" (2 Corinthians 2:16).

Some of what kills a person is named from within. "Surely vexation kills the fool, and jealousy slays the simple" (Job 5:2). "The desire of the sluggard kills him, for his hands refuse to labor" (Proverbs 21:25). Proverbs names more:
- "He dies for lack of discipline, and because of his great folly he is led astray" (Proverbs 5:23)
- "whoever hates reproof will die" (Proverbs 15:10)
- "he who despises his ways will die" (Proverbs 19:16)

Elihu says it of those who will not hear: "if they do not listen, they perish by the sword and die without knowledge" (Job 36:12). Sections 10.1, 10.5 and 10.6 follow these.

God says what he wants. "Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked, declares the Lord God, and not rather that he should turn from his way and live?" (Ezekiel 18:23). "For I have no pleasure in the death of anyone, declares the Lord God; so turn, and live" (18:32). He says it to people who had given up: "Surely our transgressions and our sins are upon us, and we rot away because of them. How then can we live?" The answer comes at once: "turn back, turn back from your evil ways, for why will you die, O house of Israel?" (33:10–11).

The turning is a considered act, and it reaches back over the past:
- "Because he considered and turned away from all the transgressions that he had committed, he shall surely live; he shall not die" (Ezekiel 18:28).
- "None of the transgressions that he has committed shall be remembered against him" (18:22).
- It reaches back the other way too: when a righteous man turns to injustice, "None of the righteous deeds that he has done shall be remembered" (18:24).
- Trust can lean the wrong way: "if he trusts in his righteousness and does injustice, none of his righteous deeds shall be remembered, but in his injustice that he has done he shall die" (33:13).

Another's death can be laid at a person's hand. The watchman who does not warn the wicked is told, "his blood I will require at your hand"; if he warns and is not heeded, "you will have delivered your soul" (Ezekiel 33:8–9). Section 10.10 follows that.

Section 10.7 follows the choosing, and Chapter 14 the turning.

Life can also be wrongly kept or taken by words. God condemns those who were "putting to death souls who should not die and keeping alive souls who should not live, by your lying to my people, who listen to lies" (Ezekiel 13:19).

## Facing death

Scripture shows the inner being under the coming of death. Often it is anguish (the calmer deaths are in "Dying to the Lord", below):
- "My heart is in anguish within me; the terrors of death have fallen upon me" (Psalm 55:4)
- David to Jonathan: "there is but a step between me and death" (1 Samuel 20:3)
- "Consider and answer me, O Lord my God; light up my eyes, lest I sleep the sleep of death" (Psalm 13:3)
- In Gethsemane: "My soul is very sorrowful, even to death" (Matthew 26:38)

Bildad says the wicked man "is torn from the tent in which he trusted and is brought to the king of terrors" (Job 18:14). He says it of Job, and God's later verdict on Job's friends stands over it (Job 42:7; 10.12). The Preacher pictures old age near its end: "they are afraid also of what is high, and terrors are in the way … and desire fails, because man is going to his eternal home" (Ecclesiastes 12:5).

The fear of dying shapes what people do. Isaac passed off his wife as his sister: "Because I thought, 'Lest I die because of her.'" (Genesis 26:9). Judah kept Shelah from Tamar, "for he feared that he would die, like his brothers" (Genesis 38:11). Lot would not flee to the hills, "lest the disaster overtake me and I die" (Genesis 19:19). Near the tabernacle the people cried, "Behold, we perish, we are undone … Are we all to perish?" (Numbers 17:12–13). And Agag came "cheerfully", saying, "Surely the bitterness of death is past" (1 Samuel 15:32). God asks his people, "who are you that you are afraid of man who dies, of the son of man who is made like grass" (Isaiah 51:12). Hebrews names that fear as bondage: Christ shared flesh and blood "that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil, and deliver all those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery" (Hebrews 2:14–15). Section 10.1 follows fear.

A death can bring fear on others. After Ananias and Sapphira died, "great fear came upon the whole church and upon all who heard of these things" (Acts 5:11).

Paul gives the nearness of death a purpose: "Indeed, we felt that we had received the sentence of death. But that was to make us rely not on ourselves but on God who raises the dead" (2 Corinthians 1:9). Jesus himself "offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears, to him who was able to save him from death, and he was heard because of his reverence" (Hebrews 5:7). Paul says the apostles live "like men sentenced to death, because we have become a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to men" (1 Corinthians 4:9).

Barzillai, at eighty, asks to go home to die: "Please let your servant return, that I may die in my own city near the grave of my father and my mother. But here is your servant Chimham" (2 Samuel 19:37). He gives his place at court to another (10.7).

## Wanting to die

Scripture is honest that people sometimes want to die. In the words of Elijah, Jonah, Job, Saul and Samson below, the Hebrew word behind "my life" or "I" is *nephesh* ("soul, life"). Most other such wishes name no inner word at all: of the 24 verses with a wish to die, 17 do not.
- Elijah "asked that he might die, saying, 'It is enough; now, O Lord, take away my life'" (1 Kings 19:4).
- Jonah: "take my life from me, for it is better for me to die than to live" (Jonah 4:3).
- Job: "I would choose strangling and death rather than my bones. I loathe my life; I would not live forever" (Job 7:15–16). A few verses earlier he spoke of "the anguish of my spirit" and "the bitterness of my soul" (7:11). The wish comes out of his nights: "When I say, 'My bed will comfort me' … then you scare me with dreams and terrify me with visions" (7:13–14). He says it to God, "Leave me alone" (7:16), and he does not act on it.
- Saul, wounded on Gilboa: "anguish has seized me, and yet my life still lingers" (2 Samuel 1:9).
- Job speaks of those "who long for death, but it comes not, and dig for it more than for hidden treasures" (Job 3:21), and asks, "Why did I not die at birth, come out from the womb and expire?" (Job 3:11); "Would that I had died before any eye had seen me" (10:18). What he wants from death is rest: "For then I would have lain down and been quiet; I would have slept; then I would have been at rest" (3:13).
- Jeremiah: "Cursed be the day on which I was born!" He wishes he had died before birth, "because he did not kill me in the womb; so my mother would have been my grave", and asks, "Why did I come out from the womb to see toil and sorrow, and spend my days in shame?" (Jeremiah 20:14, 17–18).
- Rachel, envying her sister: "Give me children, or I shall die!" (Genesis 30:1).
- The Preacher: "I thought the dead who are already dead more fortunate than the living who are still alive" (Ecclesiastes 4:2).

At the sea, fear set slavery against death and preferred slavery: "it would have been better for us to serve the Egyptians than to die in the wilderness" (Exodus 14:12; 10.6, 10.12). The complaint comes back in the wilderness: "Would that we had perished when our brothers perished before the Lord!" (Numbers 20:3; also Exodus 14:11; Numbers 21:5).

Elihu warns against the other wish: *"Do not long for the night, when peoples vanish in their place"* (Job 36:20).

Under judgment, death is chosen over life: "Death shall be preferred to life by all the remnant that remains of this evil family" (Jeremiah 8:3). "Preferred" is the choosing word. It is said as part of a judgment the Lord declares. Before it, the bones of the dead are spread "before the sun and the moon and all the host of heaven, which they have loved and served, which they have gone after" (8:2). The verse does not say that the one leads to the other. In Revelation death is sought and not found: "people will seek death and will not find it. They will long to die, but death will flee from them" (Revelation 9:6). And Job's wife urges it on him: "Do you still hold fast your integrity? Curse God and die" (Job 2:9).

Of the wishes in this section, four are answered with something other than death:
- **Elijah** is given food, twice: "Arise and eat". He goes "in the strength of that food forty days and forty nights" (1 Kings 19:5–8).
- **Jonah's** wish came with his anger at God's mercy: "angry enough to die" (Jonah 4:9). He is given a question about God's pity for Nineveh (Jonah 4:10–11).
- **Israel**, wishing they had died beside the meat pots of Egypt, is given bread from heaven (Exodus 16:3–4).
- When Israel loathed the manna and spoke against God, the answer was something to look at: "everyone who is bitten, when he sees it, shall live" (Numbers 21:8).

Three are granted, each to a man already blinded or wounded. Samson, blinded and a prisoner (Judges 16:21), is given one last act of strength (16:30). Abimelech, wounded, says to his armor-bearer, "Draw your sword and kill me, lest they say of me, 'A woman killed him.'" And "his young man thrust him through, and he died" (Judges 9:54). Saul's death is carried out by an Amalekite, whom David then condemns (2 Samuel 1:14–16).

So, of the seven, two are fed, two are answered another way, and three are granted.

### Christ first

"But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep" (1 Corinthians 15:20). "For as by a man came death, by a man has come also the resurrection of the dead" (15:21). "For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive. But each in his own order: Christ the firstfruits, then at his coming those who belong to Christ" (15:22–23). He is "the firstborn from the dead" (Colossians 1:18). "God raised the Lord and will also raise us up by his power" (1 Corinthians 6:14). Peter says death could not keep him: "God raised him up, loosing the pangs of death, because it was not possible for him to be held by it" (Acts 2:24). He and Paul read the psalm of him: "For you will not abandon my soul to Hades, or let your Holy One see corruption" (Acts 2:27). "For David, after he had served the purpose of God in his own generation, fell asleep and was laid with his fathers and saw corruption, but he whom God raised up did not see corruption" (Acts 13:36–37).

The Gospels show his risen body. They do not define it.
- **He could be touched, and he ate.** When the disciples "thought they saw a spirit", he said, "See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself. Touch me, and see. For a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have" (Luke 24:37, 39). They gave him broiled fish, "and he took it and ate before them" (24:42–43). The apostles "ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead" (Acts 10:41). To Thomas he said, "put out your hand, and place it in my side" (John 20:27).
- **He came and went.** With "the doors being locked … Jesus came and stood among them" (John 20:19). At Emmaus "their eyes were opened, and they recognized him. And he vanished from their sight" (Luke 24:31).
- **He was not known at once.** On the road, "their eyes were kept from recognizing him" (Luke 24:16). Mary "saw Jesus standing, but she did not know that it was Jesus" (John 20:14). At the lake, "the disciples did not know that it was Jesus" (21:4).

Paul also writes, "flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does the perishable inherit the imperishable" (1 Corinthians 15:50). Scripture states both: flesh and bones that can be touched, and flesh and blood that cannot inherit. I leave them side by side.

blocks.section: Flesh in the New Testament: one word, several values
blocks.text:
## Flesh in the New Testament: one word, several values

In the New Testament, flesh can still simply mean human life in the body.

- "The Word became flesh and dwelt among us" (John 1:14).
- "In the days of his flesh, Jesus offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears" (Hebrews 5:7).
- "The life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God" (Galatians 2:20).
- "If I am to live in the flesh, that means fruitful labor for me" (Philippians 1:22).
- "A thorn was given me in the flesh" (2 Corinthians 12:7).

But in Paul, and in Peter and John, flesh also becomes something else: **a way the inner person is set**, with its own desires and its own mind.

- "The desires of the flesh are against the Spirit, and the desires of the Spirit are against the flesh" (Galatians 5:17).
- "To set the mind on the flesh is death, but to set the mind on the Spirit is life and peace" (Romans 8:6).
- "I know that nothing good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh. For I have the desire to do what is right, but not the ability to carry it out" (Romans 7:18).
- "I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh I serve the law of sin" (Romans 7:25).
- "The passions of the flesh … wage war against your soul" (1 Peter 2:11).
- "The desires of the flesh and the desires of the eyes and pride of life" (1 John 2:16).

The same letters say what is to be done with these desires. "Walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh" (Galatians 5:16). "Those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires" (5:24). "Put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, to gratify its desires" (Romans 13:14). Peter speaks of living "for the rest of the time in the flesh no longer for human passions but for the will of God" (1 Peter 4:2). In that verse "the flesh" is simply life in the body, and the passions are what it is no longer lived for. The same desires can be used on others. False teachers "entice by sensual passions of the flesh those who are barely escaping from those who live in error" (2 Peter 2:18); they "indulge in the lust of defiling passion and despise authority" (2:10). And flesh can be an outward mark to boast in: "It is those who want to make a good showing in the flesh who would force you to be circumcised", and "they desire to have you circumcised that they may boast in your flesh" (Galatians 6:12–13).
Jude sets the same acts together: "relying on their dreams, defile the flesh, reject authority, and blaspheme the glorious ones" (Jude 8). Against them he sets the archangel, who "did not presume to pronounce a blasphemous judgment, but said, 'The Lord rebuke you'" (9; 13.2). They "blaspheme all that they do not understand" (10).

Here flesh is spoken of as having desires and a mind: it wants, it sets its mind, it judges "according to the flesh" (John 8:15), and it boasts "according to the flesh" (2 Corinthians 11:18).

The same word can change value within a single speech. In John 6, Jesus says, "the bread that I will give for the life of the world is my flesh" (6:51), and "whoever feeds on my flesh … has eternal life" (6:54). When the disciples take offence, he says, "It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh is no help at all. The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life" (6:63). Within a dozen verses, flesh is the gift of life and "no help at all".

blocks.section: Lines that are often drawn, but that I cannot find
blocks.text:
## Lines that are often drawn, but that I cannot find

Several confident distinctions are often taught. When I read the verses in their places, they did not hold up. Here they are, one by one.

**"The soul sins; the human spirit never does."** It is true that "the soul who sins shall die" (Ezekiel 18:4), but there the soul means the *person*, the one who answers for the sin. And while I find no verse where "the spirit" is the subject of the verb "to sin", the spirit is plainly judged. It is "haughty" before a fall (Proverbs 16:18). It was "not faithful to God" (Psalm 78:8). It is hardened (Deuteronomy 2:30). It needs to be made "right" (Psalm 51:10). It has or lacks "deceit" (Psalm 32:2). It needs cleansing from "defilement" (2 Corinthians 7:1). If Scripture has a *moral centre*, it is the heart (Chapter 12). The spirit stands beside it, not above it.

**"Animals have souls but not spirits."** The animals are "living creatures", the same phrase as the man in Genesis 2:7. But they also have "the breath of life". The flood came on "all flesh in which is the breath of life" (Genesis 6:17; 7:15), and there the word is *rûaḥ*. "They all have the same breath" (Ecclesiastes 3:19). There is "the spirit of the beast" (Ecclesiastes 3:21). "When you take away their breath, they die" (Psalm 104:29). What marks the man in Genesis 2:7 is not that he has breath and they do not. It is that **God himself breathed it into him**.

**"The soul faces the self; the spirit faces God."** The soul is the part that thirsts for God, lifts itself to God, waits for him and blesses him (Chapter 5). The spirit is anxious, provoked, hot-tempered and crushed (Chapter 6). Each faces both ways.

**"The soul goes to Sheol; the spirit goes to God."** The verses usually cited speak of the soul being *delivered from* Sheol ("you will not abandon my soul to Sheol", Psalm 16:10; "you have brought up my soul from Sheol", Psalm 30:3). Psalm 30:3 is about a living person rescued from death. Peter reads Psalm 16:10 of Christ, "not abandoned to Hades" (Acts 2:31). Neither sends the soul one way and the spirit another, and the verses that name Sheol or Hades speak of the soul and never of the spirit. And Ecclesiastes leaves the spirit's destination as a question: "Who knows whether the spirit of man goes upward?" (Ecclesiastes 3:21). See Chapter 2.

**"Spirit first, soul second, body third."** Scripture does not rank the inner words. It lists them in different orders for different purposes (Chapter 3). It gives God a soul as readily as a spirit: "my soul shall not abhor you" (Leviticus 26:11), "my soul delights" (Isaiah 42:1). It brings a dead child's life back as soul ("the life of the child came into him again", 1 Kings 17:22) as readily as spirit ("her spirit returned", Luke 8:55).

# 10.2 Knowing and hearing

Knowing belongs chiefly to the heart, as Chapter 4 showed. To pay attention is to set the heart. To understand is to have a *hearing heart*. To remember is to keep a thing in the heart. The spirit knows the self from within: "who knows a person's thoughts except the spirit of that person, which is in him?" (1 Corinthians 2:11). The soul receives what is known as something good to taste: "knowledge will be pleasant to your soul" (Proverbs 2:10).

**Hearing is the main way in.** The ear receives, and the heart keeps it or refuses it. "All my words that I shall speak to you receive in your heart, and hear with your ears" (Ezekiel 3:10). "Making your ear attentive to wisdom and inclining your heart to understanding" (Proverbs 2:2). When the heart is hard, hearing stops: "Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he would not listen" (Exodus 7:13). "They made their hearts diamond-hard lest they should hear the law" (Zechariah 7:12). A crushed spirit can block hearing as well. Israel "did not listen to Moses, because of their broken spirit and harsh slavery" (Exodus 6:9).

A refusal to hear can stand on a reading of the past. The survivors in Egypt told Jeremiah, "As for the word that you have spoken to us in the name of the Lord, we will not listen to you" (Jeremiah 44:16). Their reason was what they remembered: "For then we had plenty of food, and prospered, and saw no disaster. But since we left off making offerings to the queen of heaven and pouring out drink offerings to her, we have lacked everything" (44:17–18). They had seen the ruin (44:2; 10.13, *Seen and not taken in*) and read it the other way. I read the refusal as resting on their own account of cause and effect.

What is heard moves everything inside. Rahab says, "As soon as we heard it, our hearts melted, and there was no spirit left in any man because of you" (Joshua 2:11). Good news works the other way: "Like cold water to a thirsty soul, so is good news from a far country" (Proverbs 25:25). And hearing is a kind of eating: "Listen diligently to me, and eat what is good, and delight yourselves in rich food. Incline your ear, and come to me; hear, that your soul may live" (Isaiah 55:2–3).

Sometimes hearing is not enough, and the inner being needs to *see*. Jacob's heart went numb at the news that Joseph was alive. His spirit revived only when he saw the wagons (Genesis 45:26–27).

Understanding has a source that Scripture names in the breath: "it is the spirit in man, the breath of the Almighty, that makes him understand" (Job 32:8; Chapter 2). And hearing God himself was a matter of life. "Did any people ever hear the voice of a god speaking out of the midst of the fire, as you have heard, and still live?" (Deuteronomy 4:33). Section 10.9 follows this.

**Hearing goes both ways.** The ear is the way in, and it is also where what goes out arrives. God hears what people say: "You have heard their taunts, O Lord, all their plots against me" (Lamentations 3:61). "Then those who feared the Lord spoke with one another. The Lord paid attention and heard them" (Malachi 3:16). And refusing to hear goes with devising. "I am bringing disaster upon this people, the fruit of their devices, because they have not paid attention to my words" (Jeremiah 6:19). Jeremiah's enemies plot against him with these words: "let us not pay attention to any of his words" (Jeremiah 18:18).

What a person listens to shows what he is: *"An evildoer listens to wicked lips, and a liar gives ear to a mischievous tongue"* (Proverbs 17:4).

Who speaks can decide whether a word is heard. In the Preacher's example a poor, wise man "by his wisdom delivered the city. Yet no one remembered that poor man. But I say that wisdom is better than might, though the poor man's wisdom is despised and his words are not heard" (Ecclesiastes 9:15–16). His wisdom had saved them. I read the verse as saying that what was seen in him was his poverty, and that was why he was forgotten and not heard (10.3).

Hearing can be taken away, and then wanted. *"Behold, the days are coming, declares the Lord God, when I will send a famine on the land—not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the Lord. They shall wander from sea to sea … to seek the word of the Lord, but they shall not find it. In that day the lovely virgins and the young men shall faint for thirst"* (Amos 8:11–13). The famine is not of the word but of hearing it. The bodily thirst comes in the same day.

Before Samuel, *"the word of the Lord was rare in those days; there was no frequent vision"* (1 Samuel 3:1). The word for *rare* is the word for *precious*. When the call came, the boy did not know it: *"Samuel did not yet know the Lord, and the word of the Lord had not yet been revealed to him"* (3:7). Three times he ran to Eli, until *"Eli perceived that the Lord was calling the boy"* and taught him the answer, *"Speak, Lord, for your servant hears"* (3:8–9). The old priest, whose eyes were growing dim (3:2), knew the voice the boy could not yet place. I read hearing that had to be learned, in a time when the word was rare.

Hearing can stop at a single word. Paul tells the crowd of his vision in the temple: *"Make haste and get out of Jerusalem quickly, because they will not accept your testimony about me"* (Acts 22:18). He objected that they knew his past: *"Lord, they themselves know that in one synagogue after another I imprisoned and beat those who believed in you"* (22:19). The answer was *"Go, for I will send you far away to the Gentiles"* (22:21). Then *"Up to this word they listened to him. Then they raised their voices and said, 'Away with such a fellow from the earth! For he should not be allowed to live'"* (22:22). They heard him through the persecution and the vision; the word "Gentiles" ended their hearing. Paul had thought his past would make them listen; the Lord had said it would not.

Ears can be closed to a word that is still being spoken. "To whom shall I speak and give warning, that they may hear? Behold, their ears are uncircumcised, they cannot listen; behold, the word of the Lord is to them an object of scorn; they take no pleasure in it" (Jeremiah 6:10). The act is a hearing that does not happen. "Cannot listen" is followed by what they do with the word instead: they scorn it. Taking no pleasure in it is the measure of the scorn. I read the uncircumcised ears as hearing that lacks the mark of belonging to him. The one who must speak is left holding it: "Therefore I am full of the wrath of the Lord; I am weary of holding it in" (6:11).

Words that are heard can be pictured as tools. The Preacher *"sought to find words of delight, and uprightly he wrote words of truth"* (Ecclesiastes 12:10). *"The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails firmly fixed are the collected sayings; they are given by one Shepherd. My son, beware of anything beyond these"* (12:11–12). A goad drives an animal on; a nail holds something in place. I read the figure as two works of the same words on the hearer: they move him, and they fix in him. Delight is in the search for the words, and the words are given by one Shepherd.

What is heard can also kindle. "I was very angry when I heard their outcry and these words" (Nehemiah 5:6). And when what is heard lowers the hearers' standing or exposes their guilt, rage can refuse to hear any more. Stephen's hearers "were enraged, and they ground their teeth at him … But they cried out with a loud voice and stopped their ears and rushed together at him" (Acts 7:54, 57). James puts hearing first for this very reason: "let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger; for the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God" (James 1:19–20).

The same words, read aloud, brought fear to some and none to others. When the scroll of Jeremiah's words was read, the officials "heard all the words, they turned one to another in fear" (Jeremiah 36:16). The king cut it up column by column and burned it, and "neither the king nor any of his servants who heard all these words was afraid, nor did they tear their garments" (36:23–24).

Understanding can itself be dread: "it will be sheer terror to understand the message" (Isaiah 28:19; Chapter 13). And some hold the word in awe: "Princes persecute me without cause, but my heart stands in awe of your words" (Psalm 119:161). Section 10.9 follows those who tremble at his word.

Some things are only understood later. Of God's anger, Jeremiah says, "In the latter days you will understand it clearly" (Jeremiah 23:20). Chapter 13 follows how people read, and misread, what has happened to them.

God also says what knowing him is. Of Josiah: "He judged the cause of the poor and needy; then it was well. Is not this to know me? declares the Lord" (Jeremiah 22:16). It is said against his son, who built "by unrighteousness" and kept back his neighbour's wages (22:13): "But you have eyes and heart only for your dishonest gain, for shedding innocent blood, and for practicing oppression and violence" (22:17). Knowing God is named here in a deed done for the poor, and set against a heart and eyes given to gain (10.6).

Knowing has a beginning, and Scripture names it. "The fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge; fools despise wisdom and instruction" (Proverbs 1:7). "The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom" (Proverbs 9:10; Psalm 111:10). To man God said, "Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom, and to turn away from evil is understanding" (Job 28:28). It also runs the other way. The one who seeks wisdom "as for hidden treasures" is told, "then you will understand the fear of the Lord and find the knowledge of God" (Proverbs 2:4–5). And it can be refused: "Because they hated knowledge and did not choose the fear of the Lord" (Proverbs 1:29). The fear of God is also learned by hearing (10.9).

Learning to fear God takes a life. Israel was gathered "so that they may learn to fear me all the days that they live on the earth, and that they may teach their children so" (Deuteronomy 4:10). The ear decides much: "The ear that listens to life-giving reproof will dwell among the wise" (Proverbs 15:31). God can open the ear himself. In a dream "he opens the ears of men and terrifies them with warnings, that he may turn man aside from his deed and conceal pride from a man" (Job 33:16–17). Chapter 2 ("Living before God", "Delivered from death") gives the setting.

Wisdom, refused, says: "I also will laugh at your calamity; I will mock when terror strikes you" (Proverbs 1:26). And "whoever listens to me will dwell secure and will be at ease, without dread of disaster" (1:33).

What is known is also kept and returned to. Remembering feeds thinking: "I remember the days of old; I meditate on all that you have done; I ponder the work of your hands" (Psalm 143:5).

Hearing can be woken. "The Lord God has given me the tongue of those who are taught, that I may know how to sustain with a word him who is weary. Morning by morning he awakens; he awakens my ear to hear as those who are taught. The Lord God has opened my ear, and I was not rebellious; I turned not backward" (Isaiah 50:4–5). The order is the verses' own: the ear is woken before the tongue sustains anyone, and it is woken each morning. The next verse goes on to "I gave my back to those who strike" (50:6), so the woken ear is no shelter from suffering. An angel wakes a prophet too, and the first thing said is "What do you see?" (Zechariah 4:1–2; 13.2).

What is known can be known in heart and soul. Joshua, near death: "you know in your hearts and souls, all of you, that not one word has failed of all the good things that the Lord your God promised concerning you. All have come to pass for you; not one of them has failed" (Joshua 23:14). This is knowing from experience. He turns it into a warning straight away: "But just as all the good things that the Lord your God promised concerning you have been fulfilled for you, so the Lord will bring upon you all the evil things" (23:15). The faithfulness they know from the good is the same faithfulness that stands behind the warnings.

Receiving a word can wait on being willing. "and if you are willing to accept it, he is Elijah who is to come. He who has ears to hear, let him hear" (Matthew 11:14–15). The Bereans "received the word with all eagerness, examining the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so. Many of them therefore believed" (Acts 17:11–12). Paul calls a saying "trustworthy and deserving of full acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost" (1 Timothy 1:15). The other way is also named: scoffers "following their own sinful desires … deliberately overlook this fact" (2 Peter 3:3, 5). I read the willing, or the unwilling, as standing before the hearing in these verses.

## Beside choosing

Wanting stands beside choosing, and the words can cross. When the king says to Barzillai "all that you desire of me I will do for you" (2 Samuel 19:38), "desire" is the Hebrew verb for choosing. Elsewhere the verses set what a person wants next to what they choose:
- **Desire:** "For they shall be ashamed of the oaks that you desired; and you shall blush for the gardens that you have chosen" (Isaiah 1:29).
- **The soul's delight:** "These have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations" (Isaiah 66:3).
- **Envy, named before the choice it would lead to:** "Do not envy a man of violence and do not choose any of his ways" (Proverbs 3:31).
- **Wanting weighed against something better:** of wisdom, "nothing you desire can compare with her" (Proverbs 3:15).

A desire still has to be carried through. Paul writes "so that your readiness in desiring it may be matched by your completing it" (2 Corinthians 8:11). Section 10.7 gives the account of choosing.

A want can be met and still be refused. "David said longingly, 'Oh, that someone would give me water to drink from the well of Bethlehem'" (2 Samuel 23:15). Three men broke through the enemy camp to bring it, "But he would not drink of it. He poured it out to the Lord and said, 'Far be it from me, O Lord, that I should do this. Shall I drink the blood of the men who went at the risk of their lives?'" (23:16–17). His longing was real, and he set it aside for what the water had cost others. 10.7 (*Willing*) follows the will.

## Aimed at God

Wanting can be aimed at seeing Jesus, and the verses show it ending in different places. Greeks "came to Philip … and asked him, 'Sir, we wish to see Jesus'", and Jesus answered, "The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified" (John 12:21, 23). Herod "was very glad, for he had long desired to see him, because he had heard about him, and he was hoping to see some sign", and "he made no answer" (Luke 23:8–9). His mother and brothers stood outside "desiring to see you", and he said, "My mother and my brothers are those who hear the word of God and do it" (8:20–21).

Wanting can be aimed at the living God. "My soul thirsts for God, for the living God. When shall I come and appear before God?" (Psalm 42:2). "In the path of your judgments, O Lord, we wait for you; your name and remembrance are the desire of our soul" (Isaiah 26:8). "My soul is consumed with longing for your rules at all times" (Psalm 119:20). When Judah "had sought him with their whole desire", "he was found by them" (2 Chronicles 15:15).

Elsewhere wanting is scattered: "the wandering of the appetite", "various passions". Here it is gathered into one. "One thing have I asked of the Lord, that will I seek after: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, to gaze upon the beauty of the Lord and to inquire in his temple" (Psalm 27:4). It is asked and sought, a request and a pursuit. And it is a desire to look. Desire came in by the eye toward the tree and toward another man's wife. Here the act is the same, looking with desire, and it is turned to the Lord. I read that Scripture does not cure desiring by looking away; it changes what is looked at. The psalm says what lies around the want. It opens "whom shall I fear?" with an army encamped (27:1–3), and it says "my father and my mother have forsaken me, but the Lord will take me in" (27:10). It also says where the want started: "You have said, 'Seek my face.' My heart says to you, 'Your face, Lord, do I seek'" (27:8). The heart's seeking is an answer to an invitation.

In Psalm 16 every good is drawn into God: "I have no good apart from you" (16:2). The pictures are of an inheritance measured out: "The Lord is my chosen portion and my cup; you hold my lot. The lines have fallen for me in pleasant places" (16:5–6). Desire here is satisfied by what is allotted, not by what is grabbed. Against it stands "The sorrows of those who run after another god shall multiply" (16:4). Desire that runs after something else multiplies sorrow. The psalm ends, "You make known to me the path of life; in your presence there is fullness of joy; at your right hand are pleasures forevermore" (16:11). Three verses earlier: "because he is at my right hand, I shall not be shaken" (16:8). The psalm uses the one position twice. I read that the nearness that keeps a person unshaken is the same nearness that is the pleasure.

Longing does not give life by itself. "Turn my eyes from looking at worthless things; and give me life in your ways", and "Behold, I long for your precepts; in your righteousness give me life!" (Psalm 119:37, 40; Chapter 2, "Life asked for"). The eye is turned away from worthless things and the longing is set on the precepts, and still the life is asked for.

Longing for God's word is pictured as breathing hard: *"I open my mouth and pant, because I long for your commandments"* (Psalm 119:131). It is weighed by worth and by taste: *"More to be desired are they than gold, even much fine gold; sweeter also than honey and drippings of the honeycomb"* (Psalm 19:10). It can follow a choice: *"I have chosen your precepts. I long for your salvation, O Lord, and your law is my delight"* (119:173–174). And it can be laid open in sickness, when the nearest stand far off: *"O Lord, all my longing is before you; my sighing is not hidden from you"* (Psalm 38:9, 11; 10.11).

Steadfast love is called precious, and the valuing becomes shelter: *"How precious is your steadfast love, O God! The children of mankind take refuge in the shadow of your wings. They feast on the abundance of your house, and you give them drink from the river of your delights"* (Psalm 36:7–8). The psalm opens on the other man: *"there is no fear of God before his eyes"* (36:1; Chapter 12). What is valued here is not a gift but his love. I read that the valuing draws them near: they shelter, feast and drink in his house.

Some longing to see is not met in its time: *"many prophets and righteous people longed to see what you see, and did not see it"* (Matthew 13:17). *"The days are coming when you will desire to see one of the days of the Son of Man, and you will not see it. And they will say to you, 'Look, there!' or 'Look, here!' Do not go out or follow them"* (Luke 17:22–23). The longing is real, and it is not to be met by following whoever says "Look, here!"

A day can be wanted wrongly. *"Woe to you who desire the day of the Lord! Why would you have the day of the Lord? It is darkness, and not light, as if a man fled from a lion, and a bear met him"* (Amos 5:18–19). Jeremiah says the opposite of himself: *"nor have I desired the day of sickness"* (Jeremiah 17:16). The people want a day they do not understand, and the picture is of fleeing one danger straight into another. The prophet disowns wanting the disaster he has to announce.

Peter writes, "Like newborn infants, long for the pure spiritual milk, that by it you may grow up into salvation" (1 Peter 2:2), and adds, "if indeed you have tasted that the Lord is good" (2:3). Paul turns an eagerness for the Spirit's gifts outward: "since you are eager for manifestations of the Spirit, strive to excel in building up the church" (1 Corinthians 14:12).

## Thirst answered

Twice in John people ask for the gift and mean the thing itself. The woman at the well: "Sir, give me this water, so that I will not be thirsty or have to come here to draw water" (John 4:15). The crowd, who had followed Jesus "because you ate your fill of the loaves" (6:26): "Sir, give us this bread always" (6:34). Both times the answer moves from the thing to a person: "I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst" (6:35). The want is real, and it is not refused. It is met by coming and believing, acts toward someone, and not by a supply.

The water is pictured as a spring: "Everyone who drinks of this water will be thirsty again, but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never be thirsty again. The water that I will give him will become in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life" (John 4:13–14). Jeremiah has the opposite: "they have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters, and hewed out cisterns for themselves, broken cisterns that can hold no water" (Jeremiah 2:13; Chapter 2). A cistern holds what is poured into it, and a broken one loses it. A spring wells up from within. One is a want that must be filled again and again. The other is a want met at its source, and the source is "in him".

The thirst is answered with water: "let the one who is thirsty come; let the one who desires take the water of life without price" (Revelation 22:17). God hears the desire: "O Lord, you hear the desire of the afflicted; you will strengthen their heart" (Psalm 10:17). He gives it: "You have given him his heart's desire and have not withheld the request of his lips" (Psalm 21:2). A desire met reaches the whole person: "a desire fulfilled is a tree of life" (Proverbs 13:12), and "A desire fulfilled is sweet to the soul, but to turn away from evil is an abomination to fools" (13:19). And God himself satisfies it: "You open your hand; you satisfy the desire of every living thing" (Psalm 145:16). The creatures' thirst is met the same way (13.4).

At the feast the offer is made aloud, and the water now flows outward: *"Jesus stood up and cried out, 'If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, Out of his heart will flow rivers of living water.'"* John adds, *"Now this he said about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive"* (John 7:37–39; Chapter 6). At the well the spring wells up *"in him"*. At the feast rivers flow *"out of his heart"*. I read a want that is met and then becomes a source for others.

The one who offered the water thirsted: *"After this, Jesus, knowing that all was now finished, said (to fulfill the Scripture), 'I thirst.'"* He was given sour wine, and then he said, *"It is finished"* (John 19:28–30). The psalm puts the thirst beside the want of comfort: *"I looked for pity, but there was none, and for comforters, but I found none. They gave me poison for food, and for my thirst they gave me sour wine to drink"* (Psalm 69:20–21). He says "I thirst" knowing what it fulfils. I read the want spoken, not hidden, and answered with sour wine.

The want can be aimed at righteousness, and then it is called blessed: *"Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied"* (Matthew 5:6). God's answer to plain thirst is given with its reason. *"When the poor and needy seek water, and there is none, and their tongue is parched with thirst, I the Lord will answer them; I the God of Israel will not forsake them"* (Isaiah 41:17). *"They shall not hunger or thirst, neither scorching wind nor sun shall strike them, for he who has pity on them will lead them, and by springs of water will guide them"* (Isaiah 49:10). The end is said in nearly the same words: *"They shall hunger no more, neither thirst anymore; the sun shall not strike them, nor any scorching heat. For the Lamb in the midst of the throne will be their shepherd, and he will guide them to springs of living water, and God will wipe away every tear from their eyes"* (Revelation 7:16–17). The thirst and the tears are answered together.

A thirst met can be forgotten. *"You gave them bread from heaven for their hunger and brought water for them out of the rock for their thirst … But they and our fathers acted presumptuously and stiffened their neck"*; they *"were not mindful of the wonders that you performed among them"* (Nehemiah 9:15–17). Isaiah sets the same memory beside the wicked: *"They did not thirst when he led them through the deserts; he made water flow for them from the rock … There is no peace, says the Lord, for the wicked"* (Isaiah 48:21–22). I read a want met so fully that it was no longer felt, and the giver forgotten with it (10.3).

Thirst also comes as judgment, and the verses name the inner ground each time. Joyless service in plenty: *"Because you did not serve the Lord your God with joyfulness and gladness of heart, because of the abundance of all things, therefore you shall serve your enemies whom the Lord will send against you, in hunger and thirst"* (Deuteronomy 28:47–48). A choice of what he did not delight in: *"you did what was evil in my eyes and chose what I did not delight in"* (Isaiah 65:12), so *"my servants shall drink, but you shall be thirsty … my servants shall sing for gladness of heart, but you shall cry out for pain of heart and shall wail for breaking of spirit"* (65:13–14). The outward thirst is matched by pain of heart and a broken spirit. Drink without regard: those who *"run after strong drink"* (5:11) and *"do not regard the deeds of the Lord"* (5:12) end *"parched with thirst"*, and the lack named is knowledge: *"my people go into exile for lack of knowledge"* (Isaiah 5:13). The drinkers end thirsty.

Hunger and thirst can be borne for others. *"To the present hour we hunger and thirst, we are poorly dressed and buffeted and homeless, and we labor, working with our own hands. When reviled, we bless; when persecuted, we endure"* (1 Corinthians 4:11–12). Paul's longer list ends *"in hunger and thirst, often without food, in cold and exposure. And, apart from other things, there is the daily pressure on me of my anxiety for all the churches"* (2 Corinthians 11:27–28). The bodily wants are listed and passed over. The weight he names last is inside, and it is for others.

A bodily want can be the setting of a vision. Peter *"became hungry and wanted something to eat, but while they were preparing it, he fell into a trance"* (Acts 10:10), and saw a sheet let down full of animals (10:11–12). The verses do not say why it came then.

# 10.7 Choosing and setting direction

Scripture does not stop to define choosing. It shows a person taking a direction in two ways. A choice is made between things set before them, and the heart is set, inclined and held to what was chosen. One speech holds both. At Shechem, Joshua says *"choose this day whom you will serve"* (Joshua 24:15). When the people have chosen, he says *"Then put away the foreign gods that are among you, and incline your heart to the Lord"* (24:23). The passage then records how long the choice held (24:31). I start from that speech and set the other verses beside it.

The clearest sentence on choosing is about a child: *"when he knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good"* (Isaiah 7:15). Refusing and choosing are named together as one knowing. The man whom the book of Job calls blameless is described by what he turned from: he *"feared God and turned away from evil"* (Job 1:1).

## The words

The English "choose" stands for a few words, and the verses keep each one's own range.
- ***Bāḥar*, "to choose".** It is the ordinary Hebrew verb. The ESV renders it in more than one way:
  - "choose": *"choose this day"* (Joshua 24:15)
  - "desire": *"all that you desire of me I will do for you"* (2 Samuel 19:38)
  - "to be chosen", in the sense of preferred: *"To get understanding is to be chosen rather than silver"* (Proverbs 16:16)
- ***Bāḥîr*, "chosen one".** It is a noun from the same root, for a person or a people God chose: *"Moses, his chosen one"* (Psalm 106:23); *"Israel my chosen"* (Isaiah 45:4).
- ***Māʾas*, "to refuse, reject, despise".** It is the other side of the same act:
  - *"refuse the evil"* (Isaiah 7:15)
  - *"this people has refused the waters of Shiloah"* (8:6)
  - Job's last word: *"therefore I despise myself, and repent"* (Job 42:6)
- ***Eklegomai*, "to choose".** It is the Greek verb used for the gathering in Jerusalem choosing the seven (Acts 6:5) and the church choosing men to send (15:22, 25).
- ***Authairetos*, "of one's own accord".** One Greek word: Titus goes *"of his own accord"* (2 Corinthians 8:17).

The verbs for setting a direction are words of the heart:
- **inclining:** *"incline your heart to the Lord"* (Joshua 24:23)
- **directing:** *"direct your heart to the Lord"* (1 Samuel 7:3)
- **setting before oneself:** *"I have chosen the way of faithfulness; I set your rules before me"* (Psalm 119:30). In this verse the choosing and the setting are one sentence.

The same choosing verb is used for God. When he chooses, a person is the one chosen, and what that means for the person is set out below, in *Being chosen*. God's own choosing, in his own right, is taken up with the other beings (13.1).

## Two sides

Refusing is itself a choice. The child knows *"how to refuse the evil and choose the good"* (Isaiah 7:15). The oracle around that verse shows refusing going both ways:
- **A refusal dressed in pious words.** Ahaz, offered a sign, says *"I will not ask, and I will not put the Lord to the test"* (7:12).
- **A refusal of what was gentle.** *"this people has refused the waters of Shiloah that flow gently"* (8:6).

Each refusal in that oracle has its own consequence.

Not answering is already choosing. *"when I called, you did not answer; when I spoke, you did not listen, but you did what was evil in my eyes and chose what I did not delight in"* (Isaiah 65:12). The verse sets the not listening and the wrong choice in one sentence.

A choice can be put entirely in the negative: *"Do not envy a man of violence and do not choose any of his ways"* (Proverbs 3:31). And it can be laid out with both its sides and both its ends:
- *"cease to do evil, learn to do good"* (Isaiah 1:16–17)
- *"If you are willing and obedient, you shall eat the good of the land"* (1:19)
- *"but if you refuse and rebel, you shall be eaten by the sword"* (1:20)

## What a choice rests on

In these verses a choice does not come from nowhere. Each verse names something that stands under the choice.

**Knowing how.** The child chooses *"when he knows how"* (Isaiah 7:15). The oracle of Isaiah 1 opens with that knowing missing: *"Israel does not know, my people do not understand"* (1:3). For the person God chooses, the order runs the other way, and knowing is what the choosing is for (*Being chosen*, below).

**Being taught.** The way to choose is taught, and the teaching comes from who the Lord is:
- *"Good and upright is the Lord; therefore he instructs sinners in the way"* (Psalm 25:8)
- *"Who is the man who fears the Lord? Him will he instruct in the way that he should choose"* (25:12)
- The one who chooses asks for it: *"Make me to know your ways, O Lord; teach me your paths"* (25:4); *"graciously teach me your law"* (119:29)
- Teaching and the heart are asked for together: *"Teach me your way, O Lord, that I may walk in your truth; unite my heart to fear your name"* (86:11)

In Psalm 119 the one choosing also asks God to do the refusing with him: *"Put false ways far from me"* (119:29).

**The fear of the Lord.** In Psalm 25 it is the one who fears the Lord whom the Lord instructs (25:12). Joshua puts fear before the choice in the same order: *"fear the Lord and serve him in sincerity and in faithfulness"* (Joshua 24:14), and then *"choose this day"* (24:15). What fear does to a choice is taken up below, in *Fear and choosing*.

**What has been seen and remembered.**
- The people at Shechem choose from memory: *"it is the Lord our God who brought us and our fathers up from the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery, and who did those great signs in our sight"* (Joshua 24:17).
- Job's turning is made when he sees: *"now my eye sees you"* (Job 42:5).
- The psalmist keeps his eyes on what he chose: *"My eyes are ever toward the Lord"* (Psalm 25:15).

**What is good to the chooser.** Two verses make the chooser's own good the ground, and honour it: *"wherever it suits him"* (Deuteronomy 23:16), and *"whatever seems good to you"* (2 Samuel 19:38). In Hebrew both say "the good" to him, or in his eyes.

**Convinced that I ought.** A choice can rest on a conviction that is wrong, held with authority from others. "I myself was convinced that I ought to do many things in opposing the name of Jesus of Nazareth. And I did so in Jerusalem. I not only locked up many of the saints in prison after receiving authority from the chief priests, but when they were put to death I cast my vote against them" (Acts 26:9–10). The voice that stopped him named it: "It is hard for you to kick against the goads" (26:14).

## What draws it

What a person wants is named beside what they choose. The account of wanting is in 10.6. Here the verses set it next to the choice.
- **Desire.** *"For they shall be ashamed of the oaks that you desired; and you shall blush for the gardens that you have chosen"* (Isaiah 1:29).
- **The soul's delight.** *"These have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations"* (Isaiah 66:3).
- **Envy.** The pull is named before the choice, and the command reaches it: *"Do not envy a man of violence and do not choose any of his ways"* (Proverbs 3:31).
- **Being pleased.** *"what they said pleased the whole gathering, and they chose Stephen"* (Acts 6:5).
- **Earnestness.** Titus, *"being himself very earnest he is going to you of his own accord"* (2 Corinthians 8:17).
- **Preferring.** To choose can be to weigh one good above another: *"How much better to get wisdom than gold! To get understanding is to be chosen rather than silver"* (Proverbs 16:16). Proverbs 3 sets wisdom above all desire: *"nothing you desire can compare with her"* (3:15).

What is seen as pleasant can draw a person under a yoke. "Issachar is a strong donkey, crouching between the sheepfolds. He saw that a resting place was good, and that the land was pleasant, so he bowed his shoulder to bear, and became a servant at forced labor" (Genesis 49:14–15). The act is bowing the shoulder. What draws it is the rest and the land, seen as good and pleasant. I read a strong animal choosing to lie down, and the rest costing it its freedom.

Folly draws by what is hidden. "The woman Folly is loud; she is seductive and knows nothing", and she calls, "Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!" and "Stolen water is sweet, and bread eaten in secret is pleasant." "But he does not know that the dead are there, that her guests are in the depths of Sheol" (Proverbs 9:13, 16–18). The act is her call and the turning in. The sweetness is what she claims for stolen water. The one who turns in knows the claim and not the end.

## Whose measure

The verses ask in whose eyes, and by whose delight, a choice is good. They give more than one answer, and the setting decides which.
- **The chooser's own eyes.** *"if it is evil in your eyes to serve the Lord, choose this day"* (Joshua 24:15). Joshua leaves the view to the people, and the turning away from the Lord could begin there.
- **The Lord's eyes.** *"you did what was evil in my eyes"* (Isaiah 65:12).
- **The Lord's delight, not met.** *"chose what I did not delight in"* (65:12); *"chose that in which I did not delight"* (66:4).
- **The Lord's delight, met.** *"who choose the things that please me and hold fast my covenant"* (Isaiah 56:4). "Please" is the same word as "delight" in 65:12 and 66:4.
- **The soul's own delight, set against his.** *"their soul delights in their abominations"* (66:3), again the same word.
- **Other people's eyes, set against his choosing.** When God chooses, the verses often name a second measure held by the people around: *"everyone doing whatever is right in his own eyes"*, set against *"the place that the Lord your God will choose"* (Deuteronomy 12:8, 11); Michal's *"before the eyes of his servants' female servants"* against David's *"before the Lord"* (2 Samuel 6:20–21); a people despised *"in their sight"* (Jeremiah 33:24); *"rejected by men but in the sight of God chosen"* (1 Peter 2:4). See *Others around a choice*, below.
- **One's own "better", set against his word.** *"But Naaman was angry and went away, saying, 'Behold, I thought that he would surely come out to me …' Are not Abana and Pharpar, the rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters of Israel?"* (2 Kings 5:11–12). His own measure ("better") and his own picture of how it should go ("I thought") stood against the prophet's word. His servants answered with a question: *"My father, it is a great word the prophet has spoken to you; will you not do it? Has he actually said to you, 'Wash, and be clean'?"* (5:13). He went down, and *"his flesh was restored like the flesh of a little child"* (5:14). A measure of "better" nearly cost him the cure, and a question let him lay it down.
- **The king's eyes, or God's.** Saul proposed to pursue by night, "And they said, 'Do whatever seems good to you.' But the priest said, 'Let us draw near to God here'" (1 Samuel 14:36). God did not answer that day (14:37). When Saul swore that the guilty would die "though it be in Jonathan my son", "there was not a man among all the people who answered him", and then again, "Do what seems good to you" (14:39–40). The people give the king's eyes as the measure. The priest asks for God's first.
- **Another's will, given the whole decision.** Haman asks, "If it please the king, let it be decreed that they be destroyed" (Esther 3:9). The king gives him his ring and says, "The money is given to you, the people also, to do with them as it seems good to you" (3:11). Later the same king says to Esther and Mordecai, "you may write as you please with regard to the Jews … for an edict written in the name of the king and sealed with the king's ring cannot be revoked" (8:8). The measure is handed over twice, and the first handing cannot be undone.
- **The king's pleasure, asked for.** The same words come from the asking side. Nehemiah, asked what he was requesting, first "prayed to the God of heaven", then said, "If it pleases the king, and if your servant has found favor in your sight, that you send me to Judah" (Nehemiah 2:4–5). When it was granted he named another measure behind the king's: "And the king granted me what I asked, for the good hand of my God was upon me" (2:8). Memucan put his counsel against Vashti the same way, "If it please the king, let a royal order go out from him" (Esther 1:19), but what drove it was the fear that the women would "look at their husbands with contempt" (1:17). Esther kept the form after the king had offered "even to the half of my kingdom" (5:3): "If it please the king, let the king and Haman come today to a feast that I have prepared for the king" (5:4), and again when he asked her a second time (9:12–13). I read the form as leaving the decision with the king each time, even when he had offered to hand it over. What stands behind the asking differs: prayer, the fear of contempt, silver (Haman, above), a life (7:3).

"Good in your eyes" is not always the wrong measure. The king says *"whatever seems good to you"* to the old man who had fed him (2 Samuel 19:38), and there the chooser's own eyes are honoured. The setting changes what the same expression means (see *What changes the character*, below).

## Choosing before God

In these verses a person's choice is not the first move. It is made in front of a God who has already acted.
- At Shechem the choice comes after eleven verses of what the Lord did, beginning *"I took your father Abraham from beyond the River"* (Joshua 24:3).
- In Isaiah 65 the wrong choice is made in front of a God who says *"Here I am, here I am"* and *"I spread out my hands all the day to a rebellious people"* (65:1–2).
- At the council in Jerusalem the church's choosing follows Peter's word that *"God made a choice among you"* (Acts 15:7), in the same verb.

The verses also name God at work in a person's choosing, and set it beside the person's own accord without setting the two against each other:
- *"thanks be to God, who put into the heart of Titus the same earnest care I have for you"*, and *"being himself very earnest he is going to you of his own accord"* (2 Corinthians 8:16–17)
- the Macedonians gave *"of their own accord"*, and *"they gave themselves first to the Lord and then by the will of God to us"* (8:3, 5)
- the church's choice is joined to the Spirit's: *"it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us"* (Acts 15:28)
- the psalmist chooses, and asks God for the room to carry it out: *"I will run in the way of your commandments when you enlarge my heart!"* (Psalm 119:32)

In 2 Corinthians 8, I read the earnest care God put into Titus's heart as becoming Titus's own: the same passage calls it both. The verses name both and do not explain how they fit.

A choice can be left wholly to God. David, fleeing Absalom, sends the ark back: "If I find favor in the eyes of the Lord, he will bring me back and let me see both it and his dwelling place. But if he says, 'I have no pleasure in you,' behold, here I am, let him do to me what seems good to him" (2 Samuel 15:25–26). The act is yielding. He does not presume God's pleasure, and he does not keep the ark to secure it (13.1).

Eli yields after the word has been spoken. He made Samuel tell him all of it, "Do not hide it from me" (1 Samuel 3:17), and when he had heard the judgment on his house, "he said, 'It is the Lord. Let him do what seems good to him'" (3:18). David yields before he knows what God will do. Eli yields once he knows.

A course can change when God's pleasure is seen. "When Balaam saw that it pleased the Lord to bless Israel, he did not go, as at other times, to look for omens, but set his face toward the wilderness" (Numbers 24:1). He had gone aside before, "as at other times". Now that he sees what pleases the Lord, he does not go, and he sets his face. The next verse: "And the Spirit of God came upon him" (24:2). The Lord's pleasure itself is in 13.1.

## Being chosen
