The verb a person uses to choose is also used when God chooses a person. Then the one who chooses is God. In these verses the inner life of the one chosen is not what made them chosen. It is what the choosing is for, and what follows from it.

**The choosing comes first.** When God chooses, the verses put the inner life of the chosen after the choosing, as its purpose:
- *"my servant whom I have chosen, that you may know and believe me and understand that I am he"* (Isaiah 43:10). The witnesses he chose are *"the people who are blind, yet have eyes, who are deaf, yet have ears"* (43:8).
- *"he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him"* (Ephesians 1:4).
- *"has not God chosen those who are poor in the world to be rich in faith"* (James 2:5).
- *"Blessed is the one you choose and bring near"* (Psalm 65:4) comes straight after *"When iniquities prevail against me, you atone for our transgressions"* (65:3).

One verse names God's choosing and a person's belief together: *"God chose you as the firstfruits to be saved, through sanctification by the Spirit and belief in the truth"* (2 Thessalonians 2:13). It does not say how the two fit.

When people choose a person, the order is the other way. The gathering in Jerusalem was told to *"pick out from among you seven men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom"* (Acts 6:3), and they chose Stephen, *"a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit"* (6:5). They chose by what was already seen in him. It was seen in him to the end: *"full of the Holy Spirit"*, he prayed for those who stoned him, *"Lord, do not hold this sin against them"* (7:55, 60).

**What the chosen are moved to.** The verses set an inner response beside being chosen. Twice they name the choosing as its ground.
- **Celebrating.** David, rebuked by Michal for dancing before the ark: *"It was before the Lord, who chose me above your father and above all his house … and I will celebrate before the Lord"* (2 Samuel 6:21). Her measure was the eyes of the servants (6:20). His was the Lord. Being chosen had not kept him from being angry, afraid and unwilling when Uzzah died (6:8–10).
- **Not fearing.** *"Fear not, O Jacob my servant, Jeshurun whom I have chosen"* (Isaiah 44:2). The ground is who chose him: *"the Lord who made you, who formed you from the womb and will help you"*.
- **Satisfaction.** *"We shall be satisfied with the goodness of your house, the holiness of your temple!"* (Psalm 65:4).
- **Joy and singing.** *"So he brought his people out with joy, his chosen ones with singing"* (Psalm 105:43).
- **Gladness that another asks to share.** *"that I may rejoice in the gladness of your nation"* (Psalm 106:5). He asks it while confessing *"Both we and our fathers have sinned"* (106:6).

**What the chosen are called to.** Being chosen is given as the ground of commands:
- **Be strong and do it.** *"the Lord has chosen you to build a house for the sanctuary; be strong and do it"* (1 Chronicles 28:10), with *"serve him with a whole heart and with a willing mind, for the Lord searches all hearts"* (28:9).
- **Put on.** *"Put on then, as God's chosen ones, holy and beloved, compassionate hearts, kindness, humility, meekness, and patience"* (Colossians 3:12). What is put on is turned toward others: *"as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive"* (3:13); *"above all these put on love"* (3:14).
- **Stand firm.** *"stand firm and hold to the traditions that you were taught by us"* (2 Thessalonians 2:15).
- **Confirm it.** *"be all the more diligent to confirm your calling and election, for if you practice these qualities you will never fall"* (2 Peter 1:10). The qualities are added one to another, from faith to love (1:5–7). The effort follows what was given first: *"His divine power has granted to us all things that pertain to life and godliness"* (1:3).
- **Remember.** *"Remember the wondrous works that he has done … children of Jacob, his chosen ones!"* (Psalm 105:5–6); *"Remember these things, O Jacob … you will not be forgotten by me"* (Isaiah 44:21).

**Standing for others.** The chosen can stand between God and people who have turned from him. After the calf, *"he said he would destroy them—had not Moses, his chosen one, stood in the breach before him, to turn away his wrath from destroying them"* (Psalm 106:23). The psalm calls Moses chosen at the very point where he stands for people who *"forgot God, their Savior"* (106:21). It also says what those people did to him. They *"were jealous of Moses"* (106:16), and later *"they made his spirit bitter, and he spoke rashly with his lips"* (106:33). Standing for them did not keep him from being embittered by them. The anger he turned away is taken up in 10.13.

**Faith, and the truth.** Several verses name faith, and knowing the truth, for the chosen:
- *"the faith of God's elect and their knowledge of the truth, which accords with godliness"* (Titus 1:1)
- *"rich in faith"* (James 2:5)
- *"belief in the truth"* (2 Thessalonians 2:13)

For people already chosen, Paul prays for *"the eyes of your hearts enlightened, that you may know what is the hope to which he has called you"* (Ephesians 1:18). Faith is shown in what it does: *"faith by itself, if it does not have works, is dead"* (James 2:17).

**Being chosen is not a guarantee.** The verses say plainly that the chosen can fail:
- **A condition.** *"if you forsake him, he will cast you off forever"* (1 Chronicles 28:9).
- **Forgetting and despising.** The chosen people *"soon forgot his works"* and *"despised the pleasant land, having no faith in his promise"* (Psalm 106:13, 24). "Despised" is the refusing verb of Isaiah 7:15.
- **Not calling.** *"Yet you did not call upon me, O Jacob; but you have been weary of me, O Israel!"* (Isaiah 43:22).
- **Blindness.** Whoever lacks the qualities is *"so nearsighted that he is blind, having forgotten that he was cleansed from his former sins"* (2 Peter 1:9).

The way back is the Lord's remembering: *"For their sake he remembered his covenant"* (Psalm 106:45); *"I, I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins"* (Isaiah 43:25).

**Set against others.** In each passage the chosen stand beside others who choose otherwise, or cannot see:
- the idol-maker, whose heart is shut *"so that they cannot understand"* (Isaiah 44:18)
- those who *"refused to love the truth"* and *"had pleasure in unrighteousness"* (2 Thessalonians 2:10, 12)
- those who *"profess to know God, but they deny him by their works"* (Titus 1:16)
- an assembly that seats the rich and sends the poor to stand, having *"become judges with evil thoughts"* (James 2:4). God chose the poor: *"But you have dishonored the poor man"* (2:6).
- kings who *"are of one mind"* with the beast, against *"those with him"*, who *"are called and chosen and faithful"* (Revelation 17:13–14)

## Others around a choice

A choice does not stay between the one who chooses and the one chosen. Others stand near it: at the place God chose, turned toward it from far away, set against the person chosen, standing with them, or knowing that a choice was made. The verses seldom say what these others feel about the choosing itself. They say what they are to do and be around it, and what moves them.

**At the place God chose.** When God chooses a place, the people are not told to admire it. They are told what to be there. They are to rejoice: *"you shall rejoice before the Lord your God in all that you undertake"* (Deuteronomy 12:18). The joy rests on the blessing, not on the place: *"in which the Lord your God has blessed you"* (12:7). At the Feast of Booths the joy is what the blessing is for: *"because the Lord your God will bless you … so that you will be altogether joyful"* (16:15). The joy is never had alone. The servants, the Levite, *"the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow"* are named in it (16:11), and the one rejoicing is told in the next breath, *"You shall remember that you were a slave in Egypt"* (16:12).

Fear is learned there too, at a meal: *"that you may learn to fear the Lord your God always"* (Deuteronomy 14:23). In the same passage the people spend their money *"for whatever you desire … whatever your appetite craves"*, and *"eat there before the Lord your God and rejoice"* (14:26). Fear of the Lord, a satisfied appetite and joy belong to the one meal, and the passage does not set them against each other. When a case is *"too difficult for you"*, the decision is sought at the place, and what is asked is *"you shall be careful to do according to all that they direct you"* (17:8, 10). Presumption is the opposite, and its end is that *"all the people shall hear and fear and not act presumptuously again"* (17:13). I read this as a person's own judgement reaching its limit and being asked to yield. The passage names the limit and the carefulness, not the struggle.

**Desire, near and far.** The soul's desire comes in twice, turned two ways. Away from the place it is given room. If the place is too far, *"you may eat within your towns whenever you desire"* (Deuteronomy 12:21). In the same words, desire draws a man to the place: a Levite *"may come when he desires"*, literally with all the desire of his soul, *"to the place that the Lord will choose"* (18:6). His coming is left to that desire. It is the account of wanting (10.6) seen from beside a choice.

**Turned toward it from far off.** For people far from the chosen city, the city is the direction of their prayer. Solomon's prayer takes the hardest case: the people in captivity because they sinned, *"for there is no one who does not sin"* (1 Kings 8:46). The turning happens in the enemy's land, in steps. First *"if they turn their heart"*, then words, *"We have sinned and have acted perversely and wickedly"* (8:47), then *"if they repent with all their heart and with all their soul … and pray to you toward … the city that you have chosen"* (8:48). "Turn" and "repent" are the one verb. Solomon prays it to the one who alone knows hearts (8:39), and he asks God himself to *"incline our hearts to him"* (8:58). Nehemiah prays from exile in the same verb, holding God to his word: *"if you return to me and keep my commandments and do them, … I will gather them and bring them to the place that I have chosen"* (Nehemiah 1:9). The return is to God, and the place is where he brings those who return.

**Set against the one chosen.** Several passages show others turning on someone chosen, and each names what moves them.
- **Grumbling, and seeking more.** When God's choice of Aaron was challenged, Moses named what lay under it: *"would you seek the priesthood also? … What is Aaron that you grumble against him?"* (Numbers 16:10–11). Psalm 106 calls it jealousy (106:16). God counts the grumbling as against himself, and makes his choice plain *"to cease from me the grumblings"* (Numbers 17:5). Once it was plain, the grumbling turned to terror: *"Are we all to perish?"* (17:13).
- **Anger at what a choice costs.** Saul's anger is kindled against Jonathan: *"do I not know that you have chosen the son of Jesse to your own shame"* (1 Samuel 20:30). He gives his reason: *"neither you nor your kingdom shall be established"* (20:31). The anger is for his house, and it ends in a spear thrown at his own son (20:33). Jonathan chose in love, *"for he loved him as he loved his own soul"* (20:17). His anger in reply is grief for the one he chose: *"he was grieved for David, because his father had disgraced him"* (20:34). He keeps the choice, and seals it with an oath in the name of the Lord (20:42).
- **Contempt in the heart.** Michal *"saw King David leaping and dancing before the Lord, and she despised him in her heart"* (2 Samuel 6:16). It was inward before it was spoken, and when it came out its measure was the servants' eyes (6:20).
- **Despised and abhorred.** The servant is addressed as *"one deeply despised, abhorred by the nation"* (Isaiah 49:7), in the same verb as Michal's. The same verse turns it round, not by anything the servant does: *"Kings shall see and arise … because of the Lord, who is faithful, … who has chosen you"*.
- **A verdict drawn from ruin.** People looked at the chosen in their ruin and said *"The Lord has rejected the two clans that he chose"*, and so *"despised my people so that they are no longer a nation in their sight"* (Jeremiah 33:24).
- **Hatred.** *"because you are not of the world, but I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you"* (John 15:19). The world loves *"its own"*. The verse names the choosing as the cause. The passage says the hatred fell first on Jesus (15:18), and puts under it *"because they do not know him who sent me"* (15:21).
- **Rejection after testing.** *"a living stone rejected by men but in the sight of God chosen and precious"* (1 Peter 2:4).

**With the chosen, and for them.** Others stand with the chosen too. The psalmist asks to be let in: *"Remember me, O Lord, … that I may rejoice in the gladness of your nation"* (Psalm 106:4–5). He asks God, not the chosen, and he asks it confessing his sin (106:6). Paul writes in chains: *"I endure everything for the sake of the elect, that they also may obtain the salvation"* (2 Timothy 2:10). The elder loves the elect lady *"in truth"*, *"because of the truth that abides in us"* (2 John 1–2): the love rests on the truth, not on her being chosen. And whoever believes in the stone God chose *"will not be put to shame"* (1 Peter 2:6). For those who do not believe, the same stone is *"a stone of stumbling"* (2:8).

**Knowing that a choice was made, and not knowing.** Knowing of a choice can settle a quarrel. In the dispute at Jerusalem, Peter appeals to what they all know: *"you know that in the early days God made a choice among you, that by my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the gospel and believe"* (Acts 15:7). The purpose of God's choosing one man lay in others, that they would hear and believe, and their hearts were *"cleansed … by faith"* (15:9). The debate falls silent (15:12). Paul knows that the Thessalonians are chosen from what he saw happen: *"because our gospel came to you not only in word, but also in power and in the Holy Spirit and with full conviction"* (1 Thessalonians 1:4–5).

Not knowing does not stop God from using a man for the sake of the chosen. To Cyrus: *"For the sake of my servant Jacob, and Israel my chosen, I call you by your name, I name you, though you do not know me"* (Isaiah 45:4). Knowing is still held out to him: *"that you may know that it is I"* (45:3). Of those outside the chosen, Paul says *"Israel failed to obtain what it was seeking. The elect obtained it, but the rest were hardened"* (Romans 11:7). They were seeking, and did not see. He refuses at once to make it the end: *"did they stumble in order that they might fall? By no means!"* (11:11).

**An inner act weighed by what God chooses.** In one passage what the others offer from within is set against God's own choosing. The people fast and complain, *"Why have we humbled ourselves, and you take no knowledge of it?"*, while *"in the day of your fast you seek your own pleasure, and oppress all your workers"* (Isaiah 58:3). God answers, *"Is such the fast that I choose, a day for a person to humble himself?"* (58:5). What he chooses is turned outward: *"to let the oppressed go free"*, *"to share your bread with the hungry"*, *"not to hide yourself from your own flesh"* (58:6–7). The humbling stood beside oppression in the same people, and it was not what he chooses. The same people *"delight to know my ways"* (58:2), in the same delight word as Isaiah 66:4 in *Whose measure*.

The same passage opens on what they appear to be doing: "Yet they seek me daily and delight to know my ways, as if they were a nation that did righteousness and did not forsake the judgment of their God; they ask of me righteous judgments; they delight to draw near to God" (Isaiah 58:2). The act is seeking and drawing near. Their delight measures how eager it is, and "as if" says what it lacks. I read that eagerness to draw near can sit beside oppressing workers (58:3) without the person seeing the two together.

Malachi has the same pairing of seeking and delight, and God answers it. The people had said, "Everyone who does evil is good in the sight of the Lord, and he delights in them", and asked, "Where is the God of justice?" (Malachi 2:17). The answer takes their own words: "And the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant in whom you delight, behold, he is coming" (3:1). Then: "But who can endure the day of his coming, and who can stand when he appears? For he is like a refiner's fire" (3:2). Their seeking and their delight are taken at their word, and the question turns back on them. I read a delight in what is asked for that has not yet faced what it asks. The comparison with Isaiah 58:2 is mine; each passage says its own part. His coming as refiner is in 13.1 (*Delight*).

**Rule offered, refused, and sought.** "Rule over us, you and your son and your grandson also, for you have saved us from the hand of Midian." Gideon refused: "I will not rule over you, and my son will not rule over you; the Lord will rule over you" (Judges 8:22–23). Daniel, offered a place as third ruler for reading the writing, refused the reward and did the task: "Let your gifts be for yourself, and give your rewards to another. Nevertheless, I will read the writing to the king and make known to him the interpretation" (Daniel 5:17). Gideon's son sought what his father refused, and won it by kinship. "Which is better for you, that all seventy of the sons of Jerubbaal rule over you, or that one rule over you? Remember also that I am your bone and your flesh." And "their hearts inclined to follow Abimelech, for they said, 'He is our brother'" (Judges 9:2–3). He then killed his seventy brothers (9:5). The verses set refusing and seeking side by side in one family, and say no more about why.

## Choosing together

A people can choose as one.
- Israel at Shechem: *"we will serve the Lord"*, and they become *"witnesses against yourselves"* (Joshua 24:21–22).
- The gathering in Jerusalem, out of being pleased (Acts 6:5).
- The church, *"having come to one accord"* (Acts 15:25).

Weighing a case together is also called choosing: *"Let us choose what is right; let us know among ourselves what is good"* (Job 34:4).

An assembly can be asked to choose with the Lord named in the asking. "If it seems good to you and from the Lord our God, let us send abroad to our brothers … Then let us bring again the ark of our God to us, for we did not seek it in the days of Saul" (1 Chronicles 13:2–3). "All the assembly agreed to do so, for the thing was right in the eyes of all the people" (13:4). Two measures are named in the asking, theirs and the Lord's. The verse that records the agreement names the people's eyes.

## A choice that is honoured

Choosing is a freedom a person can lose, and the law gives it back. The escaped slave *"shall dwell with you, in your midst, in the place that he shall choose within one of your towns, wherever it suits him. You shall not wrong him"* (Deuteronomy 23:16).

The king hands the choice to the man who fed him in the wilderness: *"all that you desire of me I will do for you"* (2 Samuel 19:38). Barzillai had already weighed his own age: *"Can I discern what is pleasant and what is not?"* (19:35). His choice is still honoured.

A choice can be given back after a wrong. Warned by God in a dream, Abimelech returned Sarah, gave sheep, oxen and servants, and said, "Behold, my land is before you; dwell where it pleases you" (Genesis 20:15). To Sarah: "It is a sign of your innocence in the eyes of all who are with you, and before everyone you are vindicated" (20:16). The wrong is answered by giving the other the choice of where to live, and by clearing her before others.

## Choosing from weakness

The one who chooses in these verses is often low:
- **sorrow:** *"My soul melts away for sorrow"* (Psalm 119:28)
- **guilt and trouble:** *"pardon my guilt, for it is great"*; *"I am lonely and afflicted"* (Psalm 25:11, 16)
- **one's own verdict on oneself:** *"Behold, I am a dry tree"* (Isaiah 56:3). The Lord answers that verdict: *"I will give them an everlasting name that shall not be cut off"* (56:5).
- **age:** *"Can I discern what is pleasant and what is not?"* (2 Samuel 19:35)
- **affliction, as Elihu reads it:** *"this you have chosen rather than affliction"* (Job 36:21)

## Setting the heart

The choice at Shechem is spoken with the mouth, and Joshua does not take it as the whole. He calls at once for the heart: *"Then put away the foreign gods that are among you, and incline your heart to the Lord"* (Joshua 24:23). The people had just chosen the Lord, and the foreign gods were still among them. Samuel says it in nearly the same words: *"put away the foreign gods and the Ashtaroth from among you and direct your heart to the Lord and serve him only"* (1 Samuel 7:3). In both, putting something away goes with turning the heart.

Scripture speaks of the heart being set, inclined and directed, and of the state it is in:
- **Inclined, and asked for.** *"Incline my heart to your testimonies, and not to selfish gain!"* (Psalm 119:36). The one who prays this has just chosen (119:30), and asks God to do the inclining.
- **Whole or divided.** *"unite my heart to fear your name"* (Psalm 86:11), against *"a double heart"* (Psalm 12:2). Solomon's *"heart was not wholly true to the Lord his God"* (1 Kings 11:4).
- **Stubborn.** *"the stubbornness of their evil hearts"* runs through Jeremiah (Jeremiah 7:24).
- **Moved from within.** *"everyone whose heart stirred him, and everyone whose spirit moved him"* (Exodus 35:21) puts heart and spirit side by side in setting out to give.
- **Set, beside a wrong love.** Jehoshaphat was told, *"Should you help the wicked and love those who hate the Lord? Because of this, wrath has gone out against you from the Lord. Nevertheless, some good is found in you, for you destroyed the Asheroth out of the land, and have set your heart to seek God"* (2 Chronicles 19:2–3). A love wrongly given and a heart set to seek God stand in one king, and the prophet's verdict holds both.
- **Set to study, to do and to teach.** *"For Ezra had set his heart to study the Law of the Lord, and to do it and to teach his statutes and rules in Israel"* (Ezra 7:10). The setting has three steps, and the doing stands between the study and the teaching. The verse before ends *"for the good hand of his God was on him"* (7:9), and this one opens with *"For"*. I read the second *"For"* as giving the good hand its ground in Ezra's heart. Its opposite is Rehoboam, who *"did evil, for he did not set his heart to seek the Lord"* (2 Chronicles 12:14; 10.14).
- **Set as an aim.** The word for ambition is used three times by Paul, and its aims are not what ambition usually seeks: *"I make it my ambition to preach the gospel, not where Christ has already been named"* (Romans 15:20); *"whether we are at home or away, we make it our aim to please him. For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ"* (2 Corinthians 5:9–10); *"aspire to live quietly, and to mind your own affairs, and to work with your hands"* (1 Thessalonians 4:11). Also: *"If anyone aspires to the office of overseer, he desires a noble task"* (1 Timothy 3:1). I read the aims as going where no one has gone, pleasing him wherever one is, and quietness.

The heart's leaning is prayed against, and a rebuke is welcomed. "Do not let my heart incline to any evil, to busy myself with wicked deeds in company with men who work iniquity, and let me not eat of their delicacies! Let a righteous man strike me—it is a kindness; let him rebuke me—it is oil for my head; let my head not refuse it" (Psalm 141:4–5). The act is a prayer that the heart not lean, and a choice of the hard word over the sweet food. What he calls pleasant is his own words, to be heard when the judges fall: "then they shall hear my words, for they are pleasant" (141:6). The prayer ends, "But my eyes are toward you, O God, my Lord" (141:8).

## Holding a choice

A choice spoken is not yet a choice carried out, and the verses say so in several ways.
- **It binds the one who made it.** *"You are witnesses against yourselves that you have chosen the Lord"* (Joshua 24:22).
- **Choosing is not the same as being able.** *"You are not able to serve the Lord, for he is a holy God"* (Joshua 24:19). Joshua says this to people who have just chosen, and they answer *"No, but we will serve the Lord"* (24:21).
- **It is held by keeping it in view, and by clinging.** *"I have chosen the way of faithfulness; I set your rules before me. I cling to your testimonies, O Lord"* (Psalm 119:30–31). The verb for "cling" is the one used a few verses earlier: *"My soul clings to the dust"* (119:25). The one verb is used of the soul clinging to the dust and of the one who chose clinging to God's testimonies.
- **It is held by keeping and holding fast.** *"who keep my Sabbaths, who choose the things that please me and hold fast my covenant"* (Isaiah 56:4). The choice stands between a keeping and a holding on.
- **It is held while waiting.** *"May integrity and uprightness preserve me, for I wait for you"* (Psalm 25:21). The psalm ends still waiting and in trouble. The right choice has not ended the trouble.
- **Readiness has to be completed.** *"so that your readiness in desiring it may be matched by your completing it"* (2 Corinthians 8:11).
- **Those God has chosen are told to make it firm.** *"be all the more diligent to confirm your calling and election"* (2 Peter 1:10). See *Being chosen*.
- **It is held as a purpose set ahead.** *"I have purposed that my mouth will not transgress"* (Psalm 17:3). See *Planning*.
- **It can be guarded by another.** Mary *"sat at the Lord's feet and listened to his teaching"* (Luke 10:39). Martha asked Jesus to send her to help (10:40). He named what Mary was doing a choice, and kept it for her: *"Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken away from her"* (10:42).

The choice at Shechem held for a time: *"Israel served the Lord all the days of Joshua, and all the days of the elders who outlived Joshua and had known all the work that the Lord did for Israel"* (Joshua 24:31). The verse ties those years to people who had known the work the choice was made from. It gives the timing; it does not give the cause.

## Willing

Planning reaches ahead from the person. The will, in these verses, mostly answers what comes to the person. In the Hebrew narratives the word for being willing, *ʾāḇâ*, almost always stands just after someone has asked, urged, commanded, enticed, pleaded, warned or offered. And it is almost always a "no": *"would not"*, *"was not willing"*, *"would have none"*. In the Greek, the words for wanting and intending (*boulomai*, *boulēma*) belong to the same family as the words for planning and counsel. One of them, *boulēma*, is translated "plan" in one verse (Acts 27:43) and "will" in another (Romans 9:19). So the verses keep the will and the plan close, without making them one act.

**The will asked for.** Jesus asks people what they want.
- To blind men who had cried out against the crowd's rebuke: "What do you want me to do for you?" "Lord, let our eyes be opened." And "Jesus in pity touched their eyes" (Matthew 20:32–34). To Bartimaeus, the same question, and "your faith has made you well" (Mark 10:51–52).
- To a man ill for thirty-eight years: "Do you want to be healed?" He answers with what he lacks: "Sir, I have no one to put me into the pool" (John 5:6–7). He is healed without the pool (5:8).
- To James and John, who came saying "we want you to do for us whatever we ask of you": "What do you want me to do for you?" They asked for the places of honour, and he answered, "You do not know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I drink?" (Mark 10:35–38; Matthew 20:21–22).
- To the twelve, when many turned back: "Do you want to go away as well?" "Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life" (John 6:67–68).
The same question is answered with sight, with a lack, with ambition and with staying. I read the question as drawing the will out into words, where it can be met.

**A will redirected.** Jesus takes the will to be first and the will to follow, and turns them.
- The disciples "had argued with one another about who was the greatest". "If anyone would be first, he must be last of all and servant of all" (Mark 9:34–35). "whoever would be first among you must be slave of all. For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve" (Mark 10:44–45; Matthew 20:27–28).
- After Peter was told "you are not setting your mind on the things of God": "If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me. For whoever would save his life will lose it" (Matthew 16:23–25; Mark 8:34–35; Luke 9:23–24, "daily").
The will is not removed. Its aim is named, wanting to be first, wanting to save one's life, and it is given another way to that end.

**The will meets something put before it.** What is put forward varies:
- a request: *"Please let us pass through your land," but the king of Edom would not listen* (Judges 11:17)
- pressing, day after day, until *"the man would not spend the night"* (Judges 19:7–10)
- a command: Saul's guard *"would not put out their hand to strike the priests of the Lord"* (1 Samuel 22:17)
- an enticement, even from the nearest: *"your friend who is as your own soul entices you secretly … you shall not yield to him"* (Deuteronomy 13:6–8); *"My son, if sinners entice you, do not consent"* (Proverbs 1:10)
- a demand, answered with a line drawn: *"All that you first demanded of your servant I will do, but this thing I cannot do"* (1 Kings 20:9), after the elders said *"Do not listen or consent"* (20:8)
- a plea, and the stronger one shutting it out: Tamar said *"No, my brother, do not violate me"*, *"But he would not listen to her, and being stronger than she, he violated her"* (2 Samuel 13:12, 14)
- a warning: Abner told Asahel twice to turn aside, *"But he refused to turn aside"*, and he died (2 Samuel 2:21–23)
- a feast: the older brother *"was angry and refused to go in. His father came out and entreated him"* (Luke 15:28). His anger took the form of a will that would not go in, and the father did not wait inside for it to change (10.13).
- a wedding feast: "they would not come", and again, "they paid no attention and went off, one to his farm, another to his business" (Matthew 22:3, 5)
- a plea for patience: "Have patience with me, and I will pay you." "He refused and went and put him in prison" (Matthew 18:29–30), he who had been forgiven all his debt (18:32)
- a reign: "his citizens hated him and sent a delegation after him, saying, 'We do not want this man to reign over us'" (Luke 19:14)
- a threat: "He would not go about in Judea, because the Jews were seeking to kill him" (John 7:1), and his brothers urged him to go (7:3)
- an urging between friends: "I strongly urged him to visit you … but it was not at all his will to come now. He will come when he has opportunity" (1 Corinthians 16:12)

**The "no" can keep faith, and it can do violence.** The verb does not tell you which; the passage does, and it gives the reason every time.
- The king's servants would not kill the priests, and Doeg did (1 Samuel 22:17–18).
- David would not *"put out my hand against the Lord's anointed"*. He prayed that, as Saul's life had been precious in his sight, his own would be precious in the Lord's (26:23–24).
- The water from Bethlehem shows it most fully. David *"said longingly, 'Oh, that someone would give me water to drink'"* (2 Samuel 23:15). Three men broke through the Philistine camp to bring it. *"But he would not drink of it. He poured it out to the Lord and said, 'Far be it from me, O Lord, that I should do this. Shall I drink the blood of the men who went at the risk of their lives?'"* (23:16–17). His own longing was met, and he refused it for their sake, aloud and before the Lord (10.6 follows wanting).
- Against that stands Amnon's "would not" (2 Samuel 13:14), and the men of Gibeah who *"would not listen"* (Judges 19:25).
- Those who lay burdens on others "are not willing to move them with their finger" (Matthew 23:4), for "they preach, but do not practice" (23:3).
- At the cross Jesus was offered "wine to drink, mixed with gall, but when he tasted it, he would not drink it" (Matthew 27:34).

The same verb is used for a refusal that honours other people and for a refusal that tramples them.

**A refusal can be selective.** Saul and the people *"spared Agag and the best of the sheep … and would not utterly destroy them. All that was despised and worthless they devoted to destruction"* (1 Samuel 15:9). They refused only where they valued what they kept. God's word on it was *"he has turned back from following me"*, and *"Samuel was angry, and he cried to the Lord all night"* (15:11).

**Wanting to go back.** "But now that you have come to know God, or rather to be known by God, how can you turn back again to the weak and worthless elementary principles of the world, whose slaves you want to be once more?" (Galatians 4:9). "Tell me, you who desire to be under the law, do you not listen to the law?" (4:21). Paul is "afraid I may have labored over you in vain" (4:11). After the defeat at Ai, when "the hearts of the people melted", Joshua said, "Would that we had been content to dwell beyond the Jordan!" (Joshua 7:5, 7). In a figure: "no one after drinking old wine desires new, for he says, 'The old is good'" (Luke 5:39). I read the will turning back toward what it knew, even toward slavery, when the new has cost something.

**Content to stay.** "Moses was content to dwell with the man" (Exodus 2:21), and he named his son for being "a sojourner in a foreign land" (2:22). "the Levite was content to dwell with the man", and Micah said, "Now I know that the Lord will prosper me, because I have a Levite as priest" (Judges 17:11, 13). The same willingness to stay sits in two very different settings, and the verses say what each led to.

**Feeling holds the will.**
- Fear stops it. The armor-bearer *"would not, for he feared greatly"* (1 Samuel 31:4). David *"was afraid of the Lord that day … So David was not willing to take the ark"* (2 Samuel 6:9–10). Three months later *"it was told King David, 'The Lord has blessed the household of Obed-edom'"*, and he *"went and brought up the ark of God … with rejoicing"* (6:12). What he heard moved his will.
- Melted hearts stop it: *"Yet you would not go up"* (Deuteronomy 1:26), and *"Our brothers have made our hearts melt"* (1:28).
- Grief holds it. David, fasting for the child, *"would not"* rise or eat (2 Samuel 12:17).
- Jealousy fixes it: *"He will accept no compensation; he will refuse though you multiply gifts"* (Proverbs 6:35).

10.12 and 10.1 take these feelings up.

**Refusing God refuses something good.** The passages say what was offered:
- the land: *"It is a good land"* (Deuteronomy 1:25), and *"Yet you would not go up"* (1:26)
- rest: *"This is rest; give rest to the weary; and this is repose"; yet they would not hear* (Isaiah 28:12); and *"ask for the ancient paths, where the good way is; and walk in it, and find rest for your souls. But they said, 'We will not walk in it'"* (Jeremiah 6:16)
- the one who brought God's word: *"He received living oracles to give to us. Our fathers refused to obey him, but thrust him aside, and in their hearts they turned to Egypt"* (Acts 7:38–39)
- being filled: *"Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it." But … Israel would not submit to me* (Psalm 81:10–11)
- his Spirit and his words: *"If you turn at my reproof, behold, I will pour out my spirit to you"* (Proverbs 1:23)
- life itself, from the one who gives it: *"yet you refuse to come to me that you may have life"* (John 5:40). Here the passage says what lies behind the refusal. They had searched the Scriptures (5:39), so it was not that they did not know. *"But I know that you do not have the love of God within you … How can you believe, when you receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from the only God?"* (5:42, 44). The will refused because the desire was set on glory from people.
- being gathered: "How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!" (Matthew 23:37; Luke 13:34). His will and theirs stand in one verb (13.1).
- a light received only for a while: "He was a burning and shining lamp, and you were willing to rejoice for a while in his light" (John 5:35)

- cleansing, after reasoning: *"Come now, let us reason together … though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow … If you are willing and obedient, you shall eat the good of the land; but if you refuse and rebel, you shall be eaten by the sword"* (Isaiah 1:18–20)

Isaiah 1 invites the will with an "if", and both ways are set before it, as life and death are in the next section. Jesus does the same. A young man asked about doing: *"Teacher, what good deed must I do to have eternal life?"* He was answered with the will: *"If you would enter life, keep the commandments"* (Matthew 19:16–17). He had kept them, and still asked, *"What do I still lack?"* He was answered with the will again: *"If you would be perfect, go, sell what you possess and give to the poor … and come, follow me"* (19:20–21). *"When the young man heard this he went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions"* (19:22). He knew what he lacked. Asked for the thing he held, his will would not, and the sorrow is what that felt like. The disciples ask, *"Who then can be saved?"*, and are told, *"With man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible"* (19:25–26). *A will under another*, below, ends in the same place.

**Where willing and planning are named together.** In three passages the refusal of God stands with the person's own counsel, devices or plan:
- *"Because they hated knowledge and did not choose the fear of the Lord, would have none of my counsel and despised all my reproof, therefore they shall eat the fruit of their way, and have their fill of their own devices"* (Proverbs 1:29–31). Not choosing, not willing, and one's own devices stand in one sentence.
- *"Israel would not submit to me. So I gave them over to their stubborn hearts, to follow their own counsels"* (Psalm 81:11–12).
- Isaiah 30 opens with *"stubborn children … who carry out a plan, but not mine"* (30:1). It ends: *"In returning and rest you shall be saved; in quietness and in trust shall be your strength." But you were unwilling, and you said, "No! We will flee upon horses"* (30:15–16). The refusal and their own plan come out of their mouth together.

I read these three as Scripture's own picture of the acts working together when they go wrong: the "no" to God, and a plan of one's own in its place. The verses say what follows: being given over, and being filled with one's own devices. They do not lay out a sequence that every person goes through.

The same pairing is shown going right. David gives Solomon the plan for the temple, *"all the work to be done according to the plan"* (1 Chronicles 28:19), and then says, *"with you in all the work will be every willing man who has skill"* (28:21). A plan comes from God, and the willing carry it out.

**A plan meets another person's will.**
- It can allow for it. Abraham's servant looks ahead: *"Perhaps the woman may not be willing to follow me"* (Genesis 24:5). Abraham answers with what God will do, *"he will send his angel before you"*, and with a way out, *"if the woman is not willing … you will be free from this oath"* (24:7–8).
- It can turn when its own cost appears, and another can bind himself instead. The nearer redeemer first says of Naomi's land, *"I will redeem it"* (Ruth 4:4). Told that Ruth comes with it, he says, *"I cannot redeem it for myself, lest I impair my own inheritance"* (4:6). It is the same man in the same scene, and his will turns when his own inheritance is touched. Boaz had left room for that will and had bound his own: *"if he is not willing to redeem you, then, as the Lord lives, I will redeem you"* (3:13). Ruth's choice frames it: *"you have not gone after young men"* (3:10). One will is bound to self-interest, one by an oath, and one, Ruth's, is given in kindness.
- It can press it until it gives way. Absalom invited the king, who *"would not go"*. Then *"Absalom pressed him until he let Amnon and all the king's sons go with him"* (2 Samuel 13:25, 27). The plan ended in Amnon's death (13:28). When Joab *"would not come"* twice, Absalom set his field on fire (14:29–30).
- It can bend to a crowd. Pilate had said, *"I find no guilt in him"* (John 18:38). Then, *"wishing to satisfy the crowd"*, he *"released for them Barabbas"* (Mark 15:15).
- It can try, and give way. Pilate asked, "Whom do you want me to release for you: Barabbas, or Jesus who is called Christ? For he knew that it was out of envy that they had delivered him up" (Matthew 27:17–18). He spoke again, "desiring to release Jesus" (Luke 23:20), and asked, "Why? What evil has he done?" (Matthew 27:23). "And their voices prevailed" (Luke 23:23). "he delivered Jesus over to their will" (23:25).
- It can bend to please. Felix, "desiring to do the Jews a favor, … left Paul in prison" (Acts 24:27), after hoping "that money would be given him by Paul" (24:26). Festus, "wishing to do the Jews a favor", asked Paul to be tried in Jerusalem, and Paul appealed to Caesar (25:9–11).
- It can stand against a plan. The centurion, *"wishing to save Paul, kept them from carrying out their plan"* (Acts 27:43).
- Others can hold it back or help it on. *"when Paul wished to go in among the crowd, the disciples would not let him"* (Acts 19:30). *"when he wished to cross to Achaia, the brothers encouraged him"* (18:27).
- It can be held back by the owner of the field. "Then do you want us to go and gather them?" "No, lest in gathering the weeds you root up the wheat along with them" (Matthew 13:28–29).

**A will bound by an oath before guests.** Herod "feared John, knowing that he was a righteous and holy man … When he heard him, he was greatly perplexed, and yet he heard him gladly" (Mark 6:20). At his banquet he said to the girl, "Ask me for whatever you wish, and I will give it to you" (6:22). Her mother chose for her, and she asked "with haste": "I want you to give me at once the head of John the Baptist on a platter" (6:24–25). "And the king was exceedingly sorry, but because of his oaths and his guests he did not want to break his word to her" (6:26). His grief and his will pulled two ways, and the oath and the watching guests decided it.

**A resolve is still being weighed.** Joseph, *"being a just man and unwilling to put her to shame, resolved to divorce her quietly. But as he considered these things, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream"* (Matthew 1:19–20). He was unwilling to shame her, then he resolved, then he went on considering, and God spoke into the considering. Herod's intending went the other way. He was *"intending after the Passover to bring him out to the people. So Peter was kept in prison, but earnest prayer for him was made to God by the church"* (Acts 12:4–5). The intention was not carried out.

**The will steers.** *"Look at the ships also: though they are so large and are driven by strong winds, they are guided by a very small rudder wherever the will of the pilot directs"* (James 3:4). James uses the picture for the tongue (3:5; 10.5). In the picture, the will is what sets a whole ship's course.

**The will turned toward harm.** *"those who desire to be rich fall into temptation, into a snare"* (1 Timothy 6:9). Against this Paul sets *"godliness with contentment is great gain"* (6:6). *"whoever wishes to be a friend of the world makes himself an enemy of God"* (James 4:4), said after *"your passions are at war within you"* (4:1).

The will to harm can be stopped short. "Get away from here, for Herod wants to kill you." Jesus answered, "Go and tell that fox … I must go on my way today and tomorrow and the day following" (Luke 13:31–33). "Some of them wanted to arrest him, but no one laid hands on him", and the officers said, "No one ever spoke like this man!" (John 7:44–46). A man wronging his neighbour turned the will on Moses: "Do you want to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?" (Acts 7:28), and Moses fled (7:29). A people can be set on what ruins it: "Ephraim is oppressed, crushed in judgment, because he was determined to go after filth" (Hosea 5:11).

**The will set on godliness.** *"Indeed, all who desire to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted"* (2 Timothy 3:12). It is the same verb as *"those who desire to be rich"*. The desire for riches falls into a snare. The desire for godliness walks into persecution. Paul does not promise that the godly will has an easy road. He sets it beside his own sufferings: *"yet from them all the Lord rescued me"* (3:11).

**The willing heart.** The will can also be given freely, and the verses say where that comes from.
- At the tabernacle, *"they came, everyone whose heart stirred him, and everyone whose spirit moved him"* (Exodus 35:21; see *Setting the heart*). *"All who were of a willing heart brought"* (35:22).
- Of the craftsmen, the skill given and the heart that moves are named together: *"every craftsman in whose mind the Lord had put skill, everyone whose heart stirred him up to come to do the work"* (Exodus 36:2).
- After consecration, *"all who were of a willing heart brought burnt offerings"* (2 Chronicles 29:31).
- At the gifts for the temple, *"the people rejoiced because they had given willingly, for with a whole heart they had offered freely to the Lord. David the king also rejoiced greatly"* (1 Chronicles 29:9). David says of his own gift, *"In the uprightness of my heart I have freely offered all these things, and now I have seen your people, who are present here, offering freely and joyously to you"* (29:17).
- In battle: *"My heart goes out to the commanders of Israel who offered themselves willingly among the people. Bless the Lord"* (Judges 5:9).
- Of the churches' gift for Jerusalem: *"For they were pleased to do it, and indeed they owe it to them"* (Romans 15:27).
- It is also asked of God: *"Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me … uphold me with a willing spirit"* (Psalm 51:10, 12). The next verse goes on: *"Then I will teach transgressors your ways, and sinners will return to you"* (51:13).

So the willing heart is said both to rise in the person and to be upheld by God. Paul guards the freedom of another's will. He would have liked to keep Onesimus, *"but I preferred to do nothing without your consent in order that your goodness might not be by compulsion but of your own accord"* (Philemon 13–14).

The verses on freely offering say more about where it comes from.
- **Asked for, then given.** "Who then will offer willingly, consecrating himself today to the Lord?" (1 Chronicles 29:5). "Then the leaders of fathers' houses made their freewill offerings" (29:6). David prays over it: "But who am I, and what is my people, that we should be able thus to offer willingly? For all things come from you, and of your own have we given you" (29:14), and "all this abundance … comes from your hand and is all your own" (29:16).
- **Stirred, and helped by others.** "everyone whose spirit God had stirred to go up to rebuild", and those about them "aided them … besides all that was freely offered" (Ezra 1:5–6). Some "made freewill offerings for the house of God … according to their ability" (2:68–69).
- **Even from a foreign king.** "the silver and gold that the king and his counselors have freely offered to the God of Israel", with "the freewill offerings of the people and the priests, vowed willingly" (Ezra 7:15–16). The same decree lets "anyone … who freely offers to go to Jerusalem" go (7:13).
- **Offering oneself.** "That the leaders took the lead in Israel, that the people offered themselves willingly, bless the Lord!" (Judges 5:2). "a volunteer for the service of the Lord" (2 Chronicles 17:16). After lots were cast for who would live in Jerusalem, "the people blessed all the men who willingly offered to live in Jerusalem" (Nehemiah 11:1–2).
- **Readiness, and what it is measured by.** "a year ago started not only to do this work but also to desire to do it. So now finish doing it as well, so that your readiness in desiring it may be matched by your completing it out of what you have. For if the readiness is there, it is acceptable according to what a person has, not according to what he does not have" (2 Corinthians 8:10–12). The gift is carried "to show our good will" (8:19).
I read the willing offering as answered by gladness and blessing in these verses, and measured by what a person has, not by its size.

**The will made absolute.** Of Nebuchadnezzar: *"Whom he would, he killed, and whom he would, he kept alive; whom he would, he raised up, and whom he would, he humbled"* (Daniel 5:19). The next verse says what happened inside him: *"But when his heart was lifted up and his spirit was hardened so that he dealt proudly, he was brought down"* (5:20). He had been offered counsel (4:27). He was driven out *"until he knew that the Most High God rules the kingdom of mankind and sets over it whom he will"* (5:21). His reason returned when he lifted his eyes to heaven (4:34). His son knew all this, and Daniel says to him, *"you his son, Belshazzar, have not humbled your heart, though you knew all this"* (5:22). Knowing did not move his will.

Daniel sees it again in a later king: *"And the king shall do as he wills. He shall exalt himself and magnify himself above every god … He shall prosper till the indignation is accomplished; for what is decreed shall be done"* (Daniel 11:36). The absolute will runs, and runs only until a time already set.

The will made absolute is seen from below as well. "a mighty king shall arise, who shall rule with great dominion and do as he wills. And as soon as he has arisen, his kingdom shall be broken" (Daniel 11:3–4). Another "shall do as he wills, and none shall stand before him" (11:16), until "a commander shall put an end to his insolence" (11:18). Under such rulers a people says, "They rule over our bodies and over our livestock as they please, and we are in great distress" (Nehemiah 9:37), and says it of kings set over them "because of our sins" (Nehemiah 9:37). The same prayer remembers the land given "that they might do with them as they would" (9:24), and what followed: "they ate and were filled … Nevertheless, they were disobedient" (9:25–26). Of Elijah: "they did not recognize him, but did to him whatever they pleased. So also the Son of Man will certainly suffer at their hands" (Matthew 17:12).

**A will that cannot carry itself out.** Paul speaks of a will that is real and wants the good, and does not carry itself out. "For I do not understand my own actions. For I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate. Now if I do what I do not want, I agree with the law, that it is good. So now it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells within me" (Romans 7:15–17). "For I have the desire to do what is right, but not the ability to carry it out. For I do not do the good I want, but the evil I do not want is what I keep on doing" (7:18–19). "So I find it to be a law that when I want to do right, evil lies close at hand" (7:21). He does not deny the will. He wants the good, he hates what he does, and his wanting agrees with the law. What does the opposite he calls "no longer I". I read the will here as a true inner act that is not master in its own house. The delight and the war in the members are in 10.1 (7:22–23), the cry in Chapter 2 (7:24), and the divided service in Chapter 7 (7:25).

**A will under another.** *"So then it depends not on human will or exertion, but on God, who has mercy"* (Romans 9:16). New birth is *"not of blood nor of the will of the flesh nor of the will of man, but of God"* (John 1:13). The will can be taught and filled: *"Teach me to do your will, for you are my God!"* (Psalm 143:10); Paul prays that the Colossians *"may be filled with the knowledge of his will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding"* (Colossians 1:9). Servants work *"as bondservants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart"* (Ephesians 6:6), where "heart" is the soul word. And at Gethsemane: *"Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done"* (Luke 22:42). God's will is in 13.1 (*Willing*).

Peter was told that his own will would be overruled at the end: *"when you were young, you used to dress yourself and walk wherever you wanted, but when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will dress you and carry you where you do not want to go"* (John 21:18). His next words were about someone else: *"Lord, what about this man?"* (21:21). The answer was *"If it is my will that he remain until I come, what is that to you? You follow me!"* (21:22). Told that his own will would be overruled, he turned to compare his lot with another's, and Christ's will answered both.

**Doing the will of God.** The verses speak of God's will as something a person prays, knows, does, or fails to do.
- **Prayed.** "Your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven" (Matthew 6:10). At Gethsemane, the second time: "My Father, if this cannot pass unless I drink it, your will be done" (26:42), after "The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak" (26:41). The words he taught are the words he prays.
- **Asked within.** "if we ask anything according to his will he hears us" (1 John 5:14). And: "If you abide in me, and my words abide in you, ask whatever you wish, and it will be done for you" (John 15:7). I read the two together: the asking is free where the asker's will has been shaped by his words.
- **Known by willing it.** "If anyone's will is to do God's will, he will know whether the teaching is from God" (John 7:17). The willing comes before the knowing. Paul was "appointed … to know his will" (Acts 22:14), and was asked at once, "And now why do you wait?" (22:16). "Do not be foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is" (Ephesians 5:17).
- **Known and not done.** "you … know his will and approve what is excellent" (Romans 2:18) is said to one who boasts in God and teaches others (2:17, 19–21). "And that servant who knew his master's will but did not get ready or act according to his will, will receive a severe beating" (Luke 12:47), more than the one who did not know (12:48).
- **Said, and not done.** "Not everyone who says to me, 'Lord, Lord,' will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven" (Matthew 7:21). Of two sons, one said "I will not, but afterward he changed his mind and went", the other "I will, sir, but did not go". "Which of the two did the will of his father?" (21:29–31). Jesus turns the changed mind toward belief: "you did not afterward change your minds and believe him" (21:32).
- **What it is, where the verses say.** "give thanks in all circumstances; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you" (1 Thessalonians 5:18). "For this is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from sexual immorality" (4:3), "not in the passion of lust like the Gentiles who do not know God" (4:5). "that by doing good you should put to silence the ignorance of foolish people" (1 Peter 2:15). After confession, "do his will. Separate yourselves" (Ezra 10:11).
- **With suffering, and with endurance.** "For it is better to suffer for doing good, if that should be God's will, than for doing evil" (1 Peter 3:17), and the next verse, "For Christ also suffered" (3:18). "For you have need of endurance, so that when you have done the will of God you may receive what is promised" (Hebrews 10:36).
- **Those who do it.** "For whoever does the will of my Father in heaven is my brother and sister and mother" (Matthew 12:50; Mark 3:35), said with his hand stretched toward his disciples. "if anyone is a worshiper of God and does his will, God listens to him" (John 9:31), said by the man who had been blind.
- **God working it in them.** "equip you with everything good that you may do his will, working in us that which is pleasing in his sight" (Hebrews 13:21). God "works in you, both to will and to work" (Philippians 2:13; 10.12). The renewed mind discerns "what is the will of God" (Romans 12:2; Chapter 14). Angels do it too (13.2).

The visions picture the same will. The ram "did as he pleased and became great" (Daniel 8:4), and the horn after it "became great, even as great as the Prince of the host" (8:11; 10.15).

blocks.section: Life and death set before a person
blocks.text:
## Life and death set before a person

Scripture sets life itself before the inner being as a choice. *"I have set before you life and death, blessing and curse. Therefore choose life, that you and your offspring may live"* (Deuteronomy 30:19). The passage says what choosing life is: *"loving the Lord your God, obeying his voice and holding fast to him, for he is your life and length of days"* (30:20). It describes the other way from inside: *"if your heart turns away, and you will not hear, but are drawn away to worship other gods and serve them"* (30:17). Before the choice is set out, it says the choice can be made: *"the word is very near you. It is in your mouth and in your heart, so that you can do it"* (30:14). Turning that chooses life is a considered act: *"Because he considered and turned away from all the transgressions that he had committed, he shall surely live; he shall not die"* (Ezekiel 18:28). Chapter 2 gives the account.

Death is set before the inner being in the same words: *"Behold, I set before you the way of life and the way of death"* (Jeremiah 21:8).
- **A way can seem right and still end there.** *"There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way to death"* (Proverbs 14:12).
- **A choice can be made with death in view.** Esau: *"I am about to die; of what use is a birthright to me?"* (Genesis 25:32).
- **A death can set the direction of a life.** *"he died for all, that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him who for their sake died and was raised"* (2 Corinthians 5:15).
- **A choice between two goods can stay open.** *"Yet which I shall choose I cannot tell. I am hard pressed between the two. My desire is to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better. But to remain in the flesh is more necessary on your account"* (Philippians 1:22–24). Paul does not settle it by choosing. He goes on: *"Convinced of this, I know that I will remain and continue with you all"* (1:25).

Plans are made inside a life that is brief. *"What is your life? For you are a mist that appears for a little time and then vanishes. Instead you ought to say, 'If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that.'"* (James 4:14–15). Some choices are about life itself:
- *"Do not work for the food that perishes, but for the food that endures to eternal life"* (John 6:27)
- *"For the gate is narrow and the way is hard that leads to life, and those who find it are few"* (Matthew 7:14)

Chapter 2 ("Breath lent", "Life set before a person") gives the setting.

## What follows a choice

In these verses the outcome of a choice reaches the inner being, whether the choice was right or wrong.

**When the choice is right:**
- *"His soul shall abide in well-being, and his offspring shall inherit the land"* (Psalm 25:13). "Well-being" is the same word as "the good" in *"choose the good"* (Isaiah 7:15).
- *"The friendship of the Lord is for those who fear him, and he makes known to them his covenant"* (Psalm 25:14). The upright are *"in his confidence"* (Proverbs 3:32), which is the same word as "friendship", in the verse after *"do not choose any of his ways"*.
- *"these I will bring to my holy mountain, and make them joyful in my house of prayer"* (Isaiah 56:7), with *"a name better than sons and daughters"* (56:5).
- At Antioch *"they rejoiced because of its encouragement"*, and the men chosen were *"sent off in peace"* (Acts 15:31, 33).
- Barzillai: *"the king kissed Barzillai and blessed him"* (2 Samuel 19:39).
- The child who refuses the evil and chooses the good eats *"curds and honey"* (Isaiah 7:15), the food of *"everyone who is left in the land"* (7:22).

**When the choice is wrong:**
- **Shame at the thing chosen.** *"you shall blush for the gardens that you have chosen"* (Isaiah 1:29); *"you shall be put to shame"* (65:13); *"it is they who shall be put to shame"* (66:5).
- **The heart and the spirit.** *"you shall cry out for pain of heart and shall wail for breaking of spirit"* (Isaiah 65:14).
- **Their own fears.** *"I also will choose harsh treatment for them and bring their fears upon them"* (Isaiah 66:4).
- **Filled with one's own ways.** *"The backslider in heart will be filled with the fruit of his ways, and a good man will be filled with the fruit of his ways"* (Proverbs 14:14). It is the same filling as *"have their fill of their own devices"* (Proverbs 1:31). The verse before it: *"Even in laughter the heart may ache"* (14:13).
- **Too late.** Esau "sold his birthright for a single meal. For you know that afterward, when he desired to inherit the blessing, he was rejected, for he found no chance to repent, though he sought it with tears" (Hebrews 12:16–17).

**In three of Isaiah's oracles the outcome answers the choice in its own terms.** Each verse says it in its own figure:
- They set *"cups of mixed wine for Destiny"*, and the Lord says *"I will destine you to the sword"* (Isaiah 65:11–12). "Destiny" and "destine" share a root.
- They chose gardens and desired oaks, and *"you shall be like an oak whose leaf withers, and like a garden without water"* (1:30).
- They chose what he did not delight in, and *"I also will choose harsh treatment for them"* (66:4).

**The way back stays open.** In the same oracles the offer stands: *"Come now, let us reason together, says the Lord: though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow"* (Isaiah 1:18); *"those in her who repent"* (1:27).

## Choices weighed by another

Another person can weigh someone's choices. In the book of Job the friends do this, and the verses show how far it reaches.
- **They read the choice from the words.** Eliphaz: *"For your iniquity teaches your mouth, and you choose the tongue of the crafty. Your own mouth condemns you, and not I"* (Job 15:5–6). He goes from the mouth to the heart: *"Why does your heart carry you away, and why do your eyes flash"* (15:12).
- **They weigh it as tasting.** Elihu: *"the ear tests words as the palate tastes food. Let us choose what is right"* (34:3–4).
- **They read it in suffering.** Elihu: *"this you have chosen rather than affliction"* (36:21).
- **They cannot make the choice for the other.** *"For you must choose, and not I"* (34:33).

The book does not let these verdicts have the last word. The Lord calls Job *"a blameless and upright man, who fears God and turns away from evil"* (Job 1:8). To Eliphaz he says *"you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has"* (42:7). Elihu is not named in that verdict.

The refusing Elihu pressed is made in the end, in Elihu's own verb, when Job sees the Lord: *"but now my eye sees you; therefore I despise myself, and repent in dust and ashes"* (Job 42:5–6).

A king's choice can be questioned and still stand. Joab: "May the Lord your God add to the people a hundred times as many as they are … but why does my lord the king delight in this thing?" (2 Samuel 24:3). "But the king's word prevailed against Joab and the commanders of the army" (24:4). Afterwards "David's heart struck him after he had numbered the people" (24:10; Chapter 8). The act is a decision made over counsel. Joab names the king's delight as what he cannot understand, and the king's own heart judges it after.

## What changes the character

The same words change face with the setting, and the verses show why.
- **"Good" or "evil" in your eyes.**
  - It is the chooser's own sight, where turning from the Lord could begin (Joshua 24:15).
  - It is the chooser's own good, honoured by the king (2 Samuel 19:38).
  - It gives way to *"evil in my eyes"*, the Lord's sight (Isaiah 65:12).
  - *Why:* in Joshua and Isaiah the choice is between the Lord and other gods. With Barzillai it is where an old man who served will live.
- **Knowing good and evil.**
  - It is the knowing that stands under the choice of right and wrong (Isaiah 7:15–16).
  - It is the palate's knowing of the pleasant and the unpleasant, which fades at eighty (2 Samuel 19:35).
  - It is the weighing of words in a dispute (Job 34:3–4).
  - *Why:* the same knowing is turned to right and wrong, to taste, and to judgement.
- **Refusing.**
  - It is refusing the evil (Isaiah 7:15) and refusing the gentle waters (8:6).
  - It is refusing God's terms, as Elihu charges (Job 34:33).
  - It is Job turning it on himself in repentance (42:6).
  - *Why:* the act is the same; what it is aimed at decides whether it is right.
- **Choosing.** It is the choice of a master (Joshua 24:15), a place (Deuteronomy 23:16), a way (Psalm 119:30; Isaiah 66:3), a preference (Proverbs 16:16) and a verdict (Job 34:4). *Why:* it is turned to whatever is set before a person.
- **Delight.** It is the soul's own delight in what it chose (Isaiah 66:3), and it is the Lord's delight as the measure, either not met (65:12; 66:4) or met (56:4). *Why:* whose delight it is decides.
- **Choosing a person.**
  - God chooses before anything in the person, *"before the foundation of the world"* (Ephesians 1:4). He chooses people who are blind and deaf (Isaiah 43:8, 10), and the poor (James 2:5).
  - People choose by what is already seen: *"men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom"* (Acts 6:3).
  - *Why:* who chooses. With God, the inner life is what the choosing is for. With people, it is the measure.
- **Holiness.**
  - It is the purpose of the choosing: *"that we should be holy and blameless before him"* (Ephesians 1:4).
  - It is a name the chosen already carry, while the inner qualities are still to be put on: *"as God's chosen ones, holy and beloved"* (Colossians 3:12).
  - *Why:* the verses do not say. I set them side by side.
- **Desire beside a choice.**
  - The soul's desire for meat is given room away from the place God chose (Deuteronomy 12:21).
  - The same desire of the soul draws a Levite to that place (18:6).
  - The soul delights in its own abominations, beside a wrong choice (Isaiah 66:3).
  - *Why:* what the desire is turned toward. The first two are allowed in the same words. In the third it is what the soul delights in that decides.
- **Despising.**
  - Others despise the one chosen: Michal *"in her heart"*, by the eyes of people (2 Samuel 6:16, 20); the servant *"deeply despised"*, with kings to bow before him (Isaiah 49:7). It is the same verb in both.
  - People despise the chosen people, concluding God rejected them (Jeremiah 33:24).
  - The chosen people themselves *"despised the pleasant land"* (Psalm 106:24).
  - *Why:* who despises what. Each verse gives its own ground: honour before people, a verdict drawn from ruin, no faith in the promise.

- **Willing.**
  - It is a refusal that keeps faith (1 Samuel 22:17; 26:23), a refusal that honours others at a cost to oneself (2 Samuel 23:17), and a refusal that tramples a plea (2 Samuel 13:14).
  - It is God refused, though what he offered was good (Isaiah 28:12; 30:15).
  - It is a heart that gives freely (Exodus 35:22), and a will made absolute (Daniel 5:19).
  - *Why:* what is refused, and for whose sake. Each passage gives its reason: faith, honour, force, fear, grief, pride.

Chapter 11 ("What changes the character") gathers these with the other activities.

**Connections:**
- from feeling (10.1) and fear (10.12): fear stops a choice and sets a direction; fear is learned at the place God chose, and comes as terror on those who resisted his choice
- with feeling (10.1): rejoicing at the place God chose, shared with those who have least
- from knowing (10.2): the choice rests on knowing how, and on being taught
- from remembering (10.3): the choice is made from what was seen and remembered, and held while it is remembered
- from thinking (10.4) and wanting (10.6): desire, delight, envy and preferring stand beside the choice
- with speaking (10.5): a spoken choice makes the chooser a witness against himself
- into the deed (the path in 10.0)
- before God (10.9): a choice made before a God who has acted
- with others (10.10): choosing together, choices weighed by another, the chosen turned toward others and set against them, others set against the chosen (grumbling, anger, contempt, hatred, rejection), and others standing with them and for them
- with anger (10.13): Saul's anger at his son's choice, and Moses standing in the breach
- with others (10.10): plotting against another; a will pressed, bent to a crowd, held back or helped by friends
- with feeling (10.1), fear (10.12) and wanting (10.6): fear, grief and jealousy hold the will; longing refused for others' sake
- with life set before a person (Chapter 2)
- God's own choosing, purposing and willing: with the other beings (13.1)

---

*Working note, not part of the narrative text.* This section is built to take further reading on choosing. Expected additions, each to be woven where it belongs rather than added at the end:
- **Job's own voice about choosing** (Job 7:15; 9:14; 29:25) is to be set beside *Choices weighed by another*: the chooser's own words alongside the friends' verdicts. Job 7:15 is his own would-be choice of death, spoken to God in complaint (7:13–16), so it also goes with *Life and death set before a person*.
- **Choosing between death and life** goes with *Life and death set before a person*.
- **Will and resolve.** Planning and willing are now written (*Planning*, *Willing*), and the chapters they touch carry their parts: the heart (Chapter 4), the spirit (Chapter 6), feeling (10.1), wanting (10.6), plotting (10.10), fear (10.12), anger (10.13) and Chapter 11 §4.
- **Held, not in the text:** the shared phrasing of Deuteronomy 23:16 ("the place that he shall choose") and Deuteronomy 12:5, 14 ("the place that the Lord your God will choose"). Whether it is more than a shared form of words is open. Deuteronomy 12 has now been read in full: the forms differ (*"out of all your tribes"*, 12:5; *"in one of your tribes"*, 12:14; *"within one of your towns"*, 23:16), and in 23:16 the chooser is the escaped slave. It stays held.

blocks.section: Fear that comes upon a person
blocks.text:
## Fear that comes upon a person

Fear is felt in the heart and the body together.
- "he was afraid, and his heart trembled greatly" (1 Samuel 28:5)
- "My flesh trembles for fear of you" (Psalm 119:120)
- "My heart is in anguish within me … Fear and trembling come upon me, and horror overwhelms me" (Psalm 55:4–5)
- "fighting without and fear within" (2 Corinthians 7:5)

It has a cause outside, and often a reason inside. "I heard the sound of you in the garden, and I was afraid, because I was naked, and I hid myself" (Genesis 3:10). The sound was outside Adam. The reason was something he knew about himself.

The verses name what it rises at:
- **a report or a sight:** "We have heard the report of it; our hands fall helpless; anguish has taken hold of us, pain as of a woman in labor" (Jeremiah 6:24). "When Saul and all Israel heard these words of the Philistine, they were dismayed and greatly afraid" (1 Samuel 17:11).
- **an arrival:** the elders "came to meet him trembling and said, 'Do you come peaceably?'" (1 Samuel 16:4)
- **a discovery:** "Isaac trembled very violently" (Genesis 27:33)
- **the night, and a spirit not clearly seen:** "A spirit glided past my face; the hair of my flesh stood up. It stood still, but I could not discern its appearance" (Job 4:15–16)
- **a dream:** "I saw a dream that made me afraid. As I lay in bed the fancies and the visions of my head alarmed me" (Daniel 4:5)
- **a mistaken seeing:** the disciples saw Jesus walking on the sea "and said, 'It is a ghost!' and they cried out in fear" (Matthew 14:26). After the resurrection "they were startled and frightened and thought they saw a spirit" (Luke 24:37). Both times the answer was to be shown: "Take heart; it is I" (Matthew 14:27); "See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself. Touch me, and see" (Luke 24:39).

Terror can also come as an event, from outside.
- It strikes: "I will mock when terror strikes you, when terror strikes you like a storm" (Proverbs 1:26–27). Wisdom is the speaker. The same speech says they "did not choose the fear of the Lord" (1:29). I read the passage as setting the fear of the Lord, not chosen, beside the terror that comes.
- It comes where peace was looked for: "We looked for peace, but no good came; for a time of healing, but behold, terror" (Jeremiah 8:15).
- It is given in the curse: "the Lord will give you there a trembling heart and failing eyes and a languishing soul" (Deuteronomy 28:65). The mind itself is struck: "The Lord will strike you with madness and blindness and confusion of mind" (Deuteronomy 28:28).
- It can come where there is nothing to fear: "There they are, in great terror, where there is no terror!" (Psalm 53:5).

And it can stay, or come again. "For the thing that I fear comes upon me, and what I dread befalls me" (Job 3:25). "The sword that you fear shall overtake you there" (Jeremiah 42:16). Afterwards it is turned over in the mind: "Your heart will muse on the terror" (Isaiah 33:18).

Fear can come with no one there to cause it. Among the curses: "I will visit you with panic", and "Those who hate you shall rule over you, and you shall flee when none pursues you" (Leviticus 26:16–17).

Fear also comes with age. The Preacher pictures the last days of life, "in the day when the keepers of the house tremble, and the strong men are bent", when "one rises up at the sound of a bird" (Ecclesiastes 12:3–4). Then: "they are afraid also of what is high, and terrors are in the way" (12:5). I read the house and its keepers as the body, as the passage ends with the dust returning to the earth (12:7). No enemy stands behind these fears; they come as the body fails. The passage opens with what to do before then: "Remember also your Creator in the days of your youth, before the evil days come" (12:1; 10.3). Chapter 2 carries the same verse as the approach of death.

Fear can come with seeing what has been decided. Haman "stayed to beg for his life from Queen Esther, for he saw that harm was determined against him by the king" (Esther 7:7).

## What changes it

The verses show fear changing character, and they point to what changes it.
- **What it is turned toward.** At the sea Israel "feared greatly" as Egypt marched, and after the crossing "the people feared the Lord, and they believed in the Lord" (Exodus 14:10, 31). In between, fear spoke as a preference: "it would have been better for us to serve the Egyptians than to die in the wilderness" (14:12; 10.6, *Shaped by fear*). In the boat, fear of the storm became fear of the one who stilled it (Mark 4:41). In these cases the change came after God acted.
- **One fear set in place of another, by the same speaker.** "Do not fear, for God has come to test you, that the fear of him may be before you" (Exodus 20:20). "do not fear what they fear … Let him be your fear" (Isaiah 8:12–13). "Rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell", and then, "Fear not, therefore; you are of more value than many sparrows" (Matthew 10:28, 31).
- **Who speaks to it, and why.** God's "for I am with you" (Isaiah 41:10), and Jael's "do not be afraid" (Judges 4:18).
- **Knowing whose hand is on one.** Ezra: "I took courage, for the hand of the Lord my God was on me, and I gathered leading men from Israel to go up with me" (Ezra 7:28). The verse names the ground of the courage, and the courage turns at once into a deed. Ezra then would not ask the king for soldiers, "since we had told the king, 'The hand of our God is for good on all who seek him'" (8:22; 10.14). What he told others did the same for them (Nehemiah 2:18; 10.10).
- **Who meets it.** "When justice is done, it is a joy to the righteous but terror to evildoers" (Proverbs 21:15). One scroll was read aloud: the officials "turned one to another in fear", and "neither the king nor any of his servants who heard all these words was afraid" (Jeremiah 36:16, 24). At the signs of the end, "people fainting with fear", and to the disciples, "straighten up and raise your heads, because your redemption is drawing near" (Luke 21:26, 28).
- **One's own conduct.** "rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to bad" (Romans 13:3). "I also will choose harsh treatment for them and bring their fears upon them, because when I called, no one answered" (Isaiah 66:4). The same passage opens with the one God looks to, who "trembles at my word" (66:2). I read the passage as setting that trembling beside "their fears".
- **Pride.** "So do not become proud, but fear" (Romans 11:20). "The horror you inspire has deceived you, and the pride of your heart" (Jeremiah 49:16).
- **Where the heart is.** Fear "taught by men" while "their hearts are far from me", against fear put "in their hearts" (Isaiah 29:13; Jeremiah 32:40).
- **Faith, trust and love** (the section above).
- **Joy or silence.** The women left the tomb "with fear and great joy, and ran to tell his disciples" (Matthew 28:8). In Mark's account "they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid" (Mark 16:8). The two accounts stand side by side.
- **The same root, rendered as another movement.** *Rāgaz*, "to tremble", is also anger and grief (Psalm 4:4; 2 Samuel 18:33). *Paḥad*, "dread", is also "thrill" (Isaiah 60:5). *Phobos*, "fear", is also "respect" (Romans 13:7).

Chapter 11 (§4) gathers what changes the character of a word across all the activities. These are fear's part in it.

blocks.section: Living under God's anger > Pleading, and standing in the breach
blocks.text:
### Pleading, and standing in the breach

People plead with God in the face of his anger, and they do it boldly.

Abraham knows the distance, "I who am but dust and ashes" (Genesis 18:27), and asks again anyway: "Oh let not the Lord be angry, and I will speak again but this once" (18:32). The anger he feared never came.

Moses stands between the anger and the people. God himself leaves the door open: "Now therefore let me alone, that my wrath may burn hot against them" (Exodus 32:10). Moses does not let him alone. He argues from God's ownership of the people, from his reputation, and from his promises (32:11–13), "and the Lord relented" (32:14). He lay on his face forty days without food. What drove him was fear: "For I was afraid of the anger and hot displeasure that the Lord bore against you" (Deuteronomy 9:19). The psalm remembers it as standing "in the breach before him, to turn away his wrath" (Psalm 106:23).

Moses also used God's own words. God had proclaimed himself "slow to anger" (Exodus 34:6). Moses quoted it back: "'The Lord is slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love …' Please pardon the iniquity of this people" (Numbers 14:18–19). God answered, "I have pardoned, according to your word" (14:20).

But the breach is not always filled.
