- "I sought for a man among them who should build up the wall and stand in the breach before me for the land, that I should not destroy it, but I found none" (Ezekiel 22:30).
- Even the best could only save themselves: "even if Noah, Daniel, and Job were in it … they would deliver but their own lives by their righteousness" (Ezekiel 14:20).
- Jeremiah, who had stood before God "to speak good for them, to turn away your wrath from them", found that "they have dug a pit for my life". He then prayed for the anger to fall on them (Jeremiah 18:20–23).

And the most surprising intercessor is the sufferer. Job's friends explained his pain by God's anger. In the end God says to them, "My anger burns against you", and "my servant Job shall pray for you, for I will accept his prayer" (Job 42:7–8). The man they explained by God's anger stood between them and it.

The verses also set the leaders apart in how they bear it.
- **Moses** bears it on the people's account: "But the Lord was angry with me because of you" (Deuteronomy 3:26). He turns his own exclusion into a warning: "Take care, lest you forget the covenant of the Lord your God" (4:23).
- **Aaron** "stood between the dead and the living, and the plague was stopped" (Numbers 16:48).
- **David** asks to bear it alone: "let your hand be against me and against my father's house" (2 Samuel 24:17).

blocks.section: Humbling oneself before God > A humbling God does not take knowledge of
blocks.text:
### A humbling God does not take knowledge of

The people asked, "Why have we fasted, and you see it not? Why have we humbled ourselves, and you take no knowledge of it?" The answer: "in the day of your fast you seek your own pleasure, and oppress all your workers … Is it to bow down his head like a reed, and to spread sackcloth and ashes under him?" The fast God chooses is turned outward: "to share your bread with the hungry and bring the homeless poor into your house; when you see the naked, to cover him" (Isaiah 58:3–7).

Ahab's sackcloth and fasting were seen and answered (1 Kings 21:27–29). Israel's were not. I read the difference in what went with them. Ahab acted when the word came against him. Israel fasted while seeking its own pleasure, and left the naked it saw uncovered.

The New Testament names the same thing. The noun for humility appears as "asceticism": "Let no one disqualify you, insisting on asceticism … puffed up without reason by his sensuous mind", and "self-made religion and asceticism and severity to the body, but they are of no value in stopping the indulgence of the flesh" (Colossians 2:18, 23). What looks like lowering puffs the person up. The Pharisee's "I fast twice a week" stands on the same side (Luke 18:12).

blocks.section: Humility as a way of walking
blocks.text:
## Humility as a way of walking

**Before honour.** "humility comes before honor" is said twice (Proverbs 15:33; 18:12). The verses join it to the fear of the Lord: "The fear of the Lord is instruction in wisdom, and humility comes before honor" (15:33); "The reward for humility and fear of the Lord is riches and honor and life" (22:4). And to wisdom: "with the humble is wisdom" (11:2).

**With hearing.** In both places where "humility comes before honor", the verse beside it is about hearing.
- "The ear that listens to life-giving reproof will dwell among the wise. Whoever ignores instruction despises himself, but he who listens to reproof gains intelligence" (Proverbs 15:31–32).
- "If one gives an answer before he hears, it is his folly and shame" (Proverbs 18:13).
- James says it again: "let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger … receive with meekness the implanted word, which is able to save your souls" (James 1:19–21).
- God looks to "he who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word" (Isaiah 66:2).

I read humility, in these verses, as the ear that can take a reproof and a word, and does not answer before it hears (10.2).

**Walking with God.** "With what shall I come before the Lord … Shall I come before him with burnt offerings …? He has told you, O man, what is good; and what does the Lord require of you but to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God?" (Micah 6:6–8). The question is what to bring, and the answer is a way to walk. "Humbly" is "with your God": a walk in his company, not a gift handed over.

**Instead of the offering.** Three more passages set what God looks to against a religious act:
- the fast (Isaiah 58)
- the house and the sacrifices: "But this is the one to whom I will look: he who is humble and contrite in spirit" (Isaiah 66:1–3)
- "For you will not delight in sacrifice … The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise" (Psalm 51:16–17)

The psalm goes on, "then will you delight in right sacrifices" (51:19). The offering is not done away with. It follows the broken heart.

blocks.section: Given, then held as one's own
blocks.text:
## Given, then held as one's own

The clearest thing the verses say about pride is where it comes from. In account after account a person is given something, and the heart rises on it.
- **Strength.** Uzziah "was marvelously helped, till he was strong. But when he was strong, he grew proud, to his destruction" (2 Chronicles 26:15–16).
- **Healing.** Hezekiah was healed and given a sign, and gifts were brought "so that he was exalted in the sight of all nations". Then: "But Hezekiah did not make return according to the benefit done to him, for his heart was proud" (2 Chronicles 32:23–25).
- **Majesty.** "The Most High God gave Nebuchadnezzar your father kingship and greatness and glory and majesty … But when his heart was lifted up and his spirit was hardened so that he dealt proudly, he was brought down from his kingly throne" (Daniel 5:18–20).
- **Wealth.** "By your great wisdom in your trade you have increased your wealth, and your heart has become proud in your wealth" (Ezekiel 28:5).
- **Beauty and height.** Of the great tree God says, "I made it beautiful", and then, "its heart was proud of its height" (Ezekiel 31:9–10). Chapter 12 follows the king of Tyre's beauty the same way.

The law saw it coming: "then your heart be lifted up, and you forget the Lord your God … Beware lest you say in your heart, 'My power and the might of my hand have gotten me this wealth.' You shall remember the Lord your God, for it is he who gives you power to get wealth" (Deuteronomy 8:14, 17–18). Paul says it as a question: "What do you have that you did not receive? If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it?" (1 Corinthians 4:7).

So the standing in these verses is real. It was given. Pride holds it as if it had not been given. I read that this is the line the verses draw. It does not run between having height and having none. It runs between height that is one's own by nature, height that is given, and height that is taken as one's own.

**It credits its own hand.** The king of Assyria says, "By the strength of my hand I have done it, and by my wisdom, for I have understanding" (Isaiah 10:13). In the same passage he is the rod in the Lord's hand: "Shall the axe boast over him who hews with it?" (10:5, 15). Nebuchadnezzar: "Is not this great Babylon, which I have built by my mighty power … for the glory of my majesty?" (Daniel 4:30). I read pride here as crediting to itself what was done through it.

**It gives itself the glory.** The great city "glorified herself and lived in luxury" (Revelation 18:7). The Greek verb is the one used where people give glory to God: "so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father who is in heaven" (Matthew 5:16). Here she is the one who gives the glory and the one who receives it. What it brings her is in *Where it ends*, below.

**The same word can name an honour God gives.** "He chose our heritage for us, the pride of Jacob whom he loves" (Psalm 47:4). To a city "forsaken and hated": "I will make you majestic forever, a joy from age to age" (Isaiah 60:15). "The Lord is restoring the majesty of Jacob" (Nahum 2:2). Israel's triumph is the Lord himself: "the sword of your triumph" (Deuteronomy 33:29). Where God chooses, gives or restores it, the word is honour. And what was given can be turned. God's own sanctuary became "the pride of your power, the delight of your eyes, and the yearning of your soul" (Ezekiel 24:21). His beautiful ornament "they used for pride, and they made their abominable images … of it" (Ezekiel 7:20).

## 4. One word, opposite values

Again and again I found a single word for an inner state that is good in one place and bad in another. What decides is not the word but **what the inner being is yielding to, or holding firm against**.

- **A tender heart.** It melts before an enemy and spreads fear to others (Deuteronomy 20:8). But Josiah's heart "was penitent [tender]" before God's word, and God answered him with peace (2 Kings 22:19–20). The same softness is cowardice in one place and repentance in the other.
- **A strong heart.** "Be strong, and let your heart take courage; wait for the Lord!" (Psalm 27:14). With Absalom, the same verb gives his servants the nerve to kill: "be courageous and be valiant" (2 Samuel 13:28). With Pharaoh it is hardening: "I will harden his heart" (Exodus 4:21), literally *strengthen*.
- **A guarded heart.** "Keep your heart with all vigilance" (Proverbs 4:23). Three chapters later the same word describes the adulteress, "wily [guarded] of heart" (Proverbs 7:10).
- **Crushing.** Crushed by an enemy, the spirit collapses (Psalm 143:3–4). Offered to God, a crushed spirit is the very sacrifice he wants: "a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise" (Psalm 51:17).
- **Loving and hating one's own soul** (Chapter 5).
- **Devising.** The same Hebrew verb describes the craftsmen who worked cherubim "skillfully" into the tabernacle curtains (Exodus 26:1) and those who plot. One word for planning means "discretion" (Proverbs 2:11), "evil devices" (Proverbs 12:2), and God's own purpose: "no purpose of yours can be thwarted" (Job 42:2).
- **Planning against.** God says, "I am … devising a plan against you. Return" (Jeremiah 18:11), and the people say, "Come, let us make plots against Jeremiah" (18:18). The word and the "against" are the same. One plan is meant to bring people back, and the other is meant to silence the one who calls them.
- **Purposing.** The verb for purposing (*zāmam*) is the psalmist's resolve: "I have purposed that my mouth will not transgress" (Psalm 17:3). It is the wicked man's plot: "The wicked plots against the righteous" (Psalm 37:12). It is the wise woman's weighing: "She considers a field and buys it" (Proverbs 31:16). And it is God's fixed purpose: "I have purposed; I have not relented" (Jeremiah 4:28). I read the change as following whom it is aimed at: one's own mouth, another's harm, one's own household, or a whole land.
- **Willing.** The Hebrew word for being willing (*ʾāḇâ*) is almost always a "no". It is the guard's refusal to kill the priests (1 Samuel 22:17), David refusing the water for the men's sake (2 Samuel 23:17), Amnon refusing Tamar's plea (2 Samuel 13:14), and Israel refusing God's rest (Isaiah 30:15). God himself is "not willing to destroy" (2 Kings 8:19), and "will not be willing to forgive" the man who blesses himself in his stubbornness (Deuteronomy 29:20). The Greek word runs from Pilate "wishing to satisfy the crowd" (Mark 15:15) to God "not wishing that any should perish" (2 Peter 3:9). Each passage gives the reason: faith, honour, force, fear, grief, covenant, love, a self-blessing heart. I read the change as following what is refused, and for whose sake (10.7, *Willing*).
- **Planning ahead.** The same looking ahead is a king's honest count of his strength (Luke 14:31) and sailors' guess "on the chance that somehow" (Acts 27:12). It is a man's "aim in life" (2 Timothy 3:10) and a plot "to put him to death" (John 11:53). I read the verses as setting the difference beside how much the planner can see. The king can count, the sailors cannot see the reef, and over all of it "the Lord establishes his steps" (Proverbs 16:9).
- **Reckoning.** People misreckon: "we esteemed him stricken" (Isaiah 53:4). God reckons faith "as righteousness" (Genesis 15:6). The law reckons in order to release (Leviticus 25:50). Love refuses to reckon at all: it "is not … resentful" (1 Corinthians 13:5).
- **Likening.** Comparing is how love praises ("I compare you, my love", Song of Songs 1:9), how comfort reaches out (Lamentations 2:13), and how worship ends ("who in the skies can be compared to the Lord?", Psalm 89:6). It is also how pride rises: "I will make myself like the Most High" (Isaiah 14:14).
- **Reasoning.** The Greek word is Mary's honest pondering (Luke 1:29), the disciples' anxious circling (Mark 8:17), and a quarrel (Philippians 2:14; 1 Timothy 2:8).
- **The nose.** The Hebrew word for anger, *ʾaph*, is the nostril where God breathed in life (Genesis 2:7), the face bowed in worship (2 Chronicles 7:3), and the face lifted in pride (Psalm 10:4). It can be given a ring in love (Ezekiel 16:12) or a hook for raging (2 Kings 19:28). "Long of nostrils" is patience, in God and in the wise (Exodus 34:6; Proverbs 14:29).
- **Anger.** Jesus's anger heals (Mark 3:5). A crowd's anger stops its ears and kills (Acts 7:57–58). "Be angry and do not sin" (Ephesians 4:26).
- **Vexation.** It is provocation done to another (1 Samuel 1:6), suffering borne (1:16), and "Sorrow is better than laughter, for by sadness of face the heart is made glad" (Ecclesiastes 7:3).
- **Provoking.** Love "is not irritable" (1 Corinthians 13:5), with the same word that tells believers to "stir up one another to love and good works" (Hebrews 10:24).
- **Overflow.** One Hebrew word, *ʿebrah*, is the overflow of anger and the overflow of pride. God offers it to Job with irony: "Pour out the overflowings of your anger, and look on everyone who is proud and abase him" (Job 40:11). And "'Scoffer' is the name of the arrogant, haughty man who acts with arrogant pride" (Proverbs 21:24), where the word is the same.
- **Lifted up.** One Hebrew word names the heart that grew proud when Uzziah was strong (2 Chronicles 26:16) and Jehoshaphat's heart, "courageous in the ways of the Lord" (2 Chronicles 17:6). One family of words is God's majesty and human pride (Exodus 15:7; Jeremiah 48:29). And the boast moves: "Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom" (Jeremiah 9:23), "but let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me" (9:24). What differs is where the height comes from, and which way it faces (10.15).
- **Glory.** The verb that gives glory to God (Matthew 5:16) is the great city's own: she "glorified herself" (Revelation 18:7). The noun is the glory some take "in their shame" (Philippians 3:19), and two verses later the glory of the body to come, "like his glorious body" (3:21). The same word names glory taken where it does not belong and glory given (10.15).
- **Storm.** The same storm word, *sāʿar*, is the angry king's mind ("the mind of the king of Syria was greatly troubled", 2 Kings 6:11) and the suffering city ("O afflicted one, storm-tossed and not comforted", Isaiah 54:11).
- **Denouncing.** "How can I curse whom God has not cursed?" (Numbers 23:8). But "Whoever says to the wicked, 'You are in the right,' will be cursed by peoples, abhorred by nations" (Proverbs 24:24). The word is empty when it goes against God's verdict, and it lands when it follows justice.
- **A creed.** "Slow to anger" is used in worship, in pleading, in confession, in Jonah's complaint, in praise, in wonder, in announcing judgment, and as the ground for returning (Chapter 10.9).
- **Mourning.** Aaron is forbidden to mourn "lest … wrath come" (Leviticus 10:6). When the wrath has come, mourning is commanded (Jeremiah 4:8).
- **God's hand.** The "mighty hand" brought Israel out (Deuteronomy 6:21) and later fought "against you … in anger" (Jeremiah 21:5).
- **Fear.** One word, *yārēʾ*, "to fear", names the fear that drives a person away from God and the fear of God that keeps a person from sin. In one sentence Moses takes the first away and sets the second in its place: "Do not fear, for God has come to test you, that the fear of him may be before you, that you may not sin" (Exodus 20:20). The same people, with the same word, are afraid of Egypt and then fear the Lord (Exodus 14:10, 31). Turned round, the word describes the one who is feared: "the great and awesome God, who keeps covenant and steadfast love" (Nehemiah 1:5). Beside a choice it has three more faces. It is learned at a feast in the place God chose: "that you may learn to fear the Lord your God always" (Deuteronomy 14:23). It falls on those who hear of presumption punished: "all the people shall hear and fear and not act presumptuously again" (17:13). And it comes as terror on people who resisted God's choice once he made it plain: "Are we all to perish?" (Numbers 17:13). Section 10.1 sets out the word, and 10.7 the faces beside a choice.
- **"Do not fear."** God says it with a reason, and the reason is himself: "for I am with you" (Isaiah 41:10). Joseph says it and refuses to stand in God's place (Genesis 50:19, 21). Jael says it before the tent peg (Judges 4:18). The words are the same. What they are for is not.
- **Trembling and dread.** The Hebrew words for trembling and dread are rendered as fear, and also as "Be angry" (Psalm 4:4), "deeply moved" (2 Samuel 18:33), a heart that "trembled for the ark of God" (1 Samuel 4:13), and "your heart shall thrill and exult" (Isaiah 60:5). I read them as naming one inner stirring, which its situation turns into fear, anger, grief, care or joy (10.1).
- **"None shall make you afraid."** It is promised peace: "I will give peace in the land, and you shall lie down, and none shall make you afraid" (Leviticus 26:6). The same Hebrew phrase is used of desolation: "The cities of Aroer are deserted; they will be for flocks, which will lie down, and none will make them afraid" (Isaiah 17:2). One phrase describes rest for a people and the emptiness left when they are gone.
- **Care.** The Greek *merimnaō*, "to be anxious, to care", is rebuked when it is about my own food and clothing (Matthew 6:25) and praised when it is "genuinely concerned for your welfare" (Philippians 2:20). The Hebrew *dāʾag*, "to be anxious, to dread", is dread of what may come (Jeremiah 38:19), a father's worry for his son (1 Samuel 10:2), and sorrow for sin: "I am sorry for my sin" (Psalm 38:18). Section 10.1 sets this out.
- **Hiding.** The Hebrew *sātar*, "to hide", is God hiding a person in safety and God hiding his face, four verses apart (Psalm 27:5, 9), and a sinner asking God to hide his face from his sins (Psalm 51:9). A treasure is hidden "in his joy", and a talent hidden because "I was afraid" (Matthew 13:44; 25:25). Sections 10.9 and 10.11.
- **Murmuring.** The Hebrew *rāgan* is the people's complaint "in your tents" against God (Deuteronomy 1:27) and the whisperer's words that separate friends (Proverbs 16:28) (10.5).
- **Remembering.** It bows the soul down and it gives hope, in two consecutive verses (Lamentations 3:20–21; Chapter 10.3).
- **The bed.** It is the same place, but what happens there goes either way. "He plots trouble while on his bed" (Psalm 36:4). "I remember you upon my bed, and meditate on you in the watches of the night" (Psalm 63:6).
- **"Good" or "evil" in your eyes.** Joshua leaves the choice to the people's own sight: "if it is evil in your eyes to serve the Lord, choose this day" (Joshua 24:15). The king honours an old man's sight: "whatever seems good to you" (2 Samuel 19:38). In Isaiah the measure is the Lord's: "you did what was evil in my eyes" (Isaiah 65:12). Section 10.7 sets this out.
- **Knowing good and evil.** It is the child's knowing "how to refuse the evil and choose the good" (Isaiah 7:15). It is Barzillai's palate at eighty, with the same words: "Can I discern what is pleasant and what is not?" (2 Samuel 19:35). And it is the weighing of words in a dispute: "Let us choose what is right; let us know among ourselves what is good" (Job 34:4).
- **Refusing.** The Hebrew *māʾas*, "to refuse, reject, despise", is refusing the evil (Isaiah 7:15) and refusing "the waters of Shiloah that flow gently" (8:6). Elihu uses it of refusing God's terms (Job 34:33). Job turns it on himself: "therefore I despise myself, and repent" (42:6).
- **Choosing.** The Hebrew *bāḥar*, "to choose", is the choice of a master (Joshua 24:15), of a place to live (Deuteronomy 23:16), of a way (Psalm 119:30; Isaiah 66:3), of wisdom over silver (Proverbs 16:16), and of a verdict (Job 34:4).
- **Delight.** The Hebrew *ḥāpēṣ*, "to delight in", is the soul's own delight in what it chose: "their soul delights in their abominations" (Isaiah 66:3). It is also the Lord's delight as the measure of a choice. That delight is not met when people "chose what I did not delight in" (65:12), and met in those "who choose the things that please me" (56:4). The noun *ḥēpheṣ* names his settled purpose: "he shall fulfill all my purpose" (Isaiah 44:28). It names what a man cares about, and that stops at his death: "what do they care for their houses after them" (Job 21:21).
- **Good, said of the eye.** "Whoever has a bountiful eye will be blessed, for he shares his bread with the poor" (Proverbs 22:9). "Bountiful" is literally "good" (10.6).
- **God's delight in a person.** It is the thanks of the rescued: "he rescued me, because he delighted in me" (Psalm 18:19). It is the mockers' taunt over a sufferer: "let him rescue him, for he delights in him!" (Psalm 22:8). The claim is the same. The sufferer does not answer the mockers; he answers God: "Yet you are he who took me from the womb" (22:9) (13.1).
- **An offering.** "For you will not delight in sacrifice, or I would give it" (Psalm 51:16). Three verses on: "then will you delight in right sacrifices, in burnt offerings and whole burnt offerings" (51:19). It is the same offering. Between the two stands "a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise" (51:17) (13.1).
- **Being well pleased.** The Greek *eudokeō* is the Father's word over the Son: "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased" (Matthew 3:17). It is also Paul's word for weaknesses he had pleaded three times to lose: "I am content with weaknesses, insults, hardships, persecutions, and calamities" (2 Corinthians 12:10). Between his pleading and his contentment stands the answer, "My grace is sufficient for you" (12:9) (10.1).
- **Choosing a person.** God chooses "before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him" (Ephesians 1:4). He chooses people who are "blind, yet have eyes" (Isaiah 43:8, 10), and "those who are poor in the world to be rich in faith" (James 2:5). People choose by what they can already see: "men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom" (Acts 6:3). Section 10.7 sets this out.
- **Holiness.** It is the purpose of being chosen: "that we should be holy and blameless before him" (Ephesians 1:4). It is also a name the chosen already carry, while the inner qualities are still to be put on: "Put on then, as God's chosen ones, holy and beloved, compassionate hearts" (Colossians 3:12). The verses do not say how the two fit.
- **Desire beside a choice.** The soul's desire for meat is given room away from the place God chose: "you may eat within your towns whenever you desire" (Deuteronomy 12:21). The same words for the soul's desire draw a Levite to that place: "he may come when he desires" (18:6). And the soul's delight goes with a wrong choice: "These have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations" (Isaiah 66:3). Section 10.7 sets this out.
- **Despising.** Michal "despised him in her heart" when she saw the chosen king dancing before the Lord (2 Samuel 6:16). The same verb describes the servant, "one deeply despised", before whom kings will bow (Isaiah 49:7). People despise the chosen people, judging that God has rejected them (Jeremiah 33:24). And the chosen people themselves "despised the pleasant land" (Psalm 106:24). Each verse gives its own ground: honour before people, a verdict drawn from ruin, no faith in the promise.
- **Knowing that a choice was made.** Peter's hearers know it, and a quarrel ends in silence: "you know that in the early days God made a choice among you" (Acts 15:7, 12). Paul knows it of others from what he saw: "we know … that he has chosen you, because our gospel came to you not only in word, but also in power" (1 Thessalonians 1:4–5). Cyrus is called for the sake of the chosen "though you do not know me" (Isaiah 45:4). The world hates the chosen "because they do not know him who sent me" (John 15:21).
- **Precious.** The Hebrew *yāqār* is wisdom weighed above *"nothing you desire"* (Proverbs 3:15), the word *"rare in those days"* (1 Samuel 3:1), a visit kept *seldom* (Proverbs 25:17), *"the moon moving in splendor"* that entices a heart (Job 31:26–27), a name *"highly esteemed"* (1 Samuel 18:30), *"the lordly price"* set on a shepherd (Zechariah 11:13), and a son *"dear"* while spoken against (Jeremiah 31:20). The Greek *timios* is faith tested by fire (1 Peter 1:7), the blood of Christ (1:19), and the jewels of Babylon (Revelation 17:4). What differs is who values, what the thing is weighed against, and whether its worth is known: man does not know wisdom's worth (Job 28:13), and Saul would not give the esteem the others gave (1 Samuel 18:29–30). (10.6 *Precious*.)
- **Imperishable.** The Greek *aphthartos* and its noun name what the dead are raised: "the dead will be raised imperishable" (1 Corinthians 15:52). The same words name love, "love incorruptible" (Ephesians 6:24), the seed of new birth (1 Peter 1:23), an inheritance (1:4), "the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit" (3:4), the wreath that self-control runs for (1 Corinthians 9:25), and God himself, "immortal, invisible" (1 Timothy 1:17). (Chapter 2, *Changed*; 13.1, *Immortal*.)
- **Writhing.** The Hebrew *ḥûl*, "to twist, writhe", is a woman in labour ("Writhe and groan, O daughter of Zion, like a woman in labor", Micah 4:10), the earth before God ("tremble before him, all the earth!", Psalm 96:9), and the heart in anguish (Psalm 55:4). It is also the daughters of Shiloh who come out "to dance in the dances" (Judges 21:21), "a whirling tempest" (Jeremiah 23:19), and patient waiting: "Be still before the Lord and wait patiently for him" (Psalm 37:7). Struck people can be without it: "You have struck them down, but they felt no anguish" (Jeremiah 5:3). One twisting is pain, trembling, birth, the dance and waiting (10.12, *Fear in the body*).

blocks.section: 4. One word, opposite values > What changes the character
blocks.text:
### What changes the character

A word, or an activity, does not carry its value inside itself. The same act changes character with its circumstances. When I set the cases side by side, the verses themselves point to what makes the difference. I give these as what I have found so far, not as a fixed list.

- **Which way it faces.** For someone or against them. "Discretion will watch over you" (Proverbs 2:11). "All their thoughts are against me for evil" (Psalm 56:5). But "against" alone does not decide it. God's plan against a nation is open to its turning: "if that nation … turns from its evil, I will relent" (Jeremiah 18:8). What decides is what the act is *for*.
- **The company it keeps.** Discretion keeps company with knowledge and prudence (Proverbs 1:4; 8:12), the evil device with arrogance and pride (Psalm 10:2, 4) and a quick temper (Proverbs 14:17). Plans are established by counsel (Proverbs 20:18) and by being committed to the Lord (16:3). Whispering together makes a plot (Psalm 41:7).
- **The state of the heart it rises from.** The same tender heart is cowardice in one place and repentance in another (Deuteronomy 20:8; 2 Kings 22:19, above). Paul names the order of cause: people are "darkened in their understanding … due to their hardness of heart" (Ephesians 4:18).
- **Ease or distress.** "In the thought of one who is at ease there is contempt for misfortune" (Job 12:5). Under suffering, God's reckoning is felt as enmity: "Why do you hide your face and count me as your enemy?" (Job 13:24). This is still a small set of verses, and I hold it loosely.
- **Distress turns people both ways.** In distress Manasseh "humbled himself greatly" (2 Chronicles 33:12), and Ahaz "became yet more faithless" (28:22). The texts set the cases side by side without saying why. Under siege, "The hands of compassionate women have boiled their own children" (Lamentations 4:10; 10.10). Ease cuts both ways too: "I am exceedingly angry with the nations that are at ease" (Zechariah 1:15).
- **What it is joined with.** Anger joined with grief heals (Mark 3:5). Joined with jealousy, it "will accept no compensation" (Proverbs 6:34–35).
- **How long it lasts.** For anger, time is part of what it is. It is to end before sunset (Ephesians 4:26). It turns away as a brother forgets (Genesis 27:45). God's is "but for a moment" (Psalm 30:5). Edom "kept his wrath forever" (Amos 1:11).
- **Whether it is seen truly.** Anger kindled by a lie still acts (Genesis 39:19). The heavy hand of God, felt from fear, is misread (Matthew 25:24–25).
- **The answer it meets.** "A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger" (Proverbs 15:1). A question, or a new way of seeing, does more than a rebuke (Genesis 4:6; 45:8; Luke 15:32).
- **What the one who brings it brings first.** The same offering is refused and then delighted in, and what comes between is a broken heart (Psalm 51:16–19, §4 above). The same weakness is pleaded against and then pleases, and what comes between is God's answer (2 Corinthians 12:8–10).
- **Haste or a pause.** "Everyone who is hasty comes only to poverty" (Proverbs 21:5). "Be not quick in your spirit to become angry" (Ecclesiastes 7:9). "The heart of the righteous ponders how to answer" (Proverbs 15:28).
- **Where it happens.** The bed holds plotting and prayer (Psalm 36:4; 63:6). But one place does change what thinking can see: "until I went into the sanctuary of God; then I discerned their end" (Psalm 73:17).
- **What it is turned toward.** At the sea "they feared greatly" as Egypt marched (Exodus 14:10). After the crossing, "the people feared the Lord, and they believed in the Lord" (14:31). The sailors "were afraid" in the storm, and when the sea was calm "the men feared the Lord exceedingly" (Jonah 1:5, 16). Fear of man is set against him: "who are you that you are afraid of man who dies … and have forgotten the Lord, your Maker" (Isaiah 51:12–13). The same holds for refusing and choosing. Refusing the evil is right and refusing the gentle waters is wrong (Isaiah 7:15; 8:6). The act is the same, and what it is aimed at decides. The one knowing is turned to right and wrong, to taste and to judgement (Isaiah 7:15; 2 Samuel 19:35; Job 34:4). The one verb for choosing is turned to whatever is set before a person (10.7). The soul's desire is allowed for meat in the towns and for the Levite's coming to the chosen place (Deuteronomy 12:21; 18:6), and the soul's delight in abominations goes with a wrong choice (Isaiah 66:3).
- **Whether the heart is in it.** Fear of God can be "a commandment taught by men" while "their hearts are far from me" (Isaiah 29:13). God promises the other: "I will put the fear of me in their hearts, that they may not turn from me" (Jeremiah 32:40).
- **Who chooses.** When God chooses a person, the inner life is what the choosing is for: "that you may know and believe me and understand" (Isaiah 43:10). When people choose a person, the inner life is what they choose by (Acts 6:3, 5). The same verb is used of both (10.7).
- **Whose eyes, and whose delight.** "Evil in your eyes" is where turning from the Lord could begin (Joshua 24:15), and "good to you" is a choice the king honours (2 Samuel 19:38). In Joshua the choice is between the Lord and other gods. With Barzillai it is where an old man who served will live. Delight is the soul's own in Isaiah 66:3 and the Lord's in 65:12 and 56:4. The word is the same; whose it is decides (10.7). When God chooses, the people around often hold another measure: "everyone doing whatever is right in his own eyes" (Deuteronomy 12:8), "before the eyes of his servants' female servants" (2 Samuel 6:20), "in their sight" (Jeremiah 33:24), "rejected by men but in the sight of God chosen" (1 Peter 2:4). The words "what seems good to you" carry different acts: loyalty in Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 19:27), fear in the rulers before Jehu (2 Kings 10:5), a cover in the men of Jabesh (1 Samuel 11:10), a people handed over in a king's word (Esther 3:11), and yielding to God in Eli and David (1 Samuel 3:18; 2 Samuel 15:26). The words are the same; the setting decides (10.7, 10.10, 10.11).
- **Who speaks it, and to what end.** The same words of comfort, "do not fear", come from God, from a friend, and from one who means harm (§4 above; 10.5; 10.10).
- **Whose mouth it is in.** That God delights in a man is thanks from the one rescued and a taunt from those who watch him suffer (Psalm 18:19; 22:8, §4 above).
- **Who hears it.** The same scroll was read to the officials and to the king. The officials "turned one to another in fear" (Jeremiah 36:16). The king and his servants "who heard all these words" were not afraid (36:24).
- **Whether it pulls the person to many things or to one.** Martha was "anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is necessary" (Luke 10:41–42). Paul wants "undivided devotion to the Lord" (1 Corinthians 7:35). The double-minded man is "unstable in all his ways" (James 1:8).
- **Who acts on whom.** God hiding a person is safety, and God hiding his face is dismay (Psalm 27:5, 9). Losing heart is always done by another (10.1).
- **Whether it is brought before God.** "When I am afraid, I put my trust in you" (Psalm 56:3). Many cares, met by his consolations (Psalm 94:19). Anxiety made known to God, and his peace guarding the heart (Philippians 4:6–7). Thoughts offered to be searched (Psalm 139:23). Thoughts taken "captive to obey Christ" (2 Corinthians 10:5).
- **What comes back.** What is devised returns on the deviser (Esther 9:25; Micah 2:1–3), and the diligent plan returns as abundance (Proverbs 21:5).
- **What it is set against.** "To live" is said of a span of years, of escaping hunger or the sword, of recovering from illness, of the dead given life again, and of the heart and spirit revived (Chapter 2). The verses pair it with what it escapes: "that we may live and not die" (Genesis 42:2); "so turn, and live" (Ezekiel 18:32); "why will you die, O house of Israel?" (33:11). The breath God gives can come back out of a person as lies: "a false witness breathes out lies" (Proverbs 14:5).
- **What brings it about, and who acts.** "Die" is said of the body's end, of a sentence passed by people, of a judgment from God, of the end of a way taken, and of something that happens inside a living person: "sin came alive and I died" (Romans 7:9); "Whoever does not love abides in death" (1 John 3:14). It is said of a death undergone on purpose: "How can we who died to sin still live in it?" (Romans 6:2). It is said of a death that belongs to the Lord: "if we die, we die to the Lord" (Romans 14:8). The verses name what brings death: sin (Romans 5:12), "vexation" and "jealousy" (Job 5:2), "the desire of the sluggard" (Proverbs 21:25), and God, who says "I kill and I make alive" (Deuteronomy 32:39). "Put to death" is said both of executing a person and of "what is earthly in you" (Colossians 3:5). "Dead dog" is said of oneself in lowliness (2 Samuel 9:8) and of another in contempt (2 Samuel 16:9). Chapter 2 gives the account.
- **Who swears it, and what for.** "As the Lord lives" is said in loyalty (2 Kings 2:2), in anger (2 Samuel 12:5), in a rash vow the people overturn (1 Samuel 14:39, 45), and on the way to greed (2 Kings 5:20). The words stay the same. The verses give the measure: "in truth, in justice, and in righteousness" (Jeremiah 4:2).
- **What it is joined to.** "Long" is days promised with honouring parents (Exodus 20:12), the wicked who "prolongs his life in his evildoing" (Ecclesiastes 7:15), and, with anger, patience: "Good sense makes one slow to anger" (Proverbs 19:11). "Life" is something loathed (Job 10:1), and in Elihu's words it is itself what loathes: "his life loathes bread" (Job 33:20).
- **Who rouses, and toward what.** The same word for rousing is used when God rouses himself (Zechariah 2:13) and when he is begged to (Psalm 44:23). It is used when God stirs a spirit to build (Ezra 1:5) or to destroy (Jeremiah 51:1, 11), and when hatred stirs up strife (Proverbs 10:12). Love is not to be stirred "until it pleases" (Song of Songs 2:7). Its power shows when it is withheld: God "did not stir up all his wrath" (Psalm 78:38). And some things cannot be roused at all: the dead man "till the heavens are no more" (Job 14:12), and the idol with "no breath at all in it" (Habakkuk 2:19). Haggai gives the order on the building side: obedience, the fear of the Lord, "I am with you", then the stirring, then the work (Haggai 1:12–14; 13.1, *Stirring*).
- **Before whom it is said, and what it rests on.** "Eat, drink, be merry" is folly in the rich man who says it to his own soul over goods laid up (Luke 12:19–20), and it is commended by the Preacher as "his lot" in "the few days of his life that God has given him" (Ecclesiastes 5:18; 8:15). The words are nearly the same (10.6).
- **Whose jealousy, and for whom.** Jealousy is God's for his people against those who scorned them (Ezekiel 36:5), and over his people's own spirit, met with grace (James 4:5–6). It is Elijah's for God (1 Kings 19:10), Joshua's for Moses, refused by Moses (Numbers 11:29), a husband's that will take no compensation (Proverbs 6:34–35), and envy of the wicked that embitters the soul (Psalm 73:3, 21). The word stays the same. What differs is whose it is, whom it is for, and whether it wants God's gift kept narrow (10.6; 13.1). Zeal can be sincere, aimed at God and still wrong for lack of knowledge (Romans 10:2; Philippians 3:6). It consumes the one who has it (Psalm 69:9). It can be put on show (2 Kings 10:16), or set an oath aside (2 Samuel 21:2). Against a person it spoils what it cannot take (Genesis 26:14–15) and claims equality (Numbers 16:3; Psalm 106:16). A husband's jealousy, which may be wrong, is put before God (Numbers 5:14, 30).
- **What it is aimed at.** Job rouses himself against the godless and is upright in it (Job 17:8). He disowns rousing himself at an enemy's ruin (31:29). It is the same act of rousing oneself (10.10).
- **When the cost appears.** The nearer redeemer was willing for the land and unwilling when Ruth came with it (Ruth 4:4–6). The will turned when his own inheritance was touched (10.7).
- **Whose will, and whether it can carry itself out.** The same verb, "want", is a will that wants the good and cannot do it (Romans 7:19), a will asked out by Jesus, "What do you want me to do for you?" (Mark 10:51), a will made absolute (Daniel 11:3), a will that gives way to a crowd (Luke 23:25), and a will taken up and turned, "If anyone would be first" (Mark 9:35). Willing God's will comes before knowing it (John 7:17) (10.7).
- **Whom the need is spoken to.** The same thirst accuses Moses at Rephidim (Exodus 17:3) and asks God at Lehi (Judges 15:18) (10.6).

- **Whose desire, and whether rule stands beside it.** *tĕšûqāh*: "Your desire shall be for your husband, and he shall rule over you" (Genesis 3:16); sin's "desire is for you, and you must rule over it" (4:7); "I am my beloved's, and his desire is for me" (Song of Songs 7:10) (10.6).
- **What the panting reaches for.** The verb for panting or longing is used of a worn slave who "longs for the shadow" (Job 7:2), of the thirsty who "pant after his wealth" (Job 5:5), of the sun that "hastens" (Ecclesiastes 1:5), of the wild donkey "sniffing the wind" (Jeremiah 2:24), of the psalmist who pants for the commandments (Psalm 119:131), and of God, who will "gasp and pant" like a woman in labour (Isaiah 42:14). What it reaches for decides its character (10.6; 13.1; 13.4).

- **Who lowers whom, and before whom.** A king humbling himself before God is answered (2 Chronicles 12:7). A people humbled by God may turn or harden (2 Chronicles 33:12; 28:22). A nation humbled by an enemy is only "subdued" (Judges 3:30). The noun for humility toward one another also names a self-made severity that puffs a person up (Colossians 2:18, 23), and submission is right before God and wrong to those who would enslave the gospel (Galatians 2:5) (10.14).
- **The story around it.** A single verse rarely settles which face a word wears. Jeremiah 18:8–18 does, and so does Genesis 50:20.

I find this freeing. Scripture does not hand me a list of good feelings and bad feelings, or good thoughts and bad thoughts. Each new part of the inner life I read adds to this list, and I expect it to grow.

blocks.section: 8. God has a heart and a soul
blocks.text:
## 8. God has a heart and a soul

The inner words are not only for humans. Scripture gives God a heart and a soul, and lets them act.

- "It grieved him to his heart" (Genesis 6:6).
- "My heart recoils within me; my compassion grows warm and tender" (Hosea 11:8).
- "I will rejoice in doing them good … with all my heart and all my soul" (Jeremiah 32:41).
- "My soul delights" in his chosen servant (Isaiah 42:1). "My soul hates" empty feasts held with bloodied hands (Isaiah 1:14–15).
- He swears "by himself" (Amos 6:8), literally by his soul.
- He "does not afflict from his heart" (Lamentations 3:33).
- He holds back his anger for reasons of his own: "I will not execute my burning anger … for I am God and not a man" (Hosea 11:9).
- And the one place where his inner self turns away from a people is not hardness: "Though Moses and Samuel stood before me, yet my heart would not turn toward this people" (Jeremiah 15:1).

Leviticus 26 shows God's soul and the people's soul in a movement back and forth. God promises: "my soul shall not abhor you" (26:11). The people's "soul abhors my rules" (26:15). God answers in kind: "my soul will abhor you" (26:30). Then, at the end, God breaks the exchange: "Yet for all that … I will not spurn them, neither will I abhor them so as to destroy them utterly and break my covenant with them" (26:44). The same verb passes between two souls, and God refuses to return it a final time.

God also thinks and plans. "The counsel of the Lord stands forever, the plans of his heart to all generations" (Psalm 33:11). "My thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways" (Isaiah 55:8). Where human plans and his cross, his stand: "As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good" (Genesis 50:20). Even a cold calculation can be taken up into his purpose. Caiaphas reckoned "that it is better for you that one man should die for the people" (John 11:50). John adds: "He did not say this of his own accord, but being high priest that year he prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation" (11:51).

And God speaks in his heart. After the flood, "the Lord said in his heart, 'I will never again curse the ground because of man, for the intention of man's heart is evil from his youth'" (Genesis 8:21). Before the flood he saw "that every intention of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually" (6:5), and "the Lord regretted that he had made man on the earth, and it grieved him to his heart" (6:6). Now he names it again, and it is the reason he gives for holding back.

God names his heart with a place. "I have consecrated this house that you have built, by putting my name there forever. My eyes and my heart will be there for all time" (1 Kings 9:3; 13.1, *Choosing*).

## Choosing

The verses on a person's choosing keep speaking of God. They speak of him in his own right, not only as the one a person chooses.

**He chooses.** The verb used of a person's choosing is also used of his:
- **a place:** "the place that the Lord your God will choose out of all your tribes to put his name and make his habitation there" (Deuteronomy 12:5)
- **people, for a purpose:** "God made a choice among you, that by my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the gospel and believe" (Acts 15:7)
- **an answer to people's choosing:** "I also will choose harsh treatment for them and bring their fears upon them, because when I called, no one answered, when I spoke, they did not listen" (Isaiah 66:4). The verse gives the reason for his choice.

**He chooses before anything is in the one chosen.** "he chose us in him before the foundation of the world" (Ephesians 1:4). He chooses those whom others pass over: "has not God chosen those who are poor in the world to be rich in faith" (James 2:5). He chooses witnesses who are "blind, yet have eyes" (Isaiah 43:8), "that you may know and believe me and understand that I am he" (43:10). His choosing is spoken of with his own love and pleasure:
- "In love he predestined us for adoption to himself as sons through Jesus Christ, according to the purpose of his will" (Ephesians 1:4–5)
- "among my father's sons he took pleasure in me to make me king over all Israel" (1 Chronicles 28:4)
- "who chose me above your father and above all his house" (2 Samuel 6:21)
- Not for what they were: *"It was not because you were more in number than any other people that the Lord set his love on you and chose you, for you were the fewest of all peoples, but it is because the Lord loves you"* (Deuteronomy 7:7–8). *"Yet the Lord set his heart in love on your fathers and chose their offspring after them … Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart"* (10:15–16). His set heart is answered by a call on theirs.

**He chooses his servant with delight, and puts his Spirit on him.** Matthew applies Isaiah's words to Jesus: "Behold, my servant whom I have chosen, my beloved with whom my soul is well pleased. I will put my Spirit upon him, and he will proclaim justice to the Gentiles" (Matthew 12:18, quoting Isaiah 42:1). The one verse holds the one who chooses, whose soul is well pleased; the servant he has chosen, whom Matthew sees fulfilled in Jesus; and his Spirit, put upon him. Matthew gives the setting. The Pharisees "conspired against him, how to destroy him" (Matthew 12:14). Jesus, "aware of this, withdrew", healed them all, and "ordered them not to make him known" (12:15–16). "This was to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet Isaiah" (12:17), and the words go on: "He will not quarrel or cry aloud … a bruised reed he will not break, and a smoldering wick he will not quench, until he brings justice to victory" (12:19–20).

**He has eyes and delight, and they are the measure of a choice.** The same verse goes on: "but they did what was evil in my eyes and chose that in which I did not delight" (Isaiah 66:4). Its opposite is those "who choose the things that please me" (56:4).

**He acts first.** At Shechem he speaks of what he has done before anyone chooses: "I took your father Abraham from beyond the River" (Joshua 24:3); "I gave you a land on which you had not labored" (24:13). In Isaiah he offers himself to people who did not look for him:
- "I was ready to be sought by those who did not ask for me" (Isaiah 65:1)
- "I said, 'Here I am, here I am,' to a nation that was not called by my name" (65:1)
- "I spread out my hands all the day to a rebellious people" (65:2)

**He is good, upright and holy.** His instructing comes from his goodness: "Good and upright is the Lord; therefore he instructs sinners in the way" (Psalm 25:8). "The friendship of the Lord is for those who fear him" (25:14). Joshua tells the people who have just chosen him what he is: "he is a holy God. He is a jealous God" (Joshua 24:19).

His goodness is named toward those who wait: *"The Lord is good to those who wait for him, to the soul who seeks him"* (Lamentations 3:25). It is said straight after the soul's own word, *"'The Lord is my portion,' says my soul, 'therefore I will hope in him'"* (3:24). And it is asked for the upright under pressure: *"Do good, O Lord, to those who are good, and to those who are upright in their hearts!"* (Psalm 125:4; 10.8).

**He knows the heart, and gives.**
- "God, who knows the heart, bore witness to them, by giving them the Holy Spirit just as he did to us" (Acts 15:8).
- "thanks be to God, who put into the heart of Titus the same earnest care I have for you" (2 Corinthians 8:16).
- The church's decision is spoken as one with the Spirit's: "it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us" (Acts 15:28).

**He searches hearts, and acts on them.** "the Lord searches all hearts and understands every plan and thought" (1 Chronicles 28:9). He acts on the hearts of people who are not his chosen, and the verses give his purpose:
- of those who "refused to love the truth": "Therefore God sends them a strong delusion, so that they may believe what is false" (2 Thessalonians 2:10–11)
- of the kings who give their power to the beast: "for God has put it into their hearts to carry out his purpose by being of one mind" (Revelation 17:17)
- of the rest of Israel, who sought and did not obtain: "God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that would not see and ears that would not hear" (Romans 11:8). Paul at once refuses to make it the end: "did they stumble in order that they might fall? By no means!" (11:11). The remnant is "chosen by grace" (11:5).
- of those who do not believe: "They stumble because they disobey the word, as they were destined to do" (1 Peter 2:8). The verse gives the disobedience as the cause, and does not explain the rest.

Solomon prays to him as the one who alone knows hearts: "for you, you only, know the hearts of all the children of mankind" (1 Kings 8:39). He also asks him to do the turning: "that he may incline our hearts to him" (8:58).

**He answers those who set themselves against his choosing.** The verses show others resenting the one he chose, and they show him answering.
- **He counts it as against himself, and makes his choice plain.** "What is Aaron that you grumble against him?" (Numbers 16:11). "And the staff of the man whom I choose shall sprout. Thus I will make to cease from me the grumblings of the people of Israel, which they grumble against you" (17:5). The staff is kept "that you may make an end of their grumblings against me, lest they die" (17:10).
- **He turns contempt round by his faithfulness.** To the one "deeply despised, abhorred by the nation": "Kings shall see and arise; princes, and they shall prostrate themselves; because of the Lord, who is faithful, the Holy One of Israel, who has chosen you" (Isaiah 49:7).
- **He sets his choosing beside the fixed order of creation.** When people say "The Lord has rejected the two clans that he chose" (Jeremiah 33:24), he answers: "If I have not established my covenant with day and night and the fixed order of heaven and earth, then I will reject the offspring of Jacob and David my servant … For I will restore their fortunes and will have mercy on them" (33:25–26).
- **He is hated first.** "If the world hates you, know that it has hated me before it hated you" (John 15:18). "I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you" (15:19).

**He calls those who do not know him, for the sake of his chosen.** "For the sake of my servant Jacob, and Israel my chosen, I call you by your name, I name you, though you do not know me. … I equip you, though you do not know me, that people may know, from the rising of the sun and from the west, that there is none besides me" (Isaiah 45:4–6).

**He blesses at the place he chose, so that his people rejoice.** "because the Lord your God will bless you in all your produce and in all the work of your hands, so that you will be altogether joyful" (Deuteronomy 16:15). Those who return to him he gathers there: "I will gather them and bring them to the place that I have chosen, to make my name dwell there" (Nehemiah 1:9).

**His eyes and his heart are at the place he chose.** At night he says to Solomon: "I have heard your prayer and have chosen this place for myself as a house of sacrifice" (2 Chronicles 7:12). "Now my eyes will be open and my ears attentive to the prayer that is made in this place. For now I have chosen and consecrated this house that my name may be there forever. My eyes and my heart will be there for all time" (7:15–16). His choosing of the place goes with his hearing of the prayer made there. In the same speech he says what he will do if he is forsaken: "this house that I have consecrated for my name, I will cast out of my sight" (7:20).

**What he chooses is turned toward others.** "Is not this the fast that I choose: to loose the bonds of wickedness, to undo the straps of the yoke, to let the oppressed go free, and to break every yoke?" (Isaiah 58:6). The self-humbling offered beside oppression is not what he chooses (58:3–5).

**His wrath is turned away when his chosen one stands before him.** "Therefore he said he would destroy them—had not Moses, his chosen one, stood in the breach before him, to turn away his wrath from destroying them" (Psalm 106:23). His anger is taken up in 10.13.

**He remembers, and he does not remember.** "He remembers his covenant forever, the word that he commanded, for a thousand generations" (Psalm 105:8). "For he remembered his holy promise, and Abraham, his servant" (105:42). When his chosen people had forgotten him, "For their sake he remembered his covenant, and relented according to the abundance of his steadfast love" (106:45). Of their sins he says the opposite: "I, I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins" (Isaiah 43:25). To the one he has chosen: "you will not be forgotten by me" (44:21).

**He reasons, answers and judges.**
- He invites a people to reason with him: "Come now, let us reason together, says the Lord" (Isaiah 1:18).
- He answers a person's verdict on himself. The eunuch said "Behold, I am a dry tree" (56:3), and the Lord says "I will give them an everlasting name that shall not be cut off" (56:5).
- He gives the last word on those who weighed Job's choices: "you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has" (Job 42:7).

"he went up on the mountain and called to him those whom he desired, and they came to him. And he appointed twelve … so that they might be with him" (Mark 3:13–14). The calling follows his desire, and the purpose is that they be with him.

## Delight

The words for a person's delight and desire are used of God too. The verses say what he delights in and whom he is pleased with, and they show him doing what pleases him.

**What he delights in.**
- *"Those of crooked heart are an abomination to the Lord, but those of blameless ways are his delight"* (Proverbs 11:20).
- David, as he gives freely: *"I know, my God, that you test the heart and have pleasure in uprightness"* (1 Chronicles 29:17).
- A purpose in a heart pleases him even when he does not let it be carried out: *"Whereas it was in your heart to build a house for my name, you did well that it was in your heart. Nevertheless, you shall not build the house"* (1 Kings 8:18–19; 2 Chronicles 6:8–9).
- He *"found in David the son of Jesse a man after my heart, who will do all my will"* (Acts 13:22).
- To Jehu: *"Because you have done well in carrying out what is right in my eyes, and have done to the house of Ahab according to all that was in my heart, your sons of the fourth generation shall sit on the throne of Israel"* (2 Kings 10:30). The next verse turns to Jehu's own heart: *"But Jehu was not careful to walk in the law of the Lord, the God of Israel, with all his heart"* (10:31).
- A people valued: *"Because you are precious in my eyes, and honored, and I love you, I give men in return for you, peoples in exchange for your life"* (Isaiah 43:4). Hezekiah, delivered, says, *"in love you have delivered my life from the pit of destruction, for you have cast all my sins behind your back"* (Isaiah 38:17).
- A son held dear while spoken against. Ephraim grieves: *"after I had turned away, I relented, and after I was instructed, I struck my thigh; I was ashamed, and I was confounded, because I bore the disgrace of my youth"* (Jeremiah 31:19). God answers: *"Is Ephraim my dear son? Is he my darling child? For as often as I speak against him, I do remember him still. Therefore my heart yearns for him; I will surely have mercy on him, declares the Lord"* (31:20). Speaking against him and remembering him go on together, and the yearning is given as the reason for mercy (10.3, 10.13).
- A price paid: *"you were ransomed from the futile ways inherited from your forefathers, not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot"* (1 Peter 1:18–19). Isaiah speaks of men given in exchange for a people precious in his eyes (above). Peter names the price as the blood of Christ, and what it ransoms from as ways inherited.
- A fast he does not accept: *"Will you call this a fast, and a day acceptable to the Lord?"* (Isaiah 58:5). What he chooses instead is in *Choosing* (58:6).
- What his anger gives way to: *"He does not retain his anger forever, because he delights in steadfast love"* (Micah 7:18). The reason the anger ends is what he delights in. Isaiah puts wrath and favour in one sentence: *"for in my wrath I struck you, but in my favor I have had mercy on you"* (Isaiah 60:10), as *"his favor is for a lifetime"* (Psalm 30:5; 10.13).

**Not strength, and truth within.** "let not the mighty man boast in his might … but let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me, that I am the Lord who practices steadfast love, justice, and righteousness in the earth. For in these things I delight, declares the Lord" (Jeremiah 9:23–24). "His delight is not in the strength of the horse, nor his pleasure in the legs of a man, but the Lord takes pleasure in those who fear him, in those who hope in his steadfast love" (Psalm 147:10–11). Strength is turned down twice, once as a boast and once as a delight. And his delight looks inward: "Behold, you delight in truth in the inward being, and you teach me wisdom in the secret heart" (Psalm 51:6), said by one who has just said "in sin did my mother conceive me" (51:5). He delights in truth where it is hidden, and he teaches there.

**What he desires.** The verses also give his desire for a place, a people and a time:
- A place: *"For the Lord has chosen Zion; he has desired it for his dwelling place: 'This is my resting place forever; here I will dwell, for I have desired it'"* (Psalm 132:13–14). The other mountains are pictured looking on with envy: *"Why do you look with hatred, O many-peaked mountain, at the mount that God desired for his abode?"* (Psalm 68:16).
- His people, as his hope for them: *"I said, How I would set you among my sons, and give you a pleasant land, a heritage most beautiful of all nations. And I thought you would call me, My Father, and would not turn from following me. Surely, as a treacherous wife leaves her husband, so have you been treacherous to me"* (Jeremiah 3:19–20). His hope is spoken, and then its disappointment.
- His grief over what is his: *"they have made my pleasant portion a desolate wilderness. They have made it a desolation; desolate, it mourns to me. The whole land is made desolate, but no man lays it to heart"* (Jeremiah 12:10–11).
- His keeping of it: *"A pleasant vineyard, sing of it! I, the Lord, am its keeper; every moment I water it … I have no wrath"* (Isaiah 27:2–4).
- His word on the one who clings to him: *"Because he holds fast to me in love, I will deliver him; I will protect him, because he knows my name"* (Psalm 91:14).
- His guarding of what is left behind for worship: *"no one shall covet your land, when you go up to appear before the Lord your God three times in the year"* (Exodus 34:24).
- What comes to his house: *"the treasures of all nations shall come in, and I will fill this house with glory … The silver is mine, and the gold is mine"* (Haggai 2:7–8).
- His timing: *"When I please, I will discipline them"* (Hosea 10:10).
- The Son's desire: *"I have earnestly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer"* (Luke 22:15).
- Job hopes for God's longing: *"You would call, and I would answer you; you would long for the work of your hands"* (Job 14:15).

**Whom he is pleased with.** At Jesus' baptism *"the Holy Spirit descended on him in bodily form, like a dove; and a voice came from heaven, 'You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased'"* (Luke 3:22). In one verse the voice from heaven speaks, the Son is named, and the Spirit comes down. Matthew applies Isaiah's *"my beloved with whom my soul is well pleased"* to Jesus (Matthew 12:18; *Choosing*). Paul says that God *"was pleased to reveal his Son to me"* (Galatians 1:16). And of one who turns back: *"my righteous one shall live by faith, and if he shrinks back, my soul has no pleasure in him"* (Hebrews 10:38). Wisdom says that favour is found by finding her: *"For whoever finds me finds life and obtains favor from the Lord, but he who fails to find me injures himself; all who hate me love death"* (Proverbs 8:35–36). The finding is by daily waiting, *"watching daily at my gates, waiting beside my doors"* (8:34). At the end love and hate are turned over: to hate wisdom is to love death, a love the person does not know he has.

**The voice again, on the mountain.** Peter was saying, "Lord, it is good that we are here. If you wish, I will make three tents here", when "a voice from the cloud said, 'This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased; listen to him'" (Matthew 17:4–5). The words of the baptism come back with a command added. "When the disciples heard this, they fell on their faces and were terrified. But Jesus came and touched them, saying, 'Rise, and have no fear'" (17:6–7). The Father's pleasure, spoken to them, frightens them, and the Son lifts them. Peter recalls it years later as the ground of what he preaches: "we did not follow cleverly devised myths … we ourselves heard this very voice borne from heaven, for we were with him on the holy mountain" (2 Peter 1:16–18), and the word is to be heeded "until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts" (1:19).

**His good pleasure gives.** "Fear not, little flock, for it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom" (Luke 12:32), after "your Father knows that you need them" (12:30; 10.12). What pleases him is to give. "For since, in the wisdom of God, the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God through the folly of what we preach to save those who believe" (1 Corinthians 1:21). His pleasure chooses the way the world calls folly. "For in him all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell, and through him to reconcile to himself all things" (Colossians 1:19–20), and the next words are "And you, who once were alienated and hostile in mind, doing evil deeds" (1:21). His pleasure reaches those who were hostile to him.

**Whom he delights in, and why.** "He brought me out into a broad place; he rescued me, because he delighted in me" (2 Samuel 22:20; Psalm 18:19). His delight is the reason given for the rescue. It is given as a name: "you shall be called My Delight Is in Her, and your land Married; for the Lord delights in you" (Isaiah 62:4), in place of Forsaken and Desolate, "as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so shall your God rejoice over you" (62:5). It holds a man who falls: "The steps of a man are established by the Lord, when he delights in his way; though he fall, he shall not be cast headlong, for the Lord upholds his hand" (Psalm 37:23–24). The fall is not denied. And it can be seen by a stranger. The queen of Sheba, who "did not believe the reports until I came and my own eyes had seen it" (1 Kings 10:7), says, "Blessed be the Lord your God, who has delighted in you and set you on the throne of Israel! Because the Lord loved Israel forever, he has made you king, that you may execute justice and righteousness" (1 Kings 10:9; 2 Chronicles 9:8). She reads his delight from what she saw, and names what it is for.

**His delight in people's mouths.** Joshua and Caleb: "If the Lord delights in us, he will bring us into this land and give it to us" (Numbers 14:8), with "do not fear the people of the land" (14:9); the congregation "said to stone them with stones" (14:10). A man whose "close friend in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me" (Psalm 41:9) says, "By this I know that you delight in me: my enemy will not shout in triumph over me" (41:11). The mockers: "He trusts in the Lord; let him deliver him; let him rescue him, for he delights in him!" (Psalm 22:8). The words that are thanks in Psalm 18:19 are a taunt here, and the sufferer answers God, not them: "Yet you are he who took me from the womb" (22:9). David will not presume it: "But if he says, 'I have no pleasure in you,' behold, here I am, let him do to me what seems good to him" (2 Samuel 15:26). What each person does with it is placed with the act: not fearing (10.9), yielding (10.7), mockery (10.5) and betrayal (10.10).

**His delight claimed for evildoers.** People can put God's delight on the wrong side. "You have wearied the Lord with your words. But you say, 'How have we wearied him?' By saying, 'Everyone who does evil is good in the sight of the Lord, and he delights in them.' Or by asking, 'Where is the God of justice?'" (Malachi 2:17). His answer is that the one they ask for comes, and comes to refine: "He will sit as a refiner and purifier of silver, and he will purify the sons of Levi and refine them like gold and silver, and they will bring offerings in righteousness to the Lord" (3:3). The delight they put on his lips is answered by refining, and its end is offerings in righteousness. The people's side is in 10.7.

**What he has no pleasure in.** *"Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked, declares the Lord God, and not rather that he should turn from his way and live?"* (Ezekiel 18:23). It is said to people who accuse him: *"Yet you say, 'The way of the Lord is not just'"* (18:25). He ends, *"make yourselves a new heart and a new spirit! Why will you die, O house of Israel? For I have no pleasure in the death of anyone, declares the Lord God; so turn, and live"* (18:31–32). He says it again to people in despair, who ask, *"Surely our transgressions and our sins are upon us, and we rot away because of them. How then can we live?"* (33:10). This time it is on oath: *"As I live, declares the Lord God, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live"* (33:11). The same words answer accusing and despairing. I read that his pleasure is told to the inner state of the hearer.

The death of his own is not taken lightly either: *"Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints"* (Psalm 116:15). The word is not delight but "precious": weighty, costly. The psalmist had been in *"the snares of death"* (116:3) and was delivered (116:8). I read: not glad of it, but not careless of it. The same word was used between two men: *"my life was precious in your eyes this day"* (1 Samuel 26:21; Chapter 5).

Not pleased, though they shared it all: "and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual Rock that followed them, and the Rock was Christ. Nevertheless, with most of them God was not pleased, for they were overthrown in the wilderness" (1 Corinthians 10:3–5). The next verse says why the account is given: "that we might not desire evil as they did" (10:6; 10.6). Sharing in what he gave did not make them pleasing to him.

**Not the offering itself.** Five verses say he does not delight in sacrifice, and each sets something else in its place.
- "What to me is the multitude of your sacrifices? says the Lord; I have had enough of burnt offerings of rams and the fat of well-fed beasts; I do not delight in the blood of bulls, or of lambs, or of goats" (Isaiah 1:11). Two verses on: "I cannot endure iniquity and solemn assembly" (1:13).
- "In sacrifice and offering you have not delighted, but you have given me an open ear" (Psalm 40:6), and the answer: "I delight to do your will, O my God; your law is within my heart" (40:8).
- "For you will not delight in sacrifice, or I would give it; you will not be pleased with a burnt offering. The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise" (Psalm 51:16–17).
- "For I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice, the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings" (Hosea 6:6), after "Your love is like a morning cloud, like the dew that goes early away" (6:4). The "love" of 6:4 and the "steadfast love" of 6:6 are one Hebrew word, *ḥesed*. What he desires is the very thing their love lacks: that it last.
- Jesus sends his hearers to learn it: "Go and learn what this means: 'I desire mercy, and not sacrifice.' For I came not to call the righteous, but sinners" (Matthew 9:13); "And if you had known what this means, 'I desire mercy, and not sacrifice,' you would not have condemned the guiltless" (12:7).
- And then: "then will you delight in right sacrifices, in burnt offerings and whole burnt offerings" (Psalm 51:19). The offerings he did not delight in (51:16) he will delight in, after the broken heart.

The verses do not say he has no use for offerings; David says he would give them. Each names something inward that comes first: an ear opened, the law in the heart, a broken heart, a love that lasts. I read that the offering is weighed by what is inside the one who brings it.

**Not from those who put something else in the place of hearing.** Saul kept back the best of what was to be destroyed, "to sacrifice to the Lord your God in Gilgal" (1 Samuel 15:21). Samuel answered, "Has the Lord as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the Lord? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams" (15:22). To priests "who despise my name" (Malachi 1:6) and offer the blind and the lame: "Present that to your governor; will he accept you or show you favor?" (1:8). Then: "Oh that there were one among you who would shut the doors, that you might not kindle fire on my altar in vain! I have no pleasure in you, says the Lord of hosts, and I will not accept an offering from your hand" (1:10). He would rather the doors were shut. And of the vow made and not paid: "When you vow a vow to God, do not delay paying it, for he has no pleasure in fools. Pay what you vow" (Ecclesiastes 5:4; 10.5). I read the three together: in each, what he does not delight in is an offering or a word standing in the place of hearing, honour or doing.

Hebrews reads Psalm 40 as the words of Christ: "Sacrifices and offerings you have not desired, but a body have you prepared for me; in burnt offerings and sin offerings you have taken no pleasure. Then I said, 'Behold, I have come to do your will, O God'" (Hebrews 10:5–7). It draws the end: "And by that will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all" (10:10). What he had no pleasure in is set aside for a will done in a body.

**He does what pleases him.**
- *"The king's heart is a stream of water in the hand of the Lord; he turns it wherever he will"* (Proverbs 21:1). The word for "will" is the word for delight. The next verse: *"Every way of a man is right in his own eyes, but the Lord weighs the heart"* (21:2).
- Job: *"But he is unchangeable, and who can turn him back? What he desires, that he does"* (Job 23:13). Job does not take it as comfort: *"Therefore I am terrified at his presence"* (23:15).
- The sailors, before they throw Jonah into the sea: *"O Lord, let us not perish for this man's life, and lay not on us innocent blood, for you, O Lord, have done as it pleased you"* (Jonah 1:14). Afterwards *"the men feared the Lord exceedingly"* (1:16).
- Balaam: "When Balaam saw that it pleased the Lord to bless Israel, he did not go, as at other times, to look for omens" (Numbers 24:1). What pleased the Lord was to bless, and seeing it turned a man from his omens (10.7).
- Of his servant: *"Yet it was the will of the Lord to crush him; he has put him to grief; when his soul makes an offering for guilt, he shall see his offspring; he shall prolong his days; the will of the Lord shall prosper in his hand"* (Isaiah 53:10). Both times, "the will of the Lord" is the delight word. The verse does not explain it, and I leave it as it stands.
- Of Eli's sons: *"But they would not listen to the voice of their father, for it was the will of the Lord to put them to death"* (1 Samuel 2:25). "Will" is the delight word again. Their father had just said, *"if someone sins against the Lord, who can intercede for him?"*, and the next verse sets Samuel beside them, growing *"in favor with the Lord and also with man"* (2:26). Set beside *"I have no pleasure in the death of anyone"* (Ezekiel 18:32), the two verses seem to pull apart. I do not reconcile them. They stand as Isaiah 53:10 stands.

Three more verses say it. "Our God is in the heavens; he does all that he pleases" (Psalm 115:3), answering "Why should the nations say, 'Where is their God?'" (115:2), beside idols that "have mouths, but do not speak" (115:5). Psalm 135 says it of all creation: "Whatever the Lord pleases, he does, in heaven and on earth, in the seas and all deeps" (Psalm 135:6), after "our Lord is above all gods" (135:5). "The Lord was pleased, for his righteousness' sake, to magnify his law and make it glorious" (Isaiah 42:21). The pleasure has a reason, and it is set beside a servant who "sees many things, but does not observe them" (42:20). His word carries out what he purposes (*Purposing*). The same words are used of a king, "he does whatever he pleases" (Ecclesiastes 8:3), in 10.1.

**What makes an offering accepted.** In the law the one who brings is accepted through the offering: "he shall offer a male without blemish … that he may be accepted before the Lord. He shall lay his hand on the head of the burnt offering, and it shall be accepted for him to make atonement for him" (Leviticus 1:3–4); "you shall offer it so that you may be accepted" (19:5; 22:29; 23:11); "to be accepted it must be perfect; there shall be no blemish in it" (22:21). The high priest bears the guilt of the holy gifts "that they may be accepted before the Lord" (Exodus 28:38). In the prophets an offering is refused where the person has turned away: "they have not paid attention to my words; and as for my law, they have rejected it. What use to me is frankincense … Your burnt offerings are not acceptable" (Jeremiah 6:19–20). "You cover the Lord's altar with tears, with weeping and groaning because he no longer regards the offering or accepts it with favor from your hand … Because the Lord was witness between you and the wife of your youth, to whom you have been faithless" (Malachi 2:13–14). "The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination to the Lord, but the prayer of the upright is acceptable to him" (Proverbs 15:8). I read the acceptance as of the person, through the offering, and the refusal as falling where the person's word or covenant is broken.

**His favor.** "For you bless the righteous, O Lord; you cover him with favor as with a shield" (Psalm 5:12). "by your favor our horn is exalted" (89:17). "A false balance is an abomination to the Lord, but a just weight is his delight" (Proverbs 11:1). "the upright enjoy acceptance" (14:9). "He who finds a wife finds a good thing and obtains favor from the Lord" (18:22). After "you have done all this evil", Samuel says, "the Lord will not forsake his people, for his great name's sake, because it has pleased the Lord to make you a people for himself" (1 Samuel 12:20, 22). His favor has a time: "In a time of favor I have answered you" (Isaiah 49:8); "to proclaim the year of the Lord's favor … to comfort all who mourn" (61:2). And a prayer waits on it: "my prayer is to you, O Lord. At an acceptable time, O God, in the abundance of your steadfast love answer me" (Psalm 69:13).

**His good hand.** Ezra and Nehemiah name it as the reason things went as they did: "the king granted him all that he asked, for the hand of the Lord his God was on him" (Ezra 7:6); "he came to Jerusalem, for the good hand of his God was on him" (7:9); "by the good hand of our God on us, they brought us a man of discretion" (8:18); "the king granted me what I asked, for the good hand of my God was upon me" (Nehemiah 2:8). Ezra told the king whom it is for: "The hand of our God is for good on all who seek him, and the power of his wrath is against all who forsake him" (Ezra 8:22). What the person does on knowing it is in 10.7 (*Setting the heart*), 10.10 and 10.12 (*What changes it*).

**Delight at creation.** Wisdom speaks in the poem of Proverbs 8: "The Lord possessed me at the beginning of his work" (Proverbs 8:22), and "when he marked out the foundations of the earth, then I was beside him, like a master workman, and I was daily his delight, rejoicing before him always, rejoicing in his inhabited world and delighting in the children of man" (8:29–31). It is a figure, Wisdom speaking as a person. Delight runs from God to Wisdom, and from Wisdom to the world and to mankind, and the poem sets it at creation. I read the poem putting delight in people into the work of making the world.

His delight stands beside his choosing (*Choosing*) and his will (*Willing*). What a person delights in is in 10.1 (*Delight*).

## Majesty

The words that name human pride also name God's majesty, and the verses say what his is like.
- **It is his own.** "The Lord reigns; he is robed in majesty … Your throne is established from of old; you are from everlasting" (Psalm 93:1–2).
- **It is shown in what he does.** "I will sing to the Lord, for he has triumphed gloriously; the horse and his rider he has thrown into the sea" (Exodus 15:1). "In the greatness of your majesty you overthrow your adversaries" (15:7). The enemy's own rising is quoted in the same song: "I will pursue, I will overtake, I will divide the spoil, my desire shall have its fill of them" (15:9).
- **It turns toward help.** "There is none like God, O Jeshurun, who rides through the heavens to your help, through the skies in his majesty" (Deuteronomy 33:26). "Ascribe power to God, whose majesty is over Israel … he is the one who gives power and strength to his people" (Psalm 68:34–35).
- **It goes with what only he does.** God says to Job, "Adorn yourself with majesty and dignity … look on everyone who is proud and abase him … Then will I also acknowledge to you that your own right hand can save you" (Job 40:10–12, 14).
- **It is hidden from.** "Enter into the rock and hide in the dust from before the terror of the Lord, and from the splendor of his majesty" (Isaiah 2:10), in the day when "the Lord alone will be exalted" (2:11).
- **It is not seen by all.** "If favor is shown to the wicked, he does not learn righteousness … and does not see the majesty of the Lord" (Isaiah 26:10).
- **It is a name.** The Son "sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high" (Hebrews 1:3).

**Only he says it of himself.** "I am the Lord, and there is no other, besides me there is no God" (Isaiah 45:5); "I am God, and there is none like me" (Isaiah 46:9). The proud city says the same in its heart: "I am, and there is no one besides me" (Isaiah 47:8). I read that the words true of him are the words pride takes for itself (10.15).

**He gives height.** He gave Nebuchadnezzar "kingship and greatness and glory and majesty" (Daniel 5:18). He chose for his people "the pride of Jacob whom he loves" (Psalm 47:4). "Not from the east or from the west and not from the wilderness comes lifting up, but it is God who executes judgment, putting down one and lifting up another" (Psalm 75:6–7). Though he is high, "he regards the lowly, but the haughty he knows from afar" (Psalm 138:6).

**It is challenged, and not overturned.** "The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers take counsel together, against the Lord and against his Anointed … He who sits in the heavens laughs; the Lord holds them in derision" (Psalm 2:2–4). "But you, O Lord, laugh at them; you hold all the nations in derision" (Psalm 59:8). "Toward the scorners he is scornful, but to the humble he gives favor" (Proverbs 3:34). "God is not mocked" (Galatians 6:7). In these verses his laughter answers only those who rise against him. It is never aimed at the weak, as human mocking is (10.15).

**In the Son.** His majesty is received: "we were eyewitnesses of his majesty. For when he received honor and glory from God the Father" (2 Peter 1:16–17). His place rests on what he is: "that in everything he might be preeminent. For in him all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell" (Colossians 1:18–19). At the moment "all were astonished at the majesty of God", he said, "The Son of Man is about to be delivered into the hands of men" (Luke 9:43–44). Then he was mocked on that very standing: "Hail, King of the Jews!" (Matthew 27:29); "Prophesy! Who is it that struck you?" (Luke 22:64); "He saved others; he cannot save himself" (Mark 15:31). He "made no answer" (Luke 23:9), and he prayed, "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do" (Luke 23:34). I read that the majesty no one can overturn did not defend itself against mockery. Pride grasps a place that is not its own; he "did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped" (Philippians 2:6; *Lowering himself*, below).

## Immortal

Paul's praise names God as the one whose life has no end: "To the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, the only God, be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen" (1 Timothy 1:17). He is the one "who alone has immortality, who dwells in unapproachable light, whom no one has ever seen or can see" (6:16). The same word is what "this mortal body must put on" (1 Corinthians 15:53; Chapter 2, *Changed*).
- **He raises the dead.** Paul learned to rely "not on ourselves but on God who raises the dead" (2 Corinthians 1:9).
- **By his Spirit.** "If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in you" (Romans 8:11).
- **In the Son.** "I am the resurrection and the life" (John 11:25). "I died, and behold I am alive forevermore, and I have the keys of Death and Hades" (Revelation 1:18).
- **It is his pledge of judgment.** "He has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed; and of this he has given assurance to all by raising him from the dead" (Acts 17:31).
